stem: You send a bill of costs for £15,000.00 plus £3,000.00 VAT to Asif for work done for him on a recent probate matter.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: DR Asif's ledger account £15,000.00 - client section CR cash account £15,000.00 - client section DR Asif's ledger account £3,000.00 - client section CR HM Revenue & Customs ledger £3,000.00 - client section

DR Asif's ledger account £15,000.00 - office section CR cash account £15,000.00 - office section DR Asif's ledger account £3,000.00 - office section CR HM Revenue & Customs ledger £3,000.00 - office section
DR Asif's ledger account £18,000.00 - office section CR profit costs ledger £18,000.00 - office section

DR Asif's ledger account £15,000.00 - client section CR profit costs ledger £15,000.00 - client section DR Asif's ledger account £3,000.00 - client section CR HM Revenue & Customs ledger £3,000.00 - client section

DR Asif's ledger account £15,000.00 - office section CR profit costs ledger £15,000.00 - office section DR Asif's ledger account £3,000.00 - office section CR HM Revenue & Customs ledger £3,000.00 - office section

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. When a solicitor's office delivers a bill of costs to the client, this act is considered as a fee earned. The solicitor's office is merely informing Asif of his debt owed. Client money is not involved, as fees/profit costs are considered office money, because they belong to the solicitor. The accounting entries in Answer E accurately reflect the creation of a debit in Asif's client ledger account and the creation of a credit in the firm's profit costs ledger, as well as the recording of VAT charged on the bill of costs (output tax). A is wrong, because fees/profit costs are not client money and should therefore not be recorded in the client sections of ledgers. Further, the delivery of a bill of costs creates entries in the solicitor's profit costs ledger, not the cash ledger. Whilst the delivery of a bill of costs is considered income, no monies have been paid in as part of the act. B is wrong because the credit for profit costs is recorded in the cash account, not the profit costs ledger. See above. C is wrong because the profit costs and VAT are recorded as a single entry in the profit costs ledger. The VAT output tax needs to be recorded as a credit in the HM Revenue & Customs ledger, which accordingly requires a separate debit entry, which is in Asif's ledger account - office section D is wrong because the fees/profit costs should be recorded in the office section of the ledgers, not the client section. As above, fees/profit costs are not client money.

stem: Jim sends your firm a cheque but asks you not to present it until the end of the month. He has sufficient funds in his personal bank account to cover the cheque. The money received is earmarked for anticipated but not yet incurred costs. Jim's request was made by telephone and you have been unable to get hold of him for a written confirmation of his request for several days.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: You cannot comply with Jim's request and must return the cheque
You cannot comply with Jim's request and must pay the cheque into the office account: Debit cash sheet Credit Jim's ledger office account
You cannot comply with Jim's request and must pay the cheque into the client account: Debit cash sheet Credit Jim's ledger client account
You can comply with Jim's request and need only pay the cheque into the client account at the end of the month: Debit cash sheet Credit Jim's ledger client account
You can comply with Jim's request but must record receipt of the money in the same way as if you would pay it into the client account: Debit cash sheet Credit Jim's ledger client account

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The money received is money on account of costs, and is client money (Rule 12(2)(e) and 17(4)). Usually, the money must be paid without delay to the client account (Rule 13(1), Rules 14(1) and 17(4)). However, you are allowed not to pay the money into the client bank account, provided the client has instructed you not to do so and if it is for the client's own convenience (note Rule 13(1), Rule 15(1)). In this case, whilst you have been instructed, it is not in writing, and you are unable to confirm that instruction in writing. You must therefore comply with Rule 17(4) and pay the cheque into the client account, using the accounting entries represented in Answer C. Answer A is wrong because, whilst you cannot comply with Jim's request, there are sufficient funds held by Jim against which to draw the cheque, therefore you must pay it into the client account to comply with Rule 14(1). Answer B is wrong - besides your inability to comply with Jim's request - because money on account of costs is client money (Rule 17(4)) which must be paid into the client account (Rule 14(1)) as this scenario does not fall within the exceptions to Rule 14. Answers D and E are wrong because you are unable to comply with Jim's request, as it is not in writing and you are not able to confirm it in writing (Rule 15(1)), and must therefore pay the cheque into the client account.

stem: Your office pays £2,000.00 for monthly rent.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: No entries are required because it is not in relation to a client matter
Debit general client ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£2,000.00)
Debit rent costs ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£2,000.00)
Credit rent costs ledger Debit cash sheet office account (£2,000.00
Debit rent costs ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£2,000.00)

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. This is office money under Rule 12(7)(a), as it is money held in connection with running the practice (paying overheads). Client money is not involved. The office's rent costs ledger will record rent payments as they fall due and are paid. A rental payment is recorded as a debit because it is an expense, and the payment of the rent from the office section of the cash account is recorded as a credit. A is wrong. Rule 29 does not require accounting records to be kept in relation to office money used for office matters only. However, Rule 1(2)(e) requires that a solicitor establishes and maintains proper accounting systems, and proper internal controls over those systems, to ensure compliance with the rules. Since the money is drawn from the cash account, which may sometimes pay out monies on behalf of a client, or may sometimes have client money paid in (such as for professional disbursements incurred but not yet paid), it is necessary to ensure this transaction is recorded in order to comply with the Rules generally, and in particular Rule 1(2)(f), which requires proper accounting records to be kept to show accurately the position with regard to the money held for each client and trust. B is wrong because this is an office expense, payable with office money, and is not in relation to a client matter. D is wrong because it records a receipt of monies into the cash account (rather than a payment) and an expense incurred (as opposed to discharged) on the rent costs ledger. In essence, the CR and DR are the wrong way around. E is wrong because it pays for the rental costs using client money, a clear breach of Rules 13 and 14.

stem: On Mr Owens' instruction, you pay £75.00 out of petty cash to cover Mr Owens' photocopying charges in relation to a litigation matter, after having transferred £1,000.00 for the weekly petty cash float. You hold £500.00 for Mr Owens on ledger account of costs.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: For the petty cash transfer: Debit petty cash Credit cash sheet office account (£1,000.00) For the payment of Mr Owens' photocopying charges: Debit Mr Owens' ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£75.00)
Debit Mr Owens' ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£75.00)

For the petty cash transfer: Debit petty cash account Credit cash sheet client account (£75.00) For the payment of Mr Owens' photocopying charges: Debit Mr Owens' ledger Credit petty cash client account (£75.00)
Debit Mr Owens' ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£75.00)

For the petty cash transfer: Debit petty cash Credit cash sheet office account (£1,000.00) For the payment of Mr Owens' photocopying charges: Debit Mr Owens' ledger Credit petty cash office account (£75.00)

explanation.en: The correct answer is E, which records the weekly float transfer out of office money, and the payment out of petty cash of the photocopying charges. Office money is always used for payments from petty cash. You cannot use client money for this purpose, even if the client has enough money to cover costs. You can then make a transfer from the client ledger account to the office ledger account providing you comply with the Rules on how to withdraw money from the client ledger account (Rules 20(1)(c) and 21(3)). Answer A is wrong. The weekly petty cash float is transferred, but the photocopying charges are paid directly from the main cash account, which inaccurately records the transaction (as the money is paid out of petty cash) and is against the client's instruction if such a transaction was intentional. Answer B is wrong - the disbursement is paid directly from the client ledger account and the transfer of the weekly float is not recorded. Whilst the disbursement can be paid from the client ledger account if there is enough money held for the client (which there is in this case), you have not been instructed to pay the disbursement in this way, nor have you recorded the transfer for the weekly petty cash float. Answer C transfers £75.00 from the client ledger account to the petty cash account. Aside from this being effectively a payment from the client ledger account, the potential mixing of client money with office money in this way is a breach of Rule 1. Specifically, this is not keeping other people's money separate from money belonging to the solicitor or practice (Rule 1(2)(a)), nor is it keeping other people's money safely in a bank or building society ledger account identifiable as a client ledger account (Rule 1(2)(b)). Answer D pays the disbursement directly out of the office section of the cash account and does not record the transfer of the weekly float.

stem: Your client asks you to transfer £600,000 of £1,000,000 you hold on his behalf in the general client bank ledger account to a designated deposit ledger account. You open a separate ledger for the designated client account.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Debit client ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£600,000) Debit client designated deposit ledger Credit client ledger (money on deposit) office account (£600,000)
No entries are required other than a memorandum indicating that the sum of £600,000 is now held on deposit for the client
Debit client designated deposit ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£600,000) No further entries are required.
Debit client ledger Credit client ledger (money on deposit) client account (£600,000)
Debit client ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£600,000) Debit client designated deposit Credit client ledger (money on deposit) client account (£600,000)

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. This is a transfer from a general client ledger account (Rule 12(5(b)) and a designated deposit (Rule 12(5)(a)). Rule 20 and Rule 29(3) apply here, and answer E accurately records the appropriate ledger entries in relation to the transfer from the general client account to the designated deposit ledger account and the corresponding ledger entries. Answer A is wrong because it transfers client money from the general client ledger account to the office section of the designated deposit ledger account. This is an inaccurate accounting entry as it is turning client money into office money which is not the case and would constitute an unauthorised withdrawal (Rule 20, Rule 29(2)(b)). Answer B is wrong and breaches the requirements of Rule 29(1) and (2) that properly written up accounting records are kept at all times to show a solicitor's dealings with client money. This answer also fails to reflect the fact that there is a transfer of monies between ledger accounts, as opposed to a simple 'paper transfer'. Answer C transfers the monies without any record of the fact that this money is now being held in a separate designated deposit account for the client and has no entries on the separate ledger. It is a breach of Rule 29. Answer D is merely a paper exercise. No transfer of monies between the general client account to the designated client account has taken place, and is arguably a breach of Rule 29 as it results in inaccurate accounting records, since there is no money held in the client's designated deposit ledger account, whereas the ledger entries indicate that there is.

stem: Your office pays £890.00 plus VAT (£178.00) for surveyors' fees from the office bank ledger account on behalf of your client, Mr Valli. The invoice sent to your office by Shaky Ground Surveyors Limited is made out to Mr Valli, who currently has no money in the client bank ledger account.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: DR Mr Valli's ledger account £1,068.00 - office section CR cash account £1,068.00 - office section
DR Mr Valli's ledger account £890.00 — office section CR cash account £890.00 - office section DR HM Revenue & Customs ledger £178.00 - office section CR cash account £178.00 - office section
DR Mr Valli's ledger account £890.00 - client section CR cash account £890.00 - client section DR HM Revenue & Customs ledger £178.00 - client section CR cash account £178.00 - client section
DR Mr Valli's ledger account £1,068.00 - client section CR cash account £1,068.00 - client section
DR Mr Valli's ledger account £1,068.00 - office section CR profit costs ledger £1,068.00 - office section

explanation.en: Answer A is correct. The surveyors' invoice is addressed to your client. Therefore you must use the agency method and claim the payment including VAT from Mr Valli when a bill of costs will be presented. Note that office money must be used to pay the disbursements as you do not hold enough money on behalf of Mr Valli in the client ledger account. Answer B is wrong - these would be the entries if using the principal method, if the invoice were addressed to the firm. Because the invoice is addressed to Mr Valli, your office has not made any VAT payments on his behalf, and therefore Mr Valli has no outstanding VAT debt to your firm. Answer C is also incorrect for the same reason, as well as the entries being incorrectly entered in the client sections of the ledger account. Answer D records the payment of the surveyors' fees from the client ledger account. You do not hold any money in the client ledger account on behalf of Mr Valli to cover this payment, and would be breaching Rule 20(6), and you would potentially be using another client's money to pay the surveyors' fees, in breach of Rule 1(2)(c). Answer E effectively records the entries that would be made when a bill of costs is delivered to Mr Valli. Whilst this may be appropriate at a later stage, subject to your billing agreement with Mr Valli, in this case it does not reflect your office's payment of the surveyors' fees.

stem: You receive a cheque from a new client on ledger account of costs, and pay it in immediately.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Debit cash sheet Credit client ledger office account
Debit cash sheet Credit client ledger client account
Debit client ledger Credit cash sheet office account
Debit client ledger Credit cash sheet client account
Debit cash sheet client account Credit client ledger office account

explanation.en: Answer B is correct. Under Rule 17(4), a payment on ledger account of costs is client money, and must be paid into a client bank ledger account until the solicitor has delivered a bill of costs or other written notification of costs incurred to the client or paying party. Answer A is incorrect as client money is being paid into the office ledger account, which is a breach of Rule 14(1). Answers C and D are entries showing payments out of office or client ledger accounts, rather than payments in. Answer E is incorrect bookkeeping - the debit entry (indicating receipt/payment of cash) is made correctly in the client section, but the corresponding credit entry is made against the client's ledger account in the office section, when it should be in the client section. It is a breach of Rule 29 not to keep properly written up accounting records showing the solicitor's dealings with client money received, held or paid by the solicitor.

stem: You receive £655.00 in interest on the £65,550.00 held in the general client ledger account, paid by the bank to the office ledger account on your instructions.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Debit cash sheet Credit interest received ledger client account (£655.00)
Debit cash sheet Credit profit costs ledger office account (£655.00)
Debit cash sheet Credit interest received ledger office account (£655.00)
No entries need to be made

Record the interest received: Debit cash sheet Credit interest received ledger office account (£655.00) Then transfer the money to the client ledger account: Debit interest received ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£655.00) Debit cash sheet account Credit interest received ledger client account (£655.00)

explanation.en: Answer C is correct. Interest on general client ledger accounts is defined as office money under Rule 12(7)(b), and the bank or building society should be instructed to credit such interest to the office ledger account. The credit entry is made against the office section of the 'interest received' ledger. A is wrong because the interest on the general client ledger account is office money, not client money. Under Rule 14, only client money may be paid into or held in a client ledger account, and this payment does not fall under any of the exceptions to Rule 14. B is wrong because the credit entry is incorrectly recorded against the profit costs ledger. The interest payment is not the result of fees incurred by the solicitor on a client matter, so should not be recorded against the profit costs ledger. D is wrong. The interest on the general client ledger account is accrued as a result of holding client monies in that ledger account. Whilst it is classed as office money, it is still money owed to the clients, requiring records to be kept under Rule 29. This money can later be transferred to the client ledger account, paid directly to the appropriate client(s) by cash or office cheque, or by reducing the debt owed to the firm by a client. E is wrong because this results in the transfer of a lump sum of interest into the client ledger account, without properly accounting as to which client it relates. Rule 22(1) requires that a solicitor who holds money in a general client ledger account for a client to account to that client for a fair and reasonable amount of interest. Separate entries should be made for each sum of the £ 655.00 that is transferred from the office ledger account to the client ledger account as payment in lieu of interest, identifying each client to which it relates.

stem: You act for Giraffe Insurance in relation to the defence of a personal injury claim. Following the successful defence of a default judgment application, the Claimant is ordered to pay £1,000.00 towards the Defendant's costs. You receive a cheque from the Claimant's Solicitors made out to your firm in the sum of £1,000.00, to be paid to Giraffe Insurance.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Pay the money into the client ledger account: DR cash account £1,000.00 - client section CR Giraffe Insurance ledger £1,000.00 - client section Then issue a cheque to Giraffe Insurance using monies from the client ledger account: DR Giraffe Insurance ledger £1,000.00 - client section CR cash account £1,000.00 - client section

Pay the cheque into the office ledger account: DR cash account £1,000.00 - office section CR Giraffe Insurance ledger £1,000.00 - office section Then issue a cheque to Giraffe Insurance using monies from the office ledger account: DR Giraffe Insurance ledger £1,000.00 - office section CR cash account £1,000.00 - office section

Note receipt of the cheque, but do not pay the monies in: DR cash account £1,000.00 - client section CR Giraffe Insurance ledger £1,000.00 - client section Then forward the cheque to Giraffe Insurance and record this in the client ledger: DR Giraffe Insurance ledger £1,000.00 - client section CR cash account £1,000.00 - client section

Pay the money into the office ledger account: DR cash account £1,000.00 - office section CR Giraffe Insurance ledger £1,000.00 - office section Then transfer the monies to the client ledger account: DR Giraffe Insurance ledger £1,000.00 - office section CR cash account £1,000.00 - office section DR cash account £1,000.00 - client section CR Giraffe Insurance ledger £1,000.00 - client section Then issue a cheque made payable to Giraffe Insurance Limited using monies from the client ledger account: DR Giraffe Insurance ledger £1,000.00 - client section CR cash account £1,000.00 - client section
No entries need to be made

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. This is quite clearly client money, and is subject to accounting requirements of Rule 29. As the cheque is payable to the firm and has not been endorsed to the client, it will need to be paid into the general client ledger account, and a subsequent cheque issued to the client to be drawn from the client ledger account. Answer B is incorrect. The money is client money and cannot be paid into the office ledger account. Under Rule 14(1), client money must without delay be paid into a client ledger account and be held into a client ledger account. The exceptions to this rule do not apply in this scenario. Answer C is incorrect because this set of accounting entries reflects the scenario in which a cheque made out to the solicitors' firm is endorsed then forwarded to a third party, with no money paid into the client ledger account. Because the cheque has not been endorsed in this scenario, the money must first be paid into the general client ledger account, and a subsequent cheque issued payable to the client. Answer D breaches Rule 14(1), because it pays money into the office ledger account when there is no provision under the exceptions to Rule 14 to do so. Answer E is incorrect because Rule 29 requires that accounting records be kept to show a solicitor's dealings with client money.

stem: Sarah is entitled to a payment of £25 interest on monies you hold on her behalf in the general client account. However, she still owes £250.00 as against your bill of costs.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Debit interest expense ledger Credit Sarah's ledger office account (£25.00)
Debit Sarah's ledger Credit interest expense ledger office account (£25.00)
No payment is required, as the sum falls within the de minimis limits. Therefore no entries need to be made.
Debit interest expense Credit Sarah's ledger client account (£25.00)
Debit Sarah's ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£25.00)

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Interest on general client accounts generally is considered office money and is paid into the office account Rule 12(7)(b). Broken down, however, it is comprised of money owed to specific clients. You received interest on money you held on their behalf. Whilst you are obligated to pay fair and reasonable amount of interest to Sarah, she owes you money, and therefore a reduction in Sarah's debt in the office ledger deals with the transaction. B is wrong because it is a reverse set of entries to that which is intended; i.e. you are doubling the interest owed to Sarah with these entries. C is wrong because there is no de minimis limit (Rule 22), unless the interest policy of the firm says otherwise (note (i)(e) to Rule 22). D is wrong because it records a reduction of the debt owed by Sarah in the client section of the ledgers by the amount in lieu of interest. A debt to the firm is office money. E is wrong because it amounts to a cash payment of £25.00 to Sarah, when in fact Sarah owes you money.

stem: You act for Giraffe Insurance in relation to the defence of a personal injury claim. Following the successful defence of a default judgment application, the Claimant is ordered to pay £1,000.00 towards the Defendant's costs. You receive a cheque from the Claimant's Solicitors for £1,000.00, made payable to Giraffe Insurance.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct and preferred accounting entries?

options.en: No entries need to be made

Pay the money into the client ledger account: Debit cash sheet Credit Giraffe Insurance ledger client account (£1,000.00) Then issue a cheque to Giraffe Insurance using monies from the client ledger account: Debit Giraffe Insurance ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£1,000.00)

Note receipt of the cheque, but do not pay the monies in: Debit cash sheet Credit Giraffe Insurance ledger client account (£1,000.00) Then forward the cheque to Giraffe Insurance and record this in the client ledger: Debit Giraffe Insurance ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£1,000.00)

Pay the cheque into the office ledger account: Debit cash sheet Credit Giraffe Insurance ledger office account (£1,000.00) Then issue a cheque to Giraffe Insurance using monies from the office ledger account: Debit Giraffe Insurance ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£1,000.00)
No entries are required, but a memorandum note would be placed in the client section of the client ledger: Debit Giraffe Insurance ledger Credit Giraffe Insurance ledger client account (£1,000.00)

explanation.en: Answer E is correct. Note (iii) to Rule 29 states that a cheque made payable to a client, which is forwarded to the client by the solicitor, is not client money and falls outside the rules, although it is advisable to record the action taken. Answer E reflects an accurate memorandum note entered in the client section of the client ledger, noting receipt and forwarding of the cheque. Answer A is technically correct but not preferred. Whilst a cheque made payable to a third party is not client money and falls outside the Rules, it is advisable to record receipt and forwarding of the cheque, per note (iii) to Rule 29. This will leave an audit trail should any issues arise regarding delivery or receipt of the cheque by any parties involved. Answers B and D are incorrect as they both involve paying money into a ledger account. As this is a cheque endorsed to a third party, the solicitor is unable to pay the money in to any ledger account. To record receipt and forwarding of the cheque in this way, even if no money is actually paid in, breaches the accounting requirements of Rule 29. Answer C is incorrect as the money is not client money and therefore does not need to be recorded in this way, per note (iii) to Rule 29.

stem: You acted for Naeem in respect of a property transaction. You were instructed by Naeem to close his designated deposit ledger account (current balance: £2,500.00) and transfer all funds to the general client bank ledger account. You opened a new ledger in Naeem's name when the money was initially transferred to the designated deposit ledger account.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Transfer the money between the designated deposit account and the general client account and record the entries on the ledger account for the designated deposit account and the general client ledger account: DR Naeem's ledger account (money on deposit) £2,500.00 - client section CR Naeem's designated deposit account £2,500.00 - client section DR cash account £2,500.00 - client section CR Naeem's ledger account £2,500.00 - client section

Transfer the money from the designated deposit account to the cash account: DR cash account £2,500.00 - client section CR Naeem's designated deposit account £2,500.00 - client section Make a memorandum note in the client ledger account to indicate that a sum of money which belongs to Naeem was transferred from a designated deposit account to the general client account.

Make memorandum entries in Naeem's ledger account (money on deposit) and Naeem's client ledger: DR Naeem's ledger account (money on deposit) £2,500.00 - client section CR Naeem's ledger account £2,500.00 - client section
Transfer the money from the designated deposit account to the cash account: DR Naeem's designated deposit account £2,500.00 - client section CR cash account £2,500.00 - client section

Transfer the money between the designated deposit account and the general client account: DR Naeem's designated deposit account £2,500.00 - client section CR Naeem's ledger account (money on deposit) £2,500.00 - client section DR Naeem's ledger account £2,500.00 - client section CR cash account £2,500.00 - client section Make a memorandum note to indicate that a sum of money which belongs to Naeem was transferred from a designated deposit account to the general client account.

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. This is client money, which is transferred between two different client accounts - the designated deposit account and the general client account (Rule 20(1) (e), Rule 29(3)). Because you have opened a separate ledger in Naeem's name when the money was transferred to the designated deposit account, the transfer needs to be reflected in both this designated ledger as well as Naeem's general ledger, in order for the ledgers to balance. Because the credit entry in Naeem's designated deposit account reflects the withdrawal of the money from that account (withdrawal of cash is always a credit) and the subsequent debit entry in the money on deposit ledger ensures that the accounts show that the designated deposit account and money on deposit ledger both show a zero balance. The credit and debit entries in the client account and Naeem's account ledger show that the funds have been deposited in the client account (cash deposits are always a debit) and accounted for by way of credit entry in Naeem's client ledger (as opposed to the separate - now closed - money on deposit ledger.) B is incorrect. There would be no problem with this method if there was no ledger (money on deposit) for Naeem's designated deposit account. However, these entries do not make any entry in Naeem's ledger account (money on deposit), leaving a positive balance when the money had been transferred to the general client ledger account, breaching Rule 29 due to its inaccuracy. C is simply a paper transfer from Naeem's designated deposit ledger account to the general client ledger account - no actual transfer of funds has taken place and the money remains in the designated deposit cash account. This is a breach of Rule 29. D and E are wrong because they transfer money from the client ledger account to the designated deposit ledger account (and Answer D has the same issue of an inaccurate ledger for Naeem (money on deposit) as Answer B), which is the opposite of the client's instruction.

stem: Your client previously presented a cheque for £50,000.00 representing the deposit on a commercial property. You paid it into the general client account on his behalf. You have now been instructed to open a designated deposit account and transfer the £50,000.00 across. You are not opening a new ledger.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries to record the transfer of the £50,000.00 from the general client account to the designated deposit account?

options.en: Debit your client's ledger (money on deposit) Credit designated deposit ledger client account (£50,000.00) Debit cash sheet Credit your client's ledger client account (£50,000.00)
Debit designated deposit ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£50,000.00)

Debit designated deposit ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£50,000.00) Record a memorandum note to indicate that a sum of money which belongs to your client was transferred from a designated deposit account to a general client account

Debit cash sheet Credit designated deposit ledger client account (£50,000.00) Record a memorandum note to indicate that a sum of money which belongs to your client was transferred from a designated deposit account to a general client account

Debit designated deposit ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£50,000.00) Record a memorandum note to indicate that a sum of money which belongs to your client was transferred to a designated deposit account from a general client account

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. This is client money, which is transferred between the general client account and the designated deposit account (Rule 20(1)(e), Rule 29(3)). Answer E reflects the correct accounting entries to make in this instance where there is no designated deposit ledger account used. Answer A is wrong. These are the accounting entries you would make if you were using a designated deposit ledger account. Answers B and C reflect incorrect bookkeeping, breaching Rules 1 and 32. Double entries for each record must be made against the client or the office section of an account. A debit cannot be created against the client section whilst the credit is in the office section, or vice versa. Answer D transfers money from the designated deposit account to the cash account. This is the wrong way around. Further, there is no money currently held in the designated deposit account.

stem: Francois has accrued a sum of £15.00 interest on monies you hold on his behalf in the general client account. Francois does not owe you any money and your firm has a de minimis threshold on interest set at £17.50.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Debit interest expense Credit Francois' ledger office account (£15.00)
Debit Francois' ledger Credit interest expense office account (£15.00)
Debit interest expense Credit Francois' ledger client account (£15.00)
No payment is required, if the sum falls within de minimis limits in the firm's interest policy. Therefore no entries need to be made
Debit Francois' ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£15.00)

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Whilst you are required to account to a client for whom you hold money in a general client account for a sum in lieu of interest (Rule 22(1)), firms may set a de minimis threshold, below which they are not required to pay a sum in lieu of interest (Note (i)(e) to Rule 22). If that is the firm's policy - as is the case here - and it was explained to the client, you do not need to make any payment, therefore no entries need to be made. However, once the interest owed exceeds the de minimis limit in the firm's policy, you will be obliged to account for that sum to the client. A is wrong because it is a reduction of the debt owed by the client by the interest payment, when no reduction is required due to Rule 22(2)(d) and 25. This is a breach of Rule 29. B is wrong because it doubles the interest owed to Francois. This is a breach of Rule 29. C is wrong because it records a reduction of a debt owed by Francois - which doesn't exist - in the client section of the ledgers for the interest. E is wrong because it amounts to a cash payment of £15.00 to Francois, when you are not required to pay the interest at this stage.

stem: You have recently been instructed by Will in relation to a commercial property transaction. As part of the matter opening, Will paid in £275,000.00 into the general client account. You have now been instructed by Will to transfer £125,000.00 from that amount to a designated deposit account. You decide to open a new ledger in Will's name.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: DR designated deposit account £125,000.00 - client section CR cash account £125,000.00 - client section

DR Will's ledger account £125,000.00 - client section CR cash account £125,000.00 - client section DR designated deposit account £125,000.00 - client section CR Will's ledger account (money on deposit) £125,000.00 - client section

DR Will's ledger account (money on deposit) £125,000.00 - client section CR designated deposit account £125,000.00 - client section DR cash account £125,000.00 - client section CR Will's ledger account £125,000.00 - client section

Make memorandum entries in Will's ledger account (money on deposit) and Will's client ledger: DR Will's ledger account £125,000.00 - client section CR Will's ledger account (money on deposit) £125,000.00 - client section

DR Will's ledger account £125,000.00 - client section CR cash account £125,000.00 - client section DR designated deposit account £125,000.00 - office section CR Will's ledger account (money on deposit) £125,000.00 - office section Make a memorandum note to indicate that a sum of money which belongs to Will was transferred from a designated deposit ledger account to a general ledger account

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. This is a transfer between two client's accounts (Rule 20(1)(e), Rule 29(2). As a new ledger account has been opened for Will, we need to record the credit entry in this ledger when the money is transferred (a debit) into the designated deposit account. Answer A is wrong because it is a transfer from the cash account to the designated deposit account without any corresponding ledger entries for the client ledger and deposit ledger. This is a breach of Rule 29. Answer C is a series of incorrect accounting entries that are a reverse of the intended transaction - money is transferred from the designated deposit account (which isn't there in the first place) to the general client account. This is a breach of Rule 29. Answer D is merely a paper transfer between client accounts. No money has been transferred. This is a breach of Rule 29. Answer E transfers money from the cash account to the office section of the designated deposit account. This is client money and should not be recorded in the office section of the designated deposit account, which holds client money only. This is a breach of Rule 29.

stem: You have been informed by the bank that the cheque from your client, Mr Roswell, for £600.00 on account of costs has been dishonoured. Unfortunately, you have already paid £400.00 for search fees on behalf of Mr Roswell from the general client bank account.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Transfer office money to the client account: DR Mr Roswell's ledger account £400.00 - office section CR cash account £400.00 - office section DR cash account £400.00 - client section CR Mr Roswell's ledger account £400.00 - client section
Reverse the entries made on receipt of the cheque: DR Mr Roswell's ledger account £600.00 - client section CR cash account £600.00 - client section

Reverse the entries made on receipt of the cheque: DR Mr Roswell's ledger account £600.00 - client section CR cash account £600.00 - client section Make a memorandum entry in the cash account - client section that monies are outstanding and will be restored on clearing of the payment owed by Mr Roswell

Reverse the entries made on receipt of the cheque: DR Mr Roswell's ledger account £600.00 - client section CR cash account £600.00 - client section Transfer office money to the client account: DR Mr Roswell's ledger account £400.00 - office section CR cash account £400.00 - office section DR cash account £400.00 - client section CR Mr Roswell's ledger account £400.00 - client section

Reverse the entries made on receipt of the cheque: DR Mr Roswell's ledger account £600.00 - client section CR cash account £600.00 - client section Transfer office money to the client account: DR Mr Roswell's ledger account £600.00 - office section CR cash account £600.00 - office section DR cash account £600.00 - client section CR Mr Roswell's ledger account £600.00 - client section

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Generally, note (v) to Rule 20 cautions against drawing against uncleared cheques. Because the cheque has bounced in this scenario, other clients' money will have been used to make the payment, in breach of Rule 1. Under Rule 7, a solicitor has a duty to remedy any breach of the rules promptly upon discovery. This includes the replacement of any money improperly withheld or withdrawn from a client account. You may pay office money into a client account to replace any money that has been withdrawn from the account in breach of Rule 20 (Rule 14(2)(c). Answer D reflects the correct accounting entries that reflects the dishonoured cheque and transfers monies from the office account to the client account to remedy the breach. Answer A is wrong because whilst it transfers money from the office account to the client account to remedy the breach, the dishonoured cheque is not reflected in the records, in breach of Rule 29. Answer B is wrong because whilst it reverses the entries made on receipt of the cheque, thus restoring the debt owed by the client, it does not transfer money from the office account to the client account to remedy the breach. This omission is a breach of Rule 1, Rule 7 and Rule 29. Answer C is wrong because whilst it reverses the entries made on receipt of the cheque, it is not good enough to simply record that £400.00 is owed on the client account. Because Mr Roswell's cheque has been dishonoured, other clients' money has been used to cover the payments on Mr Roswell's behalf. This is a breach of Rule 1 and requires immediate remedy per Rule 7 - not remedy on receipt of a further cheque from Mr Roswell. Answer E is wrong because it transfers £600.00 from the office account to the client account, where only £400.00 is needed to cover the breach. This payment is not permitted under Rule 14, specifically Rule 14(2)(c), because it exceeds the sum required to replace the amount drawn in breach of Rule 20.

stem: Francesca sends your firm a cheque but asks you not to present it until the end of the month. The money received is earmarked for anticipated but not yet incurred costs. Francesca's request was made in writing.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: You cannot comply with Francesca's request and must return the cheque
You cannot comply with Francesca's request and must pay the cheque into the office account: Debit cash sheet Credit Francesca's ledger office account
You cannot comply with Francesca's request and must pay the cheque into the client account: Debit cash sheet Credit Francesca's ledger client account
You can comply with Francesca's request and need only pay the cheque into the client account at the end of the month: Debit cash sheet Credit Francesca's ledger client account
You can comply with Francesca's request but must record receipt of the money in the same way as if you would pay it into the client account: Debit cash sheet Credit Francesca's ledger client account

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The money received is money on account of costs, and is client money (Rule 17(4)). Usually, the money must be paid without delay to the client account (Rule 12(2)(e), Rule 14(1) and 17(4)). However, you are allowed not to pay the money into the client bank account, provided the client has instructed you not to do so and if it is for the client's own convenience (note (i) to Rule 14, Rule 15(1)). In this case, Francesca has instructed you in writing to withhold the money. We can assume that this request is made for Francesca's convenience. Therefore you do not need to pay the cheque into the client account without delay. However, you must record the receipt of the money in the same way as you would do if you paid it into the client bank account (note (i) and (ii) to Rule 15 and Rule 29). A and Care wrong because you can comply with Francesca's request as you have scope within Rule 15(1) to withhold the money. B is wrong because money on account of costs is client money (Rule 17(4)) which must be paid into the client account (Rule 14(1)) as this scenario does not fall within the exceptions to Rule 14. D is wrong because you need to record receipt of the money in the same way as you would do if you paid it into the client bank account (notes (i) and (ii) to Rule 15 and Rule 29). It's not acceptable to simply hold on to the cheque without recording receipt.

stem: Your office accidentally paid £2,500.00 into Ian's designated deposit account, when it was intended to be held in the general client account for Pierre. There is a separate ledger for Ian's designated deposit account. Before you discover the mistake, your office paid out £100.00 from the general client account on Pierre's behalf for search fees.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct and best accounting entries to remedy the situation?

options.en: Transfer the money from Ian's designated deposit account to the client account: DR Ian's ledger account (money on deposit) £2,500.00 - client section CR Ian's designated deposit account £2,500.00 - client section DR cash account £2,500.00 - client section CR Pierre's ledger account £2,500.00 - client section Make appropriate ledger entries to note that the previous expense was from Pierre's money

Transfer money from the office account to the general client account to cover the breach of the Rules: DR Pierre's ledger account £100.00 - office section CR cash account £100.00 - office section DR cash account £100.00 - client section CR Pierre's ledger account £100.00 - client section

Transfer money from the office account to the general client account to cover the breach of the Rules: DR Pierre's ledger account £100.00 - office section CR cash account £100.00 - office section DR cash account £100.00 - client section CR Pierre's ledger account £100.00 - client section Transfer the money from lan's designated deposit account to the client account: DR cash account £2,500.00 - client section CR Ian's designated deposit account £2,500.00 - client section

Transfer money from the office account to the general client account to cover the breach of the Rules: DR Pierre's ledger account £100.00 - office section CR cash account £100.00 - office section DR cash account £100.00 - client section CR Pierre's ledger account £100.00 - client section Transfer the money from Ian's designated deposit account to the client account: DR lan's ledger account (money on deposit) £2,500.00 - client section CR Ian's designated deposit account £2,500.00 - client section DR cash account £2,500.00 - client section CR Pierre's ledger account £2,500.00 - client section
Transfer the money from Ian's designated deposit account to the client account: DR cash account £2,500.00 - client section CR Ian's designated deposit account £2,500.00 - client section

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. This is client money. One client's money has been incorrectly paid into a designated deposit account for another client, breaching Rule 1(2)(e) and (f) and Rule 29. Money has then been paid out of the general client account for that client which is, in fact, money that belonged to another client, breaching Rule 1(2)(c). Money which has been paid into a client account in breach of the Rules must be withdrawn from the client account promptly upon discovery (Rule 7, Rule 20(1)(i) and 20(5)). Because this situation has arisen out of an accounting error, the provision of Rule 20(7) doesn't apply - Pierre's money was only ever meant to be held in the general client account. Answer B is wrong, because you are required by Rule 20 to withdraw money from the designated deposit account in which it has been wrongly deposited immediately. Whilst Answer B remedies the breach of Rule 1(2)(e) in accordance with Rule 7, it does not take into account the provisions of Rule 20, nor does it deal with the outstanding issue of lan's designated deposit account wrongly holding money on Pierre's behalf. Answer C and D build on Answer B by transferring the money from Ian's designated deposit account to Pierre's account. However, this means that there is no need to transfer office money to the general client account to cover the breach, since the transfer of Pierre's money to the general client account remedies this breach as the it reimburses the client whose money was used to pay the search fees when no money was on Pierre's behalf in the general client account. Answer E is wrong because you have a separate ledger for Ian. This set of accounting entries does not accurately updated Ian's ledger account to reflect the withdrawal of the incorrectly deposited money, breaching Rule 29. If you did not hold a separate ledger for lan, this would have been correct.

stem: You hold £600.00 in the general client account for Andre on account of costs. You are asked by Andre to pay £650.00 towards surveyor's fees, the invoice for which is addressed to Andre.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: You cannot make this payment until you receive a further £50.00 from Andre
Pay the invoice from the client account: Debit Andre's ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£650.00)
Pay the invoice from the office account: Debit Andre's ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£650.00)

Pay the invoice from the office account: Debit Andre's ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£650.00) Record the VAT: Debit HM Revenue & Customs ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£130.00) Register a note in the client ledger that the firm has paid the surveyor's VAT and that this expense must be claimed from Andre when sending him the bill of costs

Pay the invoice from the client account: Debit Andre's ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£650.00) Record the VAT: Debit HM Revenue & Customs ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£130.00) Register a note in the client ledger that the firm has paid the surveyor's VAT and that this expense must be claimed from Andre when sending him the bill of costs

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The invoice is addressed to your client. Therefore you must use the agency method and claim the payment including VAT from Andrew when a bill of costs will be presented. Note that office money must be used to pay the disbursements, since there is insufficient money held on behalf of Andre in the client account. Answer A is wrong because you can pay the invoice from the office account and include the amount on the bill of costs to deliver to Andre. B is wrong because you would be using £50.00 of another client's money to pay the invoice for Andre, a breach of Rule 1. Answers D and E are wrong as they pay the invoice using the principal method, when the invoice should be paid using the agency method (E being wrong because it would also pay the invoice out of the client account).

stem: You pay £50.00 Land Registry fees on Nigel's behalf. You do not currently hold any money on Nigel's behalf.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: The fees are paid out of the general client account: Debit Nigel's ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£50.00)
You cannot make this payment until you have £50.00 on account of costs from Nigel
The monies are paid out of Nigel's designated deposit account: Debit Nigel's ledger Credit designated deposit ledger client account (£50.00)
The monies are paid out of the office account: Debit Nigel's ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£50.00)
The fees are paid from petty cash: Debit petty cash Credit cash sheet office account (£50.00)

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. As you do not hold any money for Nigel, you would have to pay the fees from the office account then include this amount on a bill of costs to be invoiced to Nigel. A is wrong. Because you do not hold any money for Nigel, you would be paying the fees using another client's money, a breach of Rule 1(2)(c). Answer B is incorrect. You can make payments on behalf of a client using office money, as you can then recover this money from the client by way of delivery of a bill of costs. Answer C is incorrect because you do not hold any money on Nigel's behalf at all, therefore you would not have a designated deposit account for Nigel. Answer E is wrong because payment of fees is not done by way of petty cash - it is instead effected by bank transfer or cheque.

stem: Your bookkeeper has just discovered that your firm mistakenly overcharged Michael in respect of expenses made on his behalf. You pay a cheque of £75.00 to Michael to reimburse him the overpaid amount.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Debit Michael's ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£75.00)
Debit Michael's ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£75.00)
Debit Michael's ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£75.00) Debit cash sheet Credit Michael's ledger client account (£75.00)
Debit administrative errors ledger Credit Michael's ledger client account (£75.00)
No entries need to be made - you can pay Michael from the office account

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. This is money you owe to the client, and is client money. In this case, it can be paid from the office account (Rules 7(1) and 20(1)). A is wrong because you are using money from the client account to reimburse the client. Since you hold no money on Michael's behalf, you would be using other client's money to pay Michael, a breach of Rule 1. C is wrong because you are transferring money from the office account to the client account, and are not paying any money that you owe to Michael. D is wrong because this is a paper exercise that debits a separate ledger account to record the debt. You are not paying out the money you owe to Michael. E is wrong because you are dealing with client money, and are required by Rule 29 to record your dealings with client money.

stem: Emily sends your firm a cheque but asks you not to present it until the end of the month when she will have received a significant inheritance payment as currently there are no funds against which to draw the cheque yet. The money received is earmarked for anticipated but not yet incurred costs. Emily's request was made by telephone and she has gone on a 2 month safari holiday.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: You cannot comply with Emily's request and must return the cheque
You cannot comply with Emily's request and must pay the cheque into the office account: Debit cash sheet Credit Emily's ledger office account
You cannot comply with Emily's request and must pay the cheque into the client account: Debit cash sheet Credit Emily's ledger client account
You can comply with Emily's request and need only pay the cheque into the client account at the end of the month: Debit cash sheet Credit Emily's ledger client account
You can comply with Emily's request but must record receipt of the money in the same way as if you would pay it into the client account: Debit cash sheet Credit Emily's ledger client account

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. The money received is money on account of costs, and is client money (Rule 17(4)). Usually, the money must be paid without delay to the client account (Rule 12(2)(e), Rules 14(1) and 17(4)). However, you are allowed not to pay the money into the client bank account, provided the client has instructed you not to do so and if it is for the client's own convenience (note (i) to Rule 14, Rule 15). In this case, whilst you have been instructed, it is not in writing, and you are unable to confirm that instruction in writing before the time the client has requested that you pay it in. You cannot comply with Rule 17(4) by paying the cheque into the client account, as you know there are no funds against which to draw the cheque yet. Whilst, in a sense, there is no client money to speak of, you are still required to return the cheque to the client. You would enclose the cheque with a letter explaining why you cannot comply with her request. Answer B is wrong - besides your inability to comply with Emily's request - because money on account of costs is client money (Rule 17(4)) which must be paid into the client account (Rule 14(1)) as this scenario does not fall within the exceptions to Rule 14. Answer C is wrong because you know there are no funds held by Emily against which to draw the cheque. This would not be a proper system of accounting and internal controls, in breach of Rule 1(2)(e). Answers D and E are wrong because you are unable to comply with Emily's request, as it is not in writing and you are not able to confirm it in writing (Rule 15(1)). D is wrong because you need to record receipt of the money in the same way as you would do if you paid it into the client bank account (note(i) to Rules 15 and 29). It's not acceptable to simply hold on to the cheque without recording receipt.

stem: You act for John in a litigation matter. Following a successful interim application hearing in the matter, you receive an invoice from Counsel addressed to the firm for £5,000.00 plus VAT of £1,000.00. The invoice is paid the next day. You are holding £10,000.00 on ledger account of costs already for John.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Debit John's ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£5,000.00) Debit HM Revenue & Customs ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£1,000.00) Register a note in the client ledger that the firm has paid Counsel's VAT and that this expense must be claimed from John when sending him the bill of costs
Debit John's ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£6,000.00)
Debit John's ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£6,000.00)

Debit John's ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£5,000.00) Debit HM Revenue & Customs ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£1,000.00) Register a note in the client ledger that the office has paid Counsel's VAT and that this expense must be claimed from John when sending him the bill of costs
Debit John's ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£5,000.00) Make a note in the client ledger to include the VAT amount when sending the bill of costs to John

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Counsel addressed the invoice, a professional disbursement, to the solicitor and not to the client. The solicitor is therefore liable for paying both the invoice amount and VAT, which can either be recovered from the client or set-off. This is known as the principal method. Answer A reflects the true cost of the invoice to the solicitor, which is the sum stipulated on the invoice less the VAT, and an accurate reflection of this in the appropriate ledger entries. The note in the client ledger serves to ensure that the VAT relating to the disbursement is included in the bill of costs sent to the client in order that the solicitor can recover it. Answers B and C reflects the entries that would be made if the invoice were addressed to the client, in which case the solicitor simply delivers the money to the third party on behalf of the client. This is known as the agency method, and would require that the ledgers record the entirety of the payment delivered to the third party and subsequently billed to the client, including VAT. Client money can be used to pay, unless there is insufficient money on behalf of that particular client. Answer D is wrong. Because the solicitor is liable for the invoice, not the client, the payment must be made out of the office ledger account. This answer would also be wrong if the invoice were addressed to the client, and thus payable by the agency method, because the client himself is responsible for dealing with all VAT aspects of the invoice. Therefore, the invoice total in its entirety, including VAT is delivered to the client, and no separate VAT entries are made on behalf of the solicitor. Answer E reflects the appropriate ledger entries in respect of the costs but fails to deal with the VAT element. HM Revenue & Customs permits solicitors to cross out their name on a VAT receipt to replace it with the client's name. Under this method, the supply is deemed to be direct to the client who can then reclaim the input VAT if registered. However, this does not apply if the solicitor seeks to recover the VAT from the client instead, in which case appropriate ledger entries in the HM Revenue & Customs and cash accounts are required.

stem: You act for Samuel in a litigation matter. Samuel sends you a crossed cheque for £8,000.00, of which £4,000.00 represents your fees and £4,000.00 is for Counsel's fees you have incurred and paid. You process the cheque using Option 1.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries for Option 1?

options.en: The sum in respect of fees and Counsel's fees are office money. Pay the whole amount into the office account under Option 1: DR cash account £8,000.00 - office section CR Samuel's ledger account £8,000.00 - office section

The sum in respect of your firm's fees and Counsel's fees are client money. Pay the whole amount into the client account under Option 1: DR cash account £8,000.00 - client section CR Samuel's ledger account £8,000.00 - client section

The sum in respect of your firm's fees is office money and Counsel's fees are client money. Pay the entire amount in the office account: DR cash account £8,000.00 - office section CR Samuel's ledger account £8,000.00 - office section By the end of the second working day following receipt, transfer the client money into the client account: DR Samuel's ledger account £4,000.00 - office section CR cash account £4,000.00 - office section CR cash account £4,000.00 - client section DR Samuel's ledger account £4,000.00 - client section

The sum in respect of your firm's fees is office money and Counsel's fees are client money. Pay the entire amount in the client account: DR cash account £8,000.00 - client section CR Samuel's ledger account £8,000.00 - client section Within 14 days of receipt of the payment, transfer the office money into the office account: DR Samuel's ledger account £4,000.00 - client section CR cash account £4,000.00 - client section CR cash account £4,000.00 - office section DR Samuel's ledger account £4,000.00 - office section

The sum in respect of your firm's fees is office money and Counsel's fees are client money. Split the amounts between the office account and client account under Option 1: DR cash account £4,000.00 - office section CR Samuel's ledger account £4,000.00 - office section DR cash account £4,000.00 - client section CR Samuel's ledger account £4,000.00 - client section

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Money received for fees due and for which a bill of costs has been delivered is office money, as are disbursements already paid by the practice (Rule 12(7)(c)). A cheque covering both sums comprises office money entirely. Even if it was not, because the cheque is crossed, you cannot split the payment. You must therefore pay the whole amount into the office account under Option 1 (Rule 17(1)(a)(i)). All other answers are wrong for this reason because they classify paid Counsel's fees as client money. Money which is received for unpaid professional disbursements (i.e. Counsel's fees incurred but not yet paid) is client money - Rule 12(2)(c).

stem: You deliver a bill of costs to Robert for £2,500.00 plus VAT (£500.00).
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Debit Robert's ledger Credit profit costs client account (£2,500.00) Debit Robert's ledger Credit HM Revenue & Customs ledger client account (£500.00)
Debit Robert's ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£2,500.00) Credit Robert's ledger Debit HM Revenue & Customs ledger office account (£500.00
Debit Robert's ledger Credit profit costs office account (£2,500.00) Debit Robert's ledger Credit HM Revenue & Customs ledger office account (£500.00)
Debit Robert's ledger Credit profit costs client account (£3,000.00)
Debit Robert's ledger Credit profit costs office account (£3,000.00)

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Profit costs are recorded in the profit costs ledger, with the corresponding entry in the client's ledger account. Solicitors are required to charge VAT on their costs to their clients, whereas clients must pay VAT on the cost fees to the solicitor. Because VAT is paid to HM Revenue & Customs, the VAT element must be recorded on a separate ledger to comply with Rule 29, with the corresponding entry recorded in the client's ledger account. Under Rule 17(2), a solicitor must deliver a bill of costs before he can recover fees. Once this is done, fees due to the practice, and payment of those, becomes office money. Entries are therefore made in the office section of the ledgers. Answer A is wrong because the monies, which are office money, are recorded in the client section. Answer B is wrong because the entries reflect a cash payment to Robert, as opposed to a rendering of a bill of costs, and a removal of the VAT debt, rather than its creation. Answer D is wrong because the profit costs and VAT are not separated, and entered against the client section of the ledgers. Answer E is wrong because the profit costs and VAT are not separated. Because you have to account to HM Revenue & Customs for VAT, and are able to set-off output tax on input tax, you should record VAT separately in a separate ledger to comply with Rule 29.

stem: You act for a woman on the sale of her house. You also act for the bank with whom the woman has a mortgage, in respect of the mortgage redemption. You deliver a bill of costs of £600.00 plus VAT of £120.00 to the bank, although it is agreed that the woman will pay for these costs.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Deliver a bill of costs to the woman: DR woman's ledger account £600.00 - office section CR profit costs account £600.00 - office section DR woman's ledger account £120.00 - office section CR HMRC ledger account £120.00 - office section On receipt of payment from the woman, deliver payment to the bank

Create a debt to the bank in woman's ledger account: DR woman's ledger account £720.00 - office section CR bank's ledger account £720.00 - office section Request a cheque from the woman and forward it to the bank on receipt

Pay the bank from the office account: DR bank's ledger account £720.00 - office section CR cash account £720.00 - office section Deliver a bill of costs to the woman: DR woman's ledger account £ 600.00 - office section CR profit costs account £600.00 - office section DR woman's ledger account £120.00 - office section CR HMRC ledger account £120.00 - office section
Pay the bank from money held on behalf of the woman in the client account: DR bank's ledger account £720.00 - client section CR cash account £720.00 - client section

Deliver a bill of costs to the bank: DR bank's ledger account £600.00 - office section CR profit costs account £600.00 - office section DR bank's ledger account £120.00 - office section CR HMRC ledger account £120.00 - office section Transfer the debt to the client: DR woman's ledger account £720.00 - office section CR bank's ledger account £720.00 - office section You are also required to record the 'transfer' of money in the transfer journal giving details of the date of the transfer, the sum transferred and the reason why the transfer was made

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. This is a liability incurred by the client and payable to the bank. You are merely acting as an intermediary. The money is neither client nor office money. You therefore deliver a bill of costs to the bank for which the client is liable to satisfy, and record in the appropriate ledgers that it is the woman that is the debtor and remove the bank as owing the debt to your firm. Answer A is wrong because you are creating a further debt - one from the woman to your firm, which is not accurate as the woman owes no money to your firm - she owes money to the bank. This is a breach of Rule 29. Answer B is wrong since you are not a party to the debt. This is a breach of Rule 29. Answer C is wrong because it is not you that owes a debt to the bank, nor are you a party to it. This amounts to dealing with the matter using the principal method, which is not appropriate. Answer D is wrong because you have not accurately recorded the creation of the debt from the woman to the bank - you have simply paid £720.00 to the bank with no record as to what it relates to.

stem: You act for the executors of the late Mrs Abrahams. The bank opens a loan account and lends the executors £45,000 to pay the inheritance tax. Today you receive from the bank a cheque for £45,000 made payable to HMRC.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: No entry should be made in this case
Debit cash sheet Credit Late Mrs Abraham's ledger office account (£45,000) This is office money
Debit cash sheet Credit Late Mrs Abraham's ledger client account (£45,000) This is client money
Debit cash sheet Credit HMRC (in trust) ledger account (£45,000) This is client money
No entry should be made in this case, as the cheque received is neither client nor office money. The solicitor must transfer the cheque to HMRC without delay

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. No entries should be made in this case, since the cheque is payable to a third party. Therefore, the cheque received is neither client money nor office money and falls outside the Rules, although it is advisable to record the action taken (note (ili) to Rule 29). Note also that the loan account is neither a client account nor an office account. The solicitor should transfer the cheque directly to HMRC. Answer E is incorrect as there is no requirement to transfer the cheque without delay under the rules.

stem: You act for Garry's Gardening Limited and hold £350.00 in the client account. You want to make a payment of £500.00 on their behalf using one cheque.
ask: Which of the following describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Pay the sum from the client bank account: DR Garry's Gardening Limited ledger account £500.00 - client section CR cash account £500.00 - client section

Pay the sum from the office bank account: DR Garry's Gardening Limited ledger account £500.00 - office section CR cash account £500.00 - office section Then transfer £350.00 from the client account to the office account: DR Garry's Gardening Limited ledger account £350.00 - client section CR cash account £350.00 - client section DR cash account £350.00 - office section CR Garry's Gardening Limited ledger account £350.00 - office section

Transfer £350.00 from the client account to the office account: DR Garry's Gardening Limited ledger account £350.00 - client section CR cash account £350.00 - client section DR cash account £350.00 - office section CR Garry's Gardening Limited ledger account £350.00 - office section Then pay the sum from the office bank account: DR Garry's Gardening Limited ledger account £500.00 - office section CR cash account £500.00 - office section

Pay the sum from the office bank account: DR Garry's Gardening Limited ledger account £500.00 - office section CR cash account £500.00 - office section Then deliver a bill of costs to the client for the difference: DR Garry's Gardening Limited ledger account £150.00 - office section CR profit costs account £150.00 - office section

Pay the sum from the office bank account: DR Garry's Gardening Limited ledger account £500.00 - office section CR cash account £ 500.00 - office section Then deliver a bill of costs to the client for the full amount: DR Garry's Gardening Limited ledger account £500.00 - office section CR profit costs account £500.00 - office section

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. You may withdraw money from the client account to reimburse, in full or in part, money spent by you on the client's behalf (Rule 20(1)(d)). Answer A is wrong because you do not hold sufficient funds on behalf of the client to pay the full amount from the client account. You would be using another client's money to cover the difference, breaching Rule 1(2)(c). Answer C is wrong because you have not yet made the payment for which the transfer from the client account is to reimburse. Therefore this amounts to an unauthorised withdrawal from the client account, breaching Rule 20. Answers D and E are wrong because you do not need to issue a bill of costs to the client as a requirement to recover the money, without using any of the money in the client account. As some money is held in the client account to cover the payment, you can use this and recover the outstanding amount in accordance with the terms of the retainer with your client.

stem: You act for Ethan. You receive and pay in a cheque for £6,250.00 representing payment for your fees having delivered a bill of costs. Five days later, you are advised that the cheque was dishonoured.
ask: Which of the following describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Record receipt and payment of the cheque into the client account (as this was client money): DR cash account £6,250.00 - client section CR Ethan's ledger account £6,250.00 - client section When informed that the cheque was dishonoured, reverse those entries: CR Ethan's ledger account £6,250.00 - client section DR cash account £6,250.00 - client section

Record receipt and payment of the cheque into the office account (as this was office money): DR cash account £6,250.00 - office section CR Ethan's ledger account £6,250.00 - office section When informed that the cheque was dishonoured, deliver another bill of costs for that amount: DR Ethan's ledger account £6,250.00 - office section CR profit costs account £6,250.00 - office section

Record receipt and payment of the cheque into the office account (as this was office money): DR cash account £6,250.00 - office section CR Ethan's ledger account £6,250.00 - office section When informed that the cheque was dishonoured, reverse those entries: DR Ethan's ledger account £6,250.00 - office section CR cash account £6,250.00 - office section

Record receipt and payment of the cheque into the client account (as this was client money): DR cash account £6,250.00 - client section CR Ethan's ledger account £6,250.00 - client section When informed that the cheque was dishonoured, deliver another bill of costs for that amount: DR Ethan's ledger account £6,250.00 - client section CR profit costs account £6,250.00 - client section

Record receipt and payment of the cheque into the office account (as this was office money): DR cash account £6,250.00 - office section CR Ethan's ledger account £6,250.00 - office section No further entries are required, as the debt will be paid on receipt of a correctly processed cheque

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Money received to pay for fees against which a bill of costs has been delivered is office money and should generally be paid into the office account (Rule 12(7)(c) (A), Rule 17(1)). A dishonoured cheque means that those funds are not available to the solicitor, and the client's debt remains, therefore the entries should be reversed (Rule 29). A is wrong because the money is office money, not client money, and should not be paid into the client account (Rule 14). B is wrong because you have not incurred additional work for which the client should be billed. This option would effectively mean the client owes you £12,500.00 instead of £6,250.00. D is wrong because the money is office money, not client money, and in any event you have not incurred additional work for which the client should be billed. E is wrong because these entries would erroneously show that the debt is satisfied, when it is not. You would not be keeping accurate accounts as required by Rule 29.

stem: You act for Betty and Catherine in separate matters. Catherine instructs you by telephone that the £150.00 you hold on her behalf in the general client account should be considered Betty's money. This is not a private loan.
ask: Which of the following describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Record a 'paper transfer', recording the date of the transfer, the sum and reason for transfer: Debit Catherine's ledger Credit Betty's ledger client account (£150.00)
No entries need to be made, because money is not being transferred between accounts
You cannot make this transfer as you do not have Catherine's written instructions

Record a 'paper transfer', recording the date of the transfer, the sum and reason for transfer: Debit Catherine's ledger Credit Betty's ledger client account (£150.00) Then withdraw the money to Betty: Debit Betty's ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£150.00)

Record a 'paper transfer', recording the date of the transfer, the sum and reason for transfer: Debit Catherine's ledger Credit Betty's ledger client account (£150.00) Then transfer the money to the office account: Debit Betty's ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£150.00) Debit cash sheet Credit Betty's ledger office account (£150.00)

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Whilst there is no withdrawal here (because it is re-designation of funds already held in the client account, the money is transferring ownership. Therefore, a paper transfer needs to be made to track the current position regarding client money you hold (Rule 27(1), Rule 29). Answer B is wrong. The money is transferring ownership from one client to another. You must record this on the ledger to comply with Rule 29, else you will have records showing that you still hold money for Catherine, which may lead to you breaching the Rules if you subsequently make a payment out of the client account on her behalf believing that you still hold that sum on her behalf. Answer C is wrong as this is not a transfer in respect of a private loan (Rule 27(2)). Answer D is wrong as you have not been instructed to withdraw the money for Betty, simply to transfer ownership. This withdrawal is not authorised and is a breach of Rule 20. Answer E is wrong because you have not been instructed to transfer the money to the office account, such as to pay an outstanding debt owed by Betty to the firm. This would be an unauthorised client withdrawal and a breach of Rule 20.

stem: On 5 June you sent a bill to your client for £1,000.00 plus VAT (£200.00). On 6 July you are informed that the client is declared bankrupt. You therefore decide to write off the client's debts.
ask: Which of the following represents the accounting entries you must make with respect to writing off your profit costs?

options.en: Debit the client's ledger account as against the bad debts expense account: DR client's ledger account £1,200.00 - office section CR bad debts £1,200.00 - office section
Debit the HMRC ledger as against the client's ledger account: DR HMRC ledger £1,000.00 - office section CR client's ledger account £1,000.00 - office section
