Debit the client's ledger account as against the cash account: DR client's ledger account £1,000.00 - office section CR cash account £1,000.00 - office section
Debit the profit costs ledger as against the client's ledger account: DR profit costs £11,200.00 - office section CR client's ledger account £1,200.00 - office section
Debit the bad debt expense ledger as against the client's ledger account: DR bad debts £1,200.00 - office section CR client's ledger account £1,200.00 - office section

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Debit the bad debt expense ledger as against the client's ledger account. Businesses will operate a separate 'bad debts' ledger for debts that are written off. This is important in order to differentiate between an abatement (which would be recorded in the profit costs ledger or a separate abatements ledger) and a write-off due to bad debts. When a bad debt is less than six months old, VAT relief cannot yet be claimed. Therefore, the full amount of the bad debt, including VAT, must be debited to the bad debts ledger and credited against the client's ledger account. No entries are made in the HMRC register. VAT can be claimed back when a bad debt is older than six months but not older than four years and six months.

stem: You have rendered a bill for £600.00 to your client. You have learned that your client is bankrupt, but that a payment of 25% in the £ will be received in full settlement of debts, with the remainder written off as a bad debt. Do not deal with the VAT element for the purposes of this question.
ask: Which of the following represents the accounting entries you should make in respect of writing off the debt?

options.en: Debit bad debts Credit client ledger office account (£450.00)
Debit bad debts Credit client ledger office account (£150.00)
Debit client ledger Credit bad debts office account (£450.00)
Debit client ledger Credit bad debts office account (£150.00)
Debit client ledger Credit bank ledger office account (£150.00)

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. A payment of 25% in the £ means that, of the £600.00 owed, you will recover £150.00, with the rest written off. You therefore debit the bad debts ledger with the £450.00 to be written off, and credit as against the client's ledger account.

stem: Six months ago, you wrote off a client's debt of £500.00 plus VAT (£100.00) owing to the client's bankruptcy. You are now eligible for VAT relief on the bad debt.
ask: Which of the following represents the accounting entries you should make to claim the VAT relief?

options.en: Debit the HMRC account as against the bad debts ledger: DR HMRC ledger £100.00 - office section CR bad debts £100.00 - office section
Debit the bad debts ledger as against the HMRC account: DR bad debts £100.00 - office section CR HMRC ledger £100.00 - office section
Debit the client's ledger account as against the bad debts account: DR client's ledger account £100.00 - office section CR bad debts £100.00 - office section
Debit the client's ledger account as against the HMRC account: DR client's ledger account £100.00 — office section CR HMRC ledger £100.00 - office section
Debit the profit costs ledger as against the HMRC ledger: DR profit costs ledger £100.00 - office section CR HMRC ledger £100.00 - office section

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Debit the HMRC account as against the bad debts ledger. Bad debts are considered an expense. A credit entry reduces the balance of an expense account. The HMRC account is a liability. A debit entry reduces the liability owed by the firm to the entity for whom that ledger is kept. HMRC requires that any VAT on which relief sought for bad debts be entered in separate bad debts ledger. Therefore, when you claim relief, you must show this in the HMRC ledger and the bad debts ledger.

stem: You rendered a bill for £800.00 plus VAT (£160.00) to your client two weeks ago. The client presents you with a cheque for £500.00 plus VAT (£100.00), and £600.00 in total, which you pay in, and tells you that is all he can afford as he is about to go to prison for five years. You agree to write off the remainder of the debt immediately.
ask: Which of the following represents the correct accounting entries you should make at this stage in respect of the bad debt?

options.en: Debit bad debts Credit client ledger office account (£960.000)
Debit bad debts Credit client ledger office account (£360.00)
Debit bad debts Credit client ledger office account (£300.00) Debit HMRC ledger Credit client ledger office account (£60.00)
Debit profit costs Credit client ledger office account (£360.00)
Debit bad debts Credit profit costs ledger office account (£360.00)

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. When making provision for bad debt which is less than 6 months old, you debit the bad debts ledger with the full amount that is to be written off, including the VAT amount, and record the credit entry in the client's ledger account. The amount to be written off is £300.00 plus VAT (£60.00) and £360.00 in total. The VAT can be claimed from HMRC when the bad debt is older than six months but not older than four years and six months.

stem: You send your client a bill for £600.00 plus VAT (£120.00). A few days later, after discussion with the client, you agree to reduce the bill by £80.00 plus VAT (£16.00).
ask: Which of the following represents the correct procedural position and the accounting entries that you should make in respect of the abatement?

options.en: Reduce the profit costs and HMRC ledgers respectively: DR profit costs ledger account £80.00 - office section CR client's ledger account £80.00 - office section DR HMRC ledger £16.00 - office section CR client's ledger £16.00 - office section
Reduce the amount from the profit costs ledger only: DR profit costs £96.00 - office section CR client's ledger account £96.00 - office section
Reduce the amount from the HMRC ledger only: DR HMRC ledger £96.00 - office section CR client's ledger account £96.00 - office section

Reverse the entries from the profit costs and HMRC ledgers respectively: DR profit costs ledger £600.00 - office section CR client's ledger account £600.00 - office section DR HMRC ledger £120.00 - office section CR client's ledger account £120.00 - office section
The VAT is recoverable by the firm, so reverse the total amount as against the profit costs ledger: DR profit costs ledger £600.00 - office section CR client's ledger account £600.00 - office section

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Reduce the profit costs and HMRC ledgers accordingly. These accounting entries are necessary to comply with Rule 29.1. If you reduced the entire amount in either the profit costs or HMRC ledger you would not be accurately accounting for your dealings with client money and would be in breach of Rule 29.1.

stem: You act for an insurance company. You bill the profit costs to the insurance company and the VAT to the corporate policyholder. After rendering a bill to the insurance company for £1,500.00 plus VAT (£300.00), the insurer questions the bill, and you agree to deduct £300.00 plus VAT (£60.00).
ask: Which of the following reflect the correct procedure and accounting entries to show the rendering of the bill and subsequent abatement?

options.en: Profit costs include VAT. The whole amount is rendered to the insurance company: DR insurance company ledger account £1,800.00 - office section CR profit costs ledger £1,800.00 - office section Abatement of profit costs and VAT recorded against insurance company ledger: DR profit costs ledger £360.00 - office section CR insurance company ledger £360.00 - office section

Bill of costs is rendered to insurance company: DR insurance company ledger account £1,500.00 - office section CR profit costs ledger £1,500.00 - office section VAT is rendered to policyholder: DR policyholder ledger account £300.00 - office section CR HMRC ledger £300.00 - office section Full abatement of profit costs recorded against insurance company's ledger: DR profit costs £1,500.00 - office section CR insurance company ledger account £1,500.00 - office section Abatement of VAT recorded against policyholder's ledger: DR HMRC ledger £300.00 - office section CR policyholder ledger account £300.00 - office section

Bill of costs is rendered to insurance company: DR insurance company ledger account £1,500.00 - office section CR profit costs ledger £1,500.00 - office section VAT is rendered to policyholder: DR policyholder ledger account £300.00 - office section CR HMRC ledger £300.00 - office section Profit costs only are abated against insurance company: CR insurance company ledger account £300.00 - office section DR profit costs ledger £300.00 - office section

Bill of costs is rendered to insurance company: DR insurance company ledger account £1,500.00 - office section CR profit costs ledger £1,500.00 - office section VAT is rendered to policyholder: DR policyholder ledger account £300.00 - office section CR HMRC ledger £300.00 - office section VAT only is abated against policyholder: CR policyholder ledger account £60.00 - office section DR HMRC ledger £60.00 - office section

Bill of costs is rendered to insurance company: DR insurance company ledger account £1,500.00 - office section CR profit costs ledger £1,500.00 - office section VAT is rendered to policyholder: DR policyholder ledger account £300.00 - office section CR HMRC ledger £300.00 - office section Abatement of profit costs recorded against insurance company's ledger: DR profit costs £300.00 - office section CR insurance company ledger account £300.00 - office section Abatement of VAT recorded against policyholder's ledger: DR HMRC ledger £60.00 - office section CR policyholder ledger account £60.00 - office section

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The profit costs are rendered to the insurance company, VAT to the policyholder and the respective abatements occur as against the respective parties' ledgers. This is because the policyholder, not the insurance company, is liable for VAT. To record otherwise would be a breach of Rule 29.1.

ask: Where do you record an abatement of fees where a firm doesn't keep a separate abatements ledger?

options.en: DR entries in the office section of the client ledger account and CR entries in the office section of the cash account
DR entries in the office section of the abatement of fees ledger account and CR entries in the office section of the profit costs ledger
DR entries in the office section of the profit costs account and CR entries in the client section of the office ledger account only
DR entries in the office section of the profit costs ledger and HMRC ledger and CR entries in the office section of the client ledger account
DR entries in the office section of the profit costs ledger and HMRC ledger and CR entries in the office section of the cash account

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. DR entries in the office section of the profit costs ledger and HMRC ledger and CR entries in the office section of the client ledger account. An abatement of fees is not a refund of cash. It is a set of entries that reduces the amount of the bill delivered to the client by the firm; a bill creating a liability of the client for the relevant profit costs and HMRC. Where there's an abatement of profit costs, there is a corresponding abatement of VAT, so entries must be made to reflect this in both the profit costs and HMRC ledgers.

stem: You receive a cheque for £500 on account of costs from your client. You pay the cheque into your client bank account the same day. The next day, you pay a court fee of £100.00 from the office bank account and made the appropriate accounting entries.
ask: The following day, the bank informs you that your client's cheque has been dishonoured Which of the following represents the correct procedural position and the accounting entries that you should make on being informed that the cheque is dishonoured?

options.en: You must reverse the entries made on receipt of the cheque: DR client ledger account £500.00 - client section CR cash account £500.00 - client section

You must first reverse the entries made on receipt of the cheque. You must then transfer £500.00 from the office bank account to the client bank account to make good the shortfall: DR client ledger account £500.00 - client section CR cash account £500.00 - client section DR client ledger account £500.00 - office section CR cash account £500.00 - office section DR cash account £500.00 - client section CR client ledger account £500.00 - client section

You must transfer £100.00 from the client bank account to the office bank account to make good the shortfall: DR client ledger account £100.00 - client section CR cash account £100.00 - client section DR cash account £100.00 - office section CR client ledger account £100.00 - office section

You must transfer £500.00 from the office bank account to the client bank account to make good the shortfall: DR client ledger account £500.00 - office section CR cash account £500.00 - office section DR cash account £500.00 - client section CR client ledger account £500.00 - client section

You must first reverse the entries made on receipt of the cheque. You must then transfer £100.00 from the office bank account to the client bank account to make good the shortfall: DR client ledger account £500.00 - client section CR cash account £500.00 - client section DR client ledger account £100.00 - office section CR cash account £100.00 - office section DR cash account £100.00 - client section CR client ledger account £100.00 - client section

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. You must reverse the entries made on receipt of the cheque. If you do not reverse the entries, you will be in breach of Rule 29.1, which requires that you must at all times keep accounting records properly written up to show your dealings with client money. No other entries are required. This is because the court fee was paid out of the office bank account and not the client account, so no other client's money was used. Therefore, your client simply owes the firm £100.00. The entries that would have been made at the time of the court fee being paid would have reflected the £100 increase in the client's debt to the firm. Reversing the entries in respect of the dishonoured cheque takes care of the requirement to reflect that the client still owes your firm £100.00.

stem: Your firm receives a cheque from your client for £1,000.00 on account of costs. You pay the money into the client bank account.
ask: What do the rules say in respect of drawing against uncleared cheques?

options.en: The rules say that you cannot draw against an uncleared cheque
The rules say that you must wait 2 working days before drawing against an uncleared cheque
The rules say that you must wait 5 working days before drawing against an uncleared cheque
The rules say that you must wait 14 days before drawing against an uncleared cheque
The rules do not prevent you from drawing against an uncleared cheque, but you should use discretion

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The rules do not prevent you from drawing against an uncleared cheque, but you should use discretion. There is no prohibition from drawing against uncleared cheques, but guidance note (iii) to Rule 20 cautions that discretion should be used, reminding you that, if the cheque is not met, other clients' money will have been used to make the payment in breach of the rules. However, you may be able to avoid a breach of the rules by instructing the bank or building society to charge all unpaid credits to your office or personal account.

stem: You hold £650.00 on account of costs from your client. Your client presents you with an additional cheque for £450.00 to increase monies held on account, which you pay in. The next day, you pay counsel's fees of £500.00 from the client bank account in respect of your client's matter. The following day, the bank advises you that your client's cheque has been dishonoured.
ask: Which of the following represents the correct procedural position and the accounting entries that you should make on being informed that the cheque is dishonoured?

options.en: No entries need to be made - you already hold sufficient funds for the client to meet counsel's disbursements
You need only reverse the entries made on receipt of the dishonoured cheque: DR client ledger account £450.00 - client section CR cash account £450.00 - client section

You must reverse the entries made on receipt of the dishonoured cheque then transfer £500.00 from the office to the client bank account to make up the shortfall: DR client ledger account £450.00 - client section CR cash account £450.00 - client section DR client ledger account £500.00 - office section CR cash account £500.00 - office section DR cash account £500.00 - client section CR client ledger account £500.00 - client section

You must reverse the entries made on receipt of the dishonoured cheque then transfer £50.00 from the office to the client bank account to make up the shortfall: DR client ledger account £450.00 - client section CR cash account £450.00 - client section DR client ledger account £50.00 - office section CR cash account £50.00 - office section DR cash account £50.00 - client section CR client ledger account £50.00 - client section

You need only transfer £50.00 from the office to the client account to make up the shortfall: DR client ledger account £50.00 - office section CR cash account £50.00 - office section DR cash account £50.00 - client section CR client ledger account £50.00 - client section

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. You need only reverse the entries made on receipt of the dishonoured cheque. If you do not reverse the entries, you will be in breach of Rule 29.1, which requires that you must at all times keep accounting records properly written up to show your dealings with client money. No other entries need be made, because you already held sufficient funds for the client when you made the payment to counsel. There is no breach of Rule 20.6 here so no need to make any transfer from the office to the client account.

stem: Your client Mr X instructs you to pay £75.00 to cover his printing charges in relation to a litigation matter. Your firm decides to pay this from the £100.00 for the weekly petty cash float that is first transferred from the office account. You hold £1,500.00 for Mr X on account of costs.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: For the petty cash transfer from the office account: Debit petty cash Credit cash sheet office account (£100.00) For the payment of Mr X's printing charges: Debit Mr X's ledger Credit petty cash sheet office account (£75.00)
Debit Mr X's ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£75.00)
For the petty cash transfer: Debit petty cash Credit cash sheet client account (£75.00) For the payment of Mr X's printing charges: Debit Mr X's ledger Credit petty cash sheet client account (£75.00)
Debit Mr X's ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£75.00)
For the petty cash transfer: Debit petty cash Credit cash sheet office account (£100.00) For the payment of Mr X's printing charges: Debit Mr X's ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£75.00)

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. At times, the payment of small expenses in the client's name can be made from "Petty Cash". Payment for these expenses is made from the petty cash float, which is drawn from the office bank account and not from the client bank account, even where the client has sufficient money in the account. You cannot use client money, even if the client has enough money to cover costs. You can, subsequently transfer the amount paid on behalf of the client from the client ledger account to the office ledger account, providing you comply with the Rules on how to withdraw money from the client ledger account (Rules 20(1)(c) and 21(3)). Answer B is not correct. The weekly petty cash float is not recorded and you are paying out of the client account when the payment is made out of petty cash. Answer C is incorrect because you cannot transfer a petty cash float - which may be used to expenses for different clients and belongs to clients - from the client account to the petty cash account. The potential mixing of client money with office money in this way is a breach of the obligation to keep other people's money separate from money belonging to the solicitor or practice (Rule 1(2)(a)). Answer D is not correct because it does not record the transfer of the weekly float and pays out of the office account. Answer E is incorrect because the expenses are paid out of the office account, not petty cash as the record should show.

stem: You represent Mr Galloway in his electoral fraud claim and deliver a bill of £300 plus £60.00 VAT on the 5th of November.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Debit Galloway's ledger Credit profit costs ledger client account (£300.00) Debit Galloway's ledger Credit HM Revenue & Customs ledger client account (£60.00)
Debit Galloway's ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£300.00) Debit Galloway's ledger Credit HM Revenue & Customs ledger office account (£60.00)
Debit Galloway's ledger Credit profit costs ledger office account (£360.00)
Debit Galloway's ledger Credit profit costs ledger office account (£300.00) Debit Galloway's ledger Credit HM Revenue & Customs ledger office account (£60.00)
Debit Galloway's ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£300.00) Debit Galloway's ledger Credit HM Revenue & Customs ledger client account (£60.00)

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. When a solicitor's office delivers a bill of costs to the client, this act is considered as a fee earned. The solicitor's office is merely informing Galloway of his debt owed. Client money is not involved, as fees/profit costs are considered office money, because they belong to the solicitor. The accounting entries in Answer D accurately reflect the creation of a debit in Galloway's client ledger account and the creation of a credit in the firm's profit costs ledger, as well as the recording of VAT charged on the bill of costs (output tax). A is wrong because the fees/profit costs should be recorded in the office section of the ledgers, not the client section. Fees/profit costs are not client money and should therefore not be recorded in the client sections of ledgers. B is wrong because the credit for profit costs is recorded in the cash account, not the profit costs ledger. See above. C is wrong because the profit costs and VAT are recorded as a single entry in the profit costs ledger. The VAT output tax needs to be recorded as a credit in the HM Revenue & Customs ledger, which accordingly requires a separate debit entry, which is in Galloway's ledger account - office section. E is wrong, because fees/profit costs are not client money and should therefore not be recorded in the client sections of ledgers. Further, the delivery of a bill of costs creates entries in the solicitor's profit costs ledger, not the cash ledger. Whilst the delivery of a bill of costs is considered income, no monies have been paid in as part of the act.

stem: You hold £50.00 in the general client account for a client on account of costs. You are asked by the client to pay £650.00 towards interpreter's fees, the invoice for which is addressed to the client.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Pay the invoice from the office account: Debit client ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£650.00) Record the VAT: Debit HM Revenue & Customs ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£130.00) Register a note in the client ledger that the firm has paid the interpreter's VAT and that this expense must be claimed from the client when sending him the bill of costs.

Pay the invoice from the client account: Debit client ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£650.00) Record the VAT: Debit HM Revenue & Customs ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£130.00) Register a note in the client ledger that the firm has paid the interpreter's VAT and that this expense must be claimed from the client when sending him the bill of costs.
Pay the invoice from the office account: Debit client ledger Credit cash sheet office account (£650.00)
You cannot make this payment until you receive a further £600.00 from the client
Pay the invoice from the client account: Debit client ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£650.00)

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The invoice is addressed to your client. Therefore you must use the agency method and claim the payment including VAT from the client when a bill of costs will be presented. Note that office money must be used to pay the disbursements, since there is insufficient money held on behalf of the client in the client account. Answers A and B are wrong as they pay the invoice using the principal method, which is used when the invoice is addressed to the firm. The invoice should be paid using the agency method as it is addressed to the client. Answer B is also wrong because it would pay the invoice out of the client account, but there is insufficient money held on behalf of the client in the client account. You would be using £600.00 of another client's money to pay the invoice for the client, a breach of Rule 1. Answer D is wrong because you can pay the invoice from the office account and include the amount on the bill of costs to deliver to the client. E is wrong because you would be using £600.00 of another client's money to pay the invoice for the client, a breach of Rule 1.

stem: You represent a woman and a bank. The woman owes the bank £1,000. You deliver your bill of costs of £500 to the bank, but transfer the debt to the woman.
ask: Which of the following options describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: CR bank's ledger account £500 - office section DR profit costs account £500 - office section CR client's ledger account (the client is the debtor) £500 - office section DR bank's ledger account (removing the debt from the bank account) £500 - office section

DR bank's ledger account £500 - office section CR profit costs account £500 - office section DR client's ledger account (the client is the debtor) £500 - office section CR bank's ledger account (removing the debt from the bank account) £500 - office section

DR bank's ledger account £500 - client section CR profit costs account £500 - client section DR client's ledger account (the client is the debtor) £500 - client section CR bank's ledger account (removing the debt from the bank account) £500 - client section

DR bank's ledger account £500 - office section CR profit costs account £500 - office section DR client's ledger account (the client is the debtor) £1000 - office section CR bank's ledger account (removing the debt from the bank account) £500 - office section

DR bank's ledger account £500 - client section CR profit costs account £500 - client section DR client's ledger account (the client is the debtor) £1000 - office section CR bank's ledger account (removing the debt from the bank account) £1000 - office section

explanation.en: Answer B is correct. The costs incurred by the bank are recorded in the office section. This is transferred to the client by way of a formal entry which records the transfer of the debt from the bank to the client. It remains in the office section. Answer A is incorrect because it indicates a debt owed to the bank and to the client. Answer C is incorrect as the debt is erroneously recorded in the client section rather than the office section. Answer D is incorrect because the entries transferring the debt from the bank to the client do not balance, and the client is shown as owing double of what the firm is entitled to. Answer E is incorrect because the initial debt is recorded in the client section, not the office section, and the client is shown as owing twice the amount that the firm is entitled to.

stem: The practice has just received £800 on behalf of its client on account of costs (which is client money). Later that day, the practice pays £750 on behalf of the client. One day later, you are informed that the cheque bounced.
ask: Which accounting entries best reflect the actions you should take and records you should make?

options.en: Within 14 days, transfer office money to the client account: DR client's ledger account £750.00 - office section CR cash account £750.00 - office section DR cash account £750.00 - client section CR cash account £750.00 - client section
Reverse the entries made on receipt of the cheque: DR client's ledger account £800.00 - client section CR cash account £800.00 - client section

Reverse the entries made on receipt of the cheque: DR client's ledger account £800.00 - client section CR cash account £800.00 - client section Make a memorandum entry in the cash account - client section that monies are outstanding and will be restored on clearing of the payment owed by the client

You must immediately transfer funds from the office account to the client account, reversing the entries made on receipt of the cheque: DR client's ledger account £800.00 - client section CR cash account £800.00 - client section Transfer office money to the client account: DR client's ledger account £800.00 - office section CR cash account £800.00 - office section DR cash account £800.00 - client section CR client's ledger account £800.00 - client section

You must immediately transfer funds from the office account to the client account, reversing the entries made on receipt of the cheque: DR client's ledger account £800.00 - client section CR cash account £800.00 - client section Transfer office money to the client account: DR client's ledger account £750.00 - office section CR cash account £750.00 - office section DR cash account £750.00 - client section CR client's ledger account £750.00 - client section

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Generally, note (v) to Rule 20 cautions against drawing against uncleared cheques. Because the cheque has bounced in this scenario, other clients' money will have been used to make the payment, in breach of Rule 1. Under Rule 7, a solicitor has a duty to remedy any breach of the rules promptly upon discovery. This includes the replacement of any money improperly withheld or withdrawn from a client account. You may pay office money into a client account to replace any money that has been withdrawn from the account in breach of Rule 20 (Rule 14(2)(c)). Answer E reflects the correct accounting entries that reflects the dishonoured cheque and transfers monies from the office account to the client account to remedy the breach. Answer A is wrong because whilst it transfers money from the office account to the client account to remedy the breach, the dishonoured cheque is not reflected in the accounts, a breach of Rule 29. Under Rule 7, a solicitor has a duty to remedy any breach of the rules promptly upon discovery. Answer B is wrong because, whilst it reverses the entries made on receipt of the cheque - thus restoring the debt owed by the client - it does not transfer money from the office account to the client account to remedy the breach. This omission is a breach of Rules 1, 7 29. Answer C is wrong because whilst it reverses the entries made on receipt of the cheque, it is not good enough to simply record that £750.00 is owed on the client account. Because the client's cheque has been dishonoured, other clients' money has been used to cover the payments on the client's behalf. This is a breach of Rule 1 and requires immediate remedy per Rule 7 - not a remedy only after receipt of a further cheque from the client. Answer D is wrong because it transfers £800.00 from the office account to the client account, where only £750.00 is needed to cover the breach. This payment is not permitted under Rule 14, specifically Rule 14(2)(c), because it exceeds the sum required to replace the amount drawn in breach of Rule 20.

stem: You receive a cheque of £200 which is made out to your client in respect of a settlement agreement that was signed between the client and his tenant.
ask: Which of the following options best describes the correct accounting entries?

options.en: Debit cash sheet Credit client ledger client account (£200) This is client money
Debit cash sheet Credit client ledger office account (£200) This is office money which will become client money once the settlement agreement has been signed
Debit cash sheet Credit client ledger client account (£200) This is neither office nor client money, but you must still record the entry in the client ledger's account
Debit cash sheet Credit client ledger client account (£200) This is client money but you cannot deposit it
This is neither client nor office money; no entries should be recorded

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Since the cheque is payable to the client and not to your firm, you cannot pay the cheque to the office account or to the client account. It is neither client nor office money and a double entry should not be made in this case. It is recommended, though, to place a memorandum note in the client's ledger account (note (iii) to Rule 29, Chapters 2 & 5).

stem: You act for a client who is selling a flat. You are given a deposit of £100,000 by the buyer, which you are to hold as stakeholder.
ask: Which of the following best reflects the correct reasoning and best accounting entries to process the money?

options.en: This is client money until it becomes the seller's on completion. It must be paid into the client account and the client's ledger account updated to reflect this: Debit cash sheet Credit client ledger client account (£100,000)

Even though this money is paid to you by the buyer, it is considered client money generally and you are holding it jointly for both parties as trustee. You must open a separate stakeholder ledger account to record the receipt of the cash, paid into the client account: Debit cash sheet Credit stakeholder ledger client account (£100,000)

This is client money. You must open a designated client account for this deposit and pay the money in: Debit client designated deposit ledger Credit client ledger (money on deposit) client account (£100,000)

Since this is client money but you are holding it as stakeholder, and will become the seller's money on completion, you should pay it into the office account: Debit cash sheet Credit client ledger client account (£100,000)

Even though this money is paid to you by the buyer, it is client money and you are holding it jointly for both parties as trustee. You may record receipt of the cash, paid into the client account, against any existing stakeholder ledger account: Debit cash sheet Credit stakeholder ledger client account (£100,000)

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Even though this money is paid to you by the buyer, it is considered client money generally and you are holding it jointly for both parties as trustee. You must open a separate stakeholder ledger account to record the receipt of the cash, paid into the client account. You are holding the money jointly for both parties and cannot release it to the seller without the buyer's authority - this is the default method in the Law Society Standard Conditions of Sale. Since it is neither the buyer nor the seller's money at this stage, you would open a separate stakeholder ledger account to accurately record your dealings with the money and comply with Rules 29.1 and 29.2. A is wrong. Because you are holding it as stakeholder, ie. as trustee, it belongs to neither client at this stage. Recording the money in a client ledger account inappropriately deals with the money as belonging to a client, which would breach Rule 29.1. A stakeholder ledger account makes it clear of the capacity in which you are holding the money. C is wrong because you are not holding the money for one client only. Creating a designated deposit account is not a proper or accurate way of dealing with the money, and you would be in breach of Rule 29.1. D is wrong because under Rule 12.2 of the SRA Accounts Rules, money held as agent is client money. Under Rule 14.1, client money must without delay be paid into a client account and must be held in a client account. The exemptions to this Rule do not apply in these circumstances. Under Rule 29.2, all dealings with client money must be appropriately recorded in a client cash account. To pay the money into the office account, therefore, would have you in breach of the Accounts Rules. E is wrong because Rule 29.2 clearly states that all dealings with client money must be appropriately recorded on the client side of a separate client ledger account for each client or person on trust. To record all stakeholder deposits for all clients in one stakeholder ledger would be a clear breach of this rule.

stem: You have been holding £75,000 as stakeholder for parties involved in a property transaction. Completion has just been effected.
ask: Which of the following best reflects the correct reasoning and best accounting entries to process the money held as stakeholder?

options.en: As soon as the completion is effected, the money is held for the seller alone and is no longer held on trust for both parties jointly. A transfer between the client ledger accounts should be recorded: Debit stakeholder ledger Credit seller's ledger client account (£75,000)
The money held as stakeholder is paid out to the seller: Debit stakeholder ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£75,000)
The money held as stakeholder is paid out to the buyer: Debit stakeholder ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£75,000)
The completion does not affect the status of the stakeholder money, so no accounting entries need to be made

As soon as the completion is effected, the money is held for the seller alone and is no longer held on trust for both parties jointly. The money must be transferred to a designated deposit account for the seller and entries made in the designated deposit account, cash account, stakeholder and client ledgers: Debit seller's designated deposit ledger Credit cash sheet client account (£75,000) Debit stakeholder ledger Credit seller's ledger (money on deposit) client account (£75,000)

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. As soon as the completion is effected, the money is held for the seller alone and is no longer held on trust for both parties jointly. A transfer between the client ledger accounts should be recorded. Note that no money has actually physically transferred between accounts - these entries reflect the fact that the solicitor's role as stakeholder has ended and that the money now belongs to the seller alone. B is wrong because, whilst completion means that the solicitor no longer holds the money as stakeholder, it does not automatically mean that all monies held by the solicitor for the seller are immediately paid out, however they are held. This answer would involve two sets of entries on two separate ledgers to reflect the payments from the cash account - one for the £75,000 held as stakeholder and the other for the balance of the purchase price as recorded in the seller's ledger. Further, this answer would, on paper, involve a solicitor paying to one party money held on trust for both parties, without accurate records to show that, on completion, the seller then held the money. This would not be an accurate record of dealings with client monies or sums transferred between client ledger accounts, in breach of Rules 29.1 and 29.2. C is wrong for the reasons above, and because the money is paid to the seller, not the buyer! D is wrong because the effect of completion is that the money is no longer held by the solicitor on trust jointly for the parties. A paper transfer to reflect that the money now belongs to the seller is required. E is wrong because it is not mandatory for money that is no longer held as stakeholder to be transferred to a separate designated deposit account for the seller - the same can remain in the client account with a simple paper transfer reflecting the status of the money following completion.

stem: Madeleine sustained serious injuries in a road traffic accident resulting in permanent injury, ongoing loss of earnings and permanent need for care. Her likely compensation has been assessed in excess of £100,000. The other party is contesting liability.
ask: Which track is the most suitable for Madeleine to commence proceedings?

options.en: Proceedings should commence in the County Court and be transferred to the High Court
Proceedings should commence in the County Court
Proceedings should commence in the High Court
Proceedings should commence in the Magistrates' Court because it involves traffic matters
Proceedings should commence in the Crown Court because personal injury is involved

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Litigation by a victim following a road traffic collision will be a civil action rather than a criminal prosecution, although it is possible that the police could also prosecute. The civil action by the victim would therefore take place in the civil courts, which means the County Court or High Court. As the case is estimated to involve over £50,000, and involve complex contested issues, it would likely commence in the High Court. The threshold for actions can be reviewed through rules of court procedure, and litigants should ensure that they commence in the correct court.

ask: Which of the following is the first point of reference for the purpose of statutory interpretation?

options.en: The Purposive rule
Reference to Parliamentary debates
The Golden rule
The Literal rule
Reference to interpretation sections of the statute

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The interpretation of statutes starts with relying on literal meaning. Only when this creates a fallacy or an absurdity do we move the procedure forward. The next stage is to consider the whole of the statute together, the Golden rule, unless this produces some inconsistencies. At this stage, the Purposive rule is applied. The purpose behind the statute is sought to be construed. The interpretation sections or the explanatory notes in statutes are secondary aids to construction. The use of Hansard is regulated by Pepper v. Hart (1992). Pepper v. Hart has had somewhat of a rise and fall. Typically now, Hansard would only be consulted de bene esse (for what it's worth).

ask: Which of the following court does bind itself?

options.en: County Court
House of Lords
Court of Appeal
High Court
Judicial Committee of the Privy Council

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The Court of Appeal binds itself. Three exceptions to this are noted in Young v. Bristol Aeroplane Co. Ltd. (1994). The Court may choose between two of its own conflicting decisions. Where the Supreme Court of the UK overrides any Court of Appeal decision, either impliedly or explicitly, the Court of Appeal need not remain bound. The Court of Appeal may ignore decisions per incuriam, those decisions made in ignorance of existing authority, which are faulty due to ignorance. None of the other Courts bind themselves. The House of Lords is effectively replaced by the Supreme Court of the UK, by the operation of the Constitutional Reform Act 2005.

ask: Which of the following methods may be used generally by any court to avoid applying a previous precedent?

options.en: Following an obiter dictum in the previous decision
Following the ratio decidendi in the previous decision
Distinguishing the precedent
Referencing the precedent
None of the above

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Where a judge notes that the facts of a precedent were different from the facts in the present case, he effectively steps away from any obligation of applying the precedent. This is known as "distinguishing" the precedent. If the Court considering the precedent has higher precedential authority as per the doctrine of stare decisis, it may overrule the precedent and thus proceed without considering it. Obiter dicta may be noted and used to support the ratio in the present case, but it cannot be followed. Obiter dicta means, roughly, 'things noted by the way.' Examples, explanations, further details....are all obiter dicta. Where the ration decidendi is applied, the precedent has been applied. Ratio decidendi means, roughly, the 'staircase of reasoning.' This is the reasoning followed by the judge is laying out his decision. It is the kernel around which the case revolves. Referencing the precedent, without either applying, distinguishing or overruling it, is sloppy writing. This is occasionally done, but it is bad practice.

ask: Which of the following is the ratio decidendi of a case?

options.en: The judgment
The comments made by the judge in relation to the facts of the case
Explanations, illustrations and metaphors
The rule of law arising from the material facts of the case
The decision

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Ratio decidendi is the reasoning used by the judge in arriving at his judgment. Facts are unique and reasoning is transferable. Hence, the reasoning of the judge is also the rule of law arising from the judgment.

stem: Tony's wife made allegations of serious sexual assault against him. He was arrested by the police and charged with the offence of rape. His solicitor has informed Tony that this offence is triable only on indictment.
ask: In which court must Tony's trial take place in?

options.en: The Crown Court
The County Court
The Magistrates' Court
The High Court
The Divisional Court

explanation.en: A is correct. Triable only on indictment offences must be tried in the Crown Court. Rape is a serious offence that can only be tried on indictment, so Tony's trial will be heard in the Crown Court before of a judge and jury. If Tony pleads guilty, however, a jury would not be convened and a judge sitting alone will pass sentence, after hearing the submissions from the prosecution and mitigation in defence. Statute; rule; constitution: Sexual Offences Act 2003.

stem: Tessa, aged 25, was accused by the manager of Trendy Toes shoe shop of shoplifting. She was subsequently charged with theft of a pair of shoes valued at £16. Her solicitor has advised Tessa that shoplifting is an offence which is triable either-way, and she can elect one of two courts in which to stand trial.
ask: Which options will Tessa's solicitor have presented for her to elect to stand trial in?

options.en: The Crown Court or the High Court
The County Court or the Crown Court
The County Court or the Magistrates' Court
The solicitor has given wrong advice; this is a summary offence
The Crown Court or the Magistrates' Court

explanation.en: E is correct. A triable either way offence may be tried in either the Crown Court or the magistrates' court. In English criminal law a hybrid offence is called a "triable-either-way offence" and can be heard at either the Magistrates' Court or Crown Court. The decision as to which court will hear the case is determined at a Mode of Trial hearing.

stem: Rupert was seriously injured in an accident caused by the negligence of Kirstin. Rupert was awarded £150,000 damages by the High Court, which is far less than he was hoping for and plans to appeal.
ask: Which option best states the most appropriate forum for Rupert's appeal?

options.en: The most appropriate forum for Rupert to appeal is the Supreme Court
The most appropriate forum for Rupert to appeal is the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council
The most appropriate forum for Rupert to appeal is the European Court of Human Rights
The most appropriate forum for Rupert to appeal is the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division)
The most appropriate forum for Rupert to appeal is the Court of Appeal (Civil Division)

explanation.en: E is correct. The Queen's Bench Division is generally the most appropriate forum to hear complex personal injury cases. The Court of Appeal (Civil Division) is practically the only place where standard appeals of this nature can go, since appeals from the High Court are made, in most cases, to the Court of Appeal (Civil Division).

stem: The Supreme Court is hearing an appeal. There is a previous precedent on the same issue from the House of Lords (formerly the Appellate Committee of the House of Lords) in 1902.
ask: Which options are open to the Supreme Court judges in this situation?

options.en: If the Supreme Court feels it has erred, it must refer the matter to Parliament to change the law prospectively rather than undo its mistake with retrospective effect
The Supreme Court is bound by its previous decisions
The Supreme Court can depart from its previous decision if it feels it is right to do so
The Supreme Court is bound by its previous decisions, but only from the time it replaced the Appellate Committee of the House of Lords as the court of final resort in the UK
The Supreme Court may overrule its own previous decisions if there is a consensus among the other branches of the Courts of Appeal

explanation.en: C is correct. The Law Lords may decide to depart from their own previous decisions. This power is used sparingly. Please note the technical distinction between departing from a decision and overruling it; a mere legal nicety. Lead case: A v Hoare [2008] UKHL 6; [2008] 1 AC 844.

stem: A case comes before the Supreme Court. There are two previous conflicting precedents, one from the Supreme Court (previously called the Appellate Committee of the House of Lords) in 1935 and the other from the Privy Council decided in 1936.
ask: Which statement is the most accurate reflection of which precedent the Supreme Court should follow?

options.en: The Supreme Court must either follow its own past decision or follow the persuasive authority of the Privy Council
The Supreme Court is bound by its previous decision from 1935
The Supreme Court is bound by its previous decisions, but only from the time it replaced the Appellate Committee of the House of Lords as the court of final resort in the UK
The Supreme Court may depart from its own past decision, may choose to follow the persuasive authority of the Privy Council or it may follow its own previous decision
The Supreme Court is bound by the decision of the Privy Council, because that is the most recent one

explanation.en: D is correct. All options are open to the Supreme Court in this context. It may choose its own course. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council is the court of final appeal for the UK overseas territories and Crown dependencies. Its decisions have persuasive value.

stem: The Abortion Act 1967 stipulated that a pregnancy should be terminated by a registered medical practitioner. Subsequent advancements in medical techniques led to non- registered medical practitioners, such as nurses, who were perfectly able to perform these procedures, without the presence of a registered medical practitioner. In a case brought before the court, the majority found that a nurse's involvement in carrying out an abortion procedure was not unlawful, because in their opinion, the purpose for which Parliament enacted the statute was to remedy the unsatisfactory state of the law before 1967 and to make abortions more accessible to women.
ask: Which rule of statutory interpretation did the majority use in this example?

options.en: The Golden Rule
The Literal Rule
The Mischief Rule
Hansard
The Unified Common Approach

explanation.en: C is correct. The judges in the majority based their decision on the mischief rule, pointing out that the mischief Parliament was trying to remedy was the unsatisfactory state of the law before 1967 and the number of dangerous illegal abortions. Lead case: Royal College of Nursing v DHSS [1981] 1 AIl ER 545.

stem: A prisoner was involved in an incident in his cell which resulted in him sustaining personal injuries. Likely damages have been assessed at less than £25,000. The injured prisoner's claim requires the calling of a number of witnesses involves complicated issues of law and raises a real point of public importance.
ask: Which would be the most appropriate venue to allocate the prisoner's case to under these circumstances?

options.en: The most appropriate venue to allocate the prisoner's case to would be the County Court - small claims track
The most appropriate venue to allocate the prisoner's case to would be the County Court - fast track
The most appropriate venue to allocate the prisoner's case to would be the County Court - multi-track
The most appropriate venue to allocate the prisoner's case to would be the High Court - multi-track
The most appropriate venue to allocate the prisoner's case to would be the Court of Appeal (civil division)

explanation.en: D is the best answer. A complex claim, in which quantum is assessed as being less than £25,000, but which involves the calling of numerous witnesses or complicated issues of law will naturally, be allocated to the multi-track in the High Court. Even cases where no money may be at stake, but which raise points of real public importance are most appropriately allocated to the multi-track procedure.

stem: The civil procedure rules are designed to ensure that cases are dealt with proportionately to the value of the claim and the costs involved and with the parties, on an equal footing. It is this idea which underlies the whole concept of having a track allocation procedure with limited costs recoverable from the unsuccessful party.
ask: What is the ethos that the court is required to give effect to when allocating a case to its appropriate track?

options.en: The court is required to give effect to the obiter dicta of an English court
The court is required to give effect to the ratio decidendi of an English court
The court is required to give effect to a per incuriam decision of an English court
The court is required to give effect to the balance of probabilities
The court is required to give effect to the overriding objective

explanation.en: E is correct. Part of the "overriding objective" of the Civil Procedure Regulations 1998 is to ensure that cases are dealt with proportionately to the value of the claim and the costs involved and with the parties, on an equal footing. It is this idea which underlies the whole concept of having a fast track with limited costs recoverable from the unsuccessful party. Statute; rule; constitution: CPR, r. 1.1.

stem: Jury service is an important civic duty. It is not an easy task, however, involving hours of waiting to be called; starting to hear a trial, only for it to be aborted; or hours of legal argument. It can also involve the most gruesome of crimes, or highly technical and complex evidence.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes jury service selection policy?

options.en: Everyone on the electoral register from the ages of 18 to 65 may be selected, provided they have been ordinarily resident in the UK, for at least 5 years, since the age of 13
Everyone on the electoral register from the ages of 18 to 75 may be selected, provided they have been ordinarily resident in the UK, for at least 5 years, since the age of 16
Everyone on the electoral register from the ages of 21 to 70 may be selected, provided they have been ordinarily resident in the UK, for at least 5 years, since the age of 16
Everyone on the electoral register from the ages of 18 to 70 may be selected, provided they have been ordinarily resident in the UK, for at least 5 years, since the age of 18
Everyone on the electoral register from the ages of 18 to 75 may be selected, provided they have been ordinarily resident in the UK, for at least 5 years, since the age of 13

explanation.en: E is correct. Only certain people may be eligible for being jurors. Anyone who is eligible to be called as a juror may be called. There are circumstances in which they may then be released but these are limited to extreme situations in order to ensure that selection is as varied as possible. Eligibility criteria includes those between the ages of 18 and 75 and been resident in the UK for at least 5 years since the age of 13. Note: The upper age limit for jury service will rose to 75 by section 68 of the Criminal Justice and Courts Act 2015. Statute; rule; constitution: Criminal Justice Act 2003 and Juries Act 1974.

stem: Juries are most commonly found in the Crown Court, where they decide a verdict. In a typical trial, the jurors will hear a case presented by the prosecution and the defence and then the judge's summing-up. The jury members will then retire to a private room to consider a verdict, and decide if the defendant is guilty or not guilty.
ask: Which of the following is the best expression of how a jury is eligible to reach its verdict?

options.en: A majority verdict generally means that a verdict of either 10-1 or 11-1 will be acceptable
A majority verdict generally means that a verdict of either 10-2 or 11-2 will be acceptable
A majority verdict generally means that a verdict of either 10-2 or 11-1 will be acceptable
A majority verdict generally means that a verdict of either 11-2 or 11-1 will be acceptable
A jury must come to a unanimous verdict

explanation.en: C is correct. If...no verdict is forthcoming, the judge may recall the jury and instruct the jury members that they may consider a majority verdict. This generally means that a verdict of either 10-2 or 11-1 will be acceptable. In the event that one or more jury member dies or is discharged during the course of the trial, a majority verdict of 10-1 or 9-1 would be acceptable. If the jury is reduced to the minimum number of 9 members, only a unanimous verdict would be acceptable. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 17 of the Juries Act 1974.

stem: Trustees failed to take into account potential tax consequences that they should have when entering into a deed. The trustees applied to the court to set aside the deed of appointment as void rather than merely voidable.
ask: Which Court would most likely have jurisdiction in this dispute?

options.en: The Magistrates' Court would most likely have jurisdiction in this dispute
The Chancery Division would most likely have jurisdiction in this dispute
The Family Division would most likely have jurisdiction in this dispute
The Queen's Bench Division would most likely have jurisdiction in this dispute
The Crown Court would most likely have jurisdiction in this dispute

explanation.en: B is correct. The Chancery Division is principally concerned with claims arising under contracts for land, (conveyancing disputes, rectification of deeds); matters relating to trusts and the administration of estates of dead people.

stem: Loraine has been charged with shoplifting after she was arrested for stealing law books from her university book shop. She must appear in court charged with this offence.
ask: What is the burden of proof required in Loraine's case?

options.en: The burden of proof required in Loraine's case is for guilt to be proven on a balance of reasonable doubt
The burden of proof required in Loraine's case is for guilt to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt
The burden of proof required in Loraine's case is for guilt to be proven on a balance of probabilities
The burden of proof required in Loraine's case is for guilt to be proven beyond a balance of probabilities
The burden of proof required in Loraine's case is for guilt to be proven beyond no doubt

explanation.en: B is correct. The prosecution has the legal burden of convincing the fact finder of Loraine's guilt beyond reasonable doubt (the criminal standard).

stem: Two months after a case was decided in the Court of Appeal, another case with very similar facts came before the High Court. The judge in the case says he is bound to follow the decision in the previous case.
ask: Which of the following is the legal doctrine which the High Court judge must follow?

options.en: The legal doctrine which the High Court judge must follow is ratio decidendi
The legal doctrine which the High Court judge must follow is res ipsa loquitur
The legal doctrine which the High Court judge must follow is stare decisis
The legal doctrine which the High Court judge must follow is Magna Carta
The legal doctrine which the High Court judge must follow is ejusdem generis

explanation.en: C is correct. The doctrine of judicial precedent involves an application of the principle of stare decisis, i.e. to stand by what has already been decided

stem: A court referred to the proper construction in a word. It held that a statute had no application to the case of betting carried on upon a race-course during the actual progress of a race meeting whether or not such betting took place within or without doors or in any particular "house, office, room or other place," so long as it was within the boundaries of the race course.
ask: Under which legal doctrine does the phrase "house, office, room or other place," fall under?

options.en: The phrase falls under the legal doctrine of obiter dicta
The phrase falls under the legal doctrine of the stare decisis
The phrase falls under the legal doctrine of per incuriam
The phrase falls under the legal doctrine of ejusdem generis
The phrase falls under the legal doctrine of ratio decidendi

explanation.en: D is correct. The ejusdem generis doctrine refers to a series of particular words is used followed by general words (e.g. 'house, office, room... or other place'), the general words must be construed with reference to the particular words.

stem: Justice Garner looked at several older cases. He noted that one case in particular seemed of importance to him and referred to the doctrine of binding precedent.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes why Justice Garner would be bound by the decision of the previous court?

options.en: Justice Garner would be bound by the decision of the previous court under the doctrine of ejusdem generis
Justice Garner would be bound by the decision of the previous court if the previous case contained an obiter dicta statement
Justice Garner would be bound by the decision of the previous court if it was a per incuriam decision
Justice Garner would be bound by the decision of the previous court if it was a decision of a higher court
Justice Garner would be bound by the decision of the previous court if it was a case that has been distinguished

explanation.en: D is correct. The doctrine of binding precedent states that any previous decision of a higher court it is binding on a judge who is dealing with a subsequent case where the facts are of sufficient similarity to the previous case.

stem: Justice Smith noted that, Justice Jones sitting alone in the High Court, had in his thorough judgment of the case described the events with meticulous care. In those circumstances, remarked Justice Smith, it was not necessary for him to rehearse the factual background in detail.
ask: Assuming he was sitting alone as a High Court judge, (and assuming that the case cannot be distinguished), which statement best describes the binding effect, if any, of Justice Jones' judgment?

options.en: Justice Jones' judgment is only binding on other High Court judges sitting alone
Justice Jones' judgment is only binding on a County Court judge
Justice Jones' judgment is binding on the bench in a Divisional Court of the High Court
Justice Jones' judgment is binding on the Chancery Division of the High Court of Justice
Justice Jones' judgment is binding on the Court of Appeal (Civil Division)

explanation.en: B is correct. A single High Court judge is bound by decisions of higher courts including the Divisional Courts of his Division, but (technically) not by a decision of another High Court judge sitting alone (although he would treat it as strong persuasive authority). Only the County Court judge is lower in the hierarchy therefore.

stem: Justice Smith, sitting alone in a case in the Queen's Bench Division, referred approvingly to several previous cases, which he said were 'on all fours' with the case at hand. The cases he referred to were from: a bench of the Queen's Bench Division, a bench of the Chancery Court, a bench of the Family Division and the High Court of Justiciary in Scotland.
ask: Which case would have the persuasive authority?

options.en: None of the cases referred to by Justice Smith would be persuasive
The case with persuasive authority is from the Chancery Court
The case with persuasive authority is from the Family Division
The case with persuasive authority is from the High Court of Justiciary in Scotland
The case with persuasive authority is from the Queen's Bench Division

explanation.en: D is correct. Since the decisions from: the Queen's Bench Division, the Chancery Court and the Family Division were not from a judge sitting alone; these decisions are binding on a judge sitting alone in the High Court. A decision by the High Court of Justiciary in Scotland would only have persuasive effect.

stem: A defendant was convicted of the summary offence of common assault in the Magistrates' Court following a plea of not guilty. He disputes his conviction and wishes to appeal.
ask: What is the most appropriate method, if any, for the defendant to appeal his conviction?

options.en: The most appropriate method for the defendant to appeal his conviction in the Magistrates' Court is by way of appeal to the Crown Court
The most appropriate method for the defendant to appeal his conviction in the Magistrates' Court is by way of appeal to the Court of Appeal (Civil Division)
The most appropriate method for the defendant to appeal his conviction in the Magistrates' Court is by way of appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division)
The most appropriate method for the defendant to appeal his conviction in the Magistrates' Court is by way of appeal to the Magistrates' Court
There is no right of appeal from the Magistrates' Court for summary only offences such as common assault

explanation.en: A is correct. A defendant who has been convicted in the magistrates' court following a plea of not guilty may appeal against either conviction or sentence, or both, to the Crown Court. However, a defendant who pleaded guilty can normally only appeal their sentence. Note: Difference between convicted and sentenced - If a defendant is convicted that means they are found guilty of a crime by jury or judge. After a defendant is convicted, they are sentenced, which means the judge or jury decide what punishment is appropriate.

stem: Where the court finds that the current dispute is fundamentally distinct from all previous cases, judges have the authority and duty to make law by creating precedent. Thereafter, the new decision becomes precedent, and will bind future courts.
ask: Which is the best description of the process where the court finds that the current dispute is fundamentally distinct from all previous cases?

options.en: Where the court finds that the current dispute is fundamentally distinct from all previous cases, it is called obiter dicta
Where the court finds that the current dispute is fundamentally distinct from all previous cases, it is called stare decisis
Where the court finds that the current dispute is fundamentally distinct from all previous cases, it is called the overriding objective
Where the court finds that the current dispute is fundamentally distinct from all previous cases, it is called the West Lothian question
Where the court finds that the current dispute is fundamentally distinct from all previous cases, it is called a matter of first impression

explanation.en: E is correct. If the court finds that the current dispute is fundamentally distinct from all previous cases (called a "matter of first impression"), judges have the authority and duty to make law by creating precedent.

stem: A defendant was convicted on indictment in the Crown Court. He would like to appeal the jury's decision on a mixed question of fact and law.
ask: What is the most appropriate method, if any, for the defendant to appeal his conviction?

options.en: The most appropriate method for the defendant to appeal his conviction in the Crown Court is by way of appeal to the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court
The most appropriate method for the defendant to appeal his conviction in the Crown Court is by way of appeal to the Supreme Court
The most appropriate method for the defendant to appeal his conviction in the Crown Court is by way of appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division)
The most appropriate method for the defendant to appeal his conviction in the Crown Court is by way of appeal to the Magistrates' Court
There is only a right of appeal from the Crown Court on a question of law; not mixed questions of fact and law

explanation.en: C is correct. A person convicted on indictment may appeal to the Court of Appeal against his conviction and/or sentence in the Crown Court.

stem: Parliament may delegate to another authority the power to make rules and regulations in an area where parliamentary language is general. These rules have the force of law.
ask: Which of the following is a form of delegated legislation?

options.en: Acts of Parliament are a form of delegated legislation
Conventions are a form of delegated legislation
Statutory Instruments are a form of delegated legislation
Representation Orders are a form of delegated legislation
Treaties are a form of delegated legislation

explanation.en: C is correct. Delegated or subordinate legislation is made by ministers (regulations in the form of so-called 'statutory instruments') and other bodies outside of central government (e.g. local authority bye-laws).

stem: A solicitor should always consider, at first interview, whether it may be possible to negotiate a settlement, directly, with the opponent - and without the use of the courts and the legal process or any other form of intermediary - instead of incurring the expense of issuing legal proceedings. More often than not, Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) may settle such matters without civil litigation.
ask: In which ADR mechanism will a third party decide the outcome?

options.en: Conciliation and negotiated settlement are the ADR mechanisms whereby a third-party decides the outcome
Mediation and arbitration are the ADR mechanisms whereby a third-party decides the outcome
Conciliation and mediation are the ADR mechanisms whereby a third-party decides the outcome
Arbitration is the ADR mechanism whereby a third-party decides the outcome
Mediation is the ADR mechanism whereby a third-party decides the outcome

explanation.en: D is correct. In both conciliation and mediation, the parties must attempt to reach a mutual decision. In conciliation, a third party will attempt to assist them to achieve this. It is only in arbitration that the third party - the arbitrator or arbitration panel - reaches a decision.

stem: Lay magistrates' (also called Justices of the Peace) training is based on competences. These are essentially a description of what a magistrate needs to know and needs to be able to do so that he/or she can fulfil the role. Competences include a checklist of observable behaviour and level of knowledge magistrates will need to demonstrate.
ask: Which one of the following statements is most appropriate when describing lay magistrates?

options.en: Lay magistrates are legally qualified but are advised on points of law, practice and procedure by a legally qualified or experienced court clerk
Magistrates are not legally qualified but have the benefit of a legal adviser in court
Lay magistrates are properly qualified solicitors who sit as part time judges at the Magistrates' Court
Lay magistrates are properly qualified barristers who sit as part time judges at the Magistrates' Court
Lay magistrates are drawn from those with professional backgrounds such as solicitors or doctors, but bus drivers, mechanics, the unemployed and the like may not serve on the magistrates' bench

explanation.en: B is correct. Magistrates are not legally qualified but are continually trained and have the benefit of a legal adviser in court.

stem: The unity and consistency of the common law were sustained by the early dominant position acquired by the royal courts. While the former Saxon king's council dealt only with great affairs of state, the succeeding Norman court assumed wide judicial powers. Its judges declared the common law.
ask: Which of the following statement is the most accurate with regards to common law in the English legal system?

options.en: Common law is a legal system that gives great precedential weight to common law on the principle that it is fair to treat different facts similarly on different occasions
Common law is an equitable system that gives great precedential weight to common law on the principle that it is unfair to treat similar facts similarly on different occasions
Common law is a legal system that gives great precedential weight to common law on the principle that it is more fair to treat similar facts differently on different occasions
Common law is a legal system that gives great precedential weight to common law on the principle that it is unfair to treat similar facts differently on different occasions
Common law is a legal system that gives great precedential weight to common law on the principle that it is unfair to treat different facts similarly on different occasions

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. A "common law system" is a legal system that gives great precedential weight to common law on the principle that it is unfair to treat similar facts differently on different occasions. Thus when a judge decided a new problem in a case brought before him, this became a new rule of law and was followed by subsequent judges. In later times this practice crystallised into the form which is known as the binding force of judicial precedent, and the judges felt bound to follow previous decisions instead of merely looking to them for guidance. By these means the common law earned the status of a system.

stem: Historically, rules concerning situations under law were categorised as legal or equitable. The common law developed a system whereby seeming contradictory rights existed within the same structure. In this respect, equitable remedies are separate from common law remedies.
ask: Which of the following statement best describes a principle of Equity?

options.en: Equitable remedies work mainly by forcing a person to do something
Where the common law and equity conflict, the common law shall prevail
Those who come to equity may come with 'unclean hands'
Equitable remedies are rarely directed at a particular person
Equitable remedies are available to a successful claimant as of right

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Remedies at law are generally paid in some amount of money whereas equitable remedies result in a court ordering one party to do or not do some action, e.g., an injunction.

stem: The 'mischief' rule is derived from precedent in which it was resolved that four matters had to be considered in considering what 'mischief' the statute was intended to remedy. These are: (1) what the common law was, before the statute was passed; (2) what the mischief and defect was which was not remedied by the common law; (3) what remedy is given by the present statute; and (4) the true reason for the remedy.
ask: Which one of the following represents another name used to refer to the mischief rule?

options.en: Another name used to refer to the mischief rule is the Golden Rule
Another name used to refer to the mischief rule is the rule in Heydon's case
Another name used to refer to the mischief rule is the Defect Rule
Another name used to refer to the mischief rule is the Ejusdem Generis Rule
Another name used to refer to the mischief rule is the Literal Rule

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. The "mischief" rule is a departure from the foregoing two rules, in that it concentrates not solely on the words of the statute, but on the purpose for which Parliament enacted the statute. It is derived from Heydon's Case (1584). Lead case: Heydon's Case (1584).

stem: Justice Wilbersteyn was trying to find Parliament's intention behind the recently introduced Red Squirrel Hunting Act. Unfortunately the wording of the Act was ambiguous where it stated, 'the unspeakable in pursuit of the inedible'. He decided, therefore, to resort to intrinsic aids to help with his interpretation.
ask: Which of the following would Justice Wilbersteyn most likely have used as an intrinsic aid for this purpose?

options.en: Justice Wilbersteyn would most likely have used the Act's Preamble as an intrinsic aid to help with his interpretation
Justice Wilbersteyn would most likely have used a dictionary as an intrinsic aid to help with his interpretation
Justice Wilbersteyn would most likely have used other legislative history as an intrinsic aid to help with his interpretation
Justice Wilbersteyn would most likely have used previous case law as an intrinsic aid to help with his interpretation
Justice Wilbersteyn would most likely have used other statutes as an intrinsic aid to help with his interpretation

explanation.en: A is correct. Intrinsic aids include materials which can provide insights to interpret the words of the provision at issue such as preambles. Lead case: Pepper V Hart [1993] 1 All ER 42.

stem: Lord Justice Coyne referred to a previous important case and noted with approval an observation made by the judge in the prior case. He conceded that, although the facts of the previous case were very different to the ones before him, the judge's observation was nevertheless extremely well made. Had the case at hand been based on similar facts, he would have followed the decision.
ask: Which of the following is the most relevant to legal doctrine to Lord Justice Coyne's statement?

options.en: The statement falls under the legal doctrine of obiter dicta
The statement falls under the legal doctrine of the stare decisis
The statement falls under the legal doctrine of per incuriam
The statement falls under the legal doctrine of ejusdem generis
The statement falls under the legal doctrine of ratio decidendi

explanation.en: A is correct. Obiter dicta are legal reasons or pronouncements which are not necessary for the decision in the case and hence are not ratio and not binding.

stem: Mr. Smith brought a case against Mr. Jones, claiming damages because of Mr. Jones' alleged breach of contract. Mr. Jones says that if Mr. Smith sues him he will lodge a counter claim against Mr. Smith for misrepresentation. The case was allocated to the County Court.
ask: What are the legal terms for the parties in this matter?

options.en: Mr. Smith is the defendant and Mr. Jones is the claimant in this matter
Mr. Smith is the prosecutor and Mr. Jones is the defendant in this matter
Mr. Smith is the plaintiff and Mr. Jones is the defendant in this matter
Mr. Smith is the defendant and Mr. Jones is the plaintiff in this matter
Mr. Jones is the defendant and Mr. Smith is the claimant in this matter

explanation.en: E is correct. The person who instigates the complaint or action against the defendant is called the claimant in civil cases. C is incorrect, as the term 'Claimant' has replaced 'Plaintiff' after the Civil Procedure Rules 1998 came into effect in 1999.

stem: A single decision of a higher court is undeniably binding on subsequent inferior courts. Certain higher courts, however, regard themselves as bound by their own decisions whilst others do not.
ask: Which of the following bodies is permitted to lay down precedents binding on themselves?
