options.en: The Court of Appeal, Civil Division, holds itself bound by its previous decisions
The Crown Court holds itself bound by its previous decisions
The County Court holds itself bound by its previous decisions
The Family Division holds itself bound by its previous decisions
The Chancery Division holds itself bound by its previous decisions

explanation.en: A is correct. The Court of Appeal (CA), Civil Division, holds itself bound by its previous decisions as well as those by the Supreme Court. There are, however, three exceptions to this rule: (1) where the CA has two conflicting decisions of its own in the case before it; (2) if the CA's decision would be inconsistent with a previous Supreme Court decision; and (3) if the earlier decision was given per incuriam, although it cannot ignore a decision of the Supreme Court on the same basis.

stem: Interactions between common law, constitutional law, statutory law and regulatory law give rise to considerable complexity. The doctrine of binding precedent, however, lies at the heart of all common law systems.
ask: Which of the following is an example of binding precedent?

options.en: An example of binding precedent is the opinion of the Justice Minister
An example of binding precedent is a judgment of a Scottish Court
An example of binding precedent is a dissenting judgment in the English Court of Appeal
An example of binding precedent is an obiter dicta of an English court
An example of binding precedent is when a case is distinguished, on its facts, or on the point of law involved

explanation.en: E is correct. An example of binding precedent is when a case is distinguished, on its facts, or on the point of law involved. A case is distinguished where an earlier case is rejected as authority, either because the material facts differ or because the statement of law in the previous case is too narrow to be properly applied to the new set of facts. In this way new binding authority is created.

stem: The Court of Appeal is divided into two separate divisions: the Civil Division, and the Criminal Division. Both Divisions are, of course, bound by decisions of the Supreme Court. The decisions of each division are binding upon the High Court and all other lower courts.
ask: Which one of the following, if any, is a reason that can justify the Court of Appeal Civil Division in refusing to follow one of its former decisions which it cannot distinguish?

options.en: Where a former Court of Appeal decision was given per curiam
Where the court is faced by previous conflicting decisions of the Court of Appeal
Where the decision conflicts with an opinion of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council
Where a previous decision of the Court of Appeal, although not expressly overruled, stands with a subsequent judgment of the Supreme Court
The Court of Appeal Civil Division is not bound by its previous decisions

explanation.en: B is correct. In Young v Bristol Aeroplane Co Ltd (1944), the Court of Appeal, Civil Division, identified three exceptional situations where it would disregard its own previous decision; one of which stated that it would disregard its own previous decision where two Court of Appeal decisions conflict. Lead case: Young v Bristol Aeroplane Co Ltd (1944). Please note that option A refers to 'per curiam' (by the court as a whole rather than by a single justice, i.e., without identifying any particular judge), whereas one of the three exceptional cases where the Court of Appeal can ignore its own decisions is known as 'per incuriam' (through lack of care).

stem: Despite the possibility of two venues for trial, almost all criminal cases, however serious, commence in the Magistrates' Courts. A criminal case that starts in the Magistrates' Court may begin either by the defendant being brought forcibly before Magistrates, or by appearing on a certain day before the Magistrates.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes how criminal prosecution generally begins?

options.en: A criminal prosecution can begin by summons or to protect a vulnerable person
A criminal prosecution can begin by charge following arrest or by summons
A criminal prosecution can begin by charge following arrest or the issuing of proceedings
A criminal prosecution can begin by summons or the issuing and serving of proceedings
A criminal prosecution can begin by charge following arrest or the issuing and serving of proceedings

explanation.en: B is correct. A criminal case that starts in the Magistrates' Court may begin either by the defendant being charged and then being brought forcibly before Magistrates, or by summons to the defendant to appear on a certain day before the Magistrates.

stem: A mentally disordered and vulnerable person has been charged with an indictable-only offence. You, as the solicitor, must explain to him what an indictable offence is in the simplest terms you can think of.
ask: Which one of the following is the most basic but accurate description of an indictable offence?

options.en: An indictable offence is a serious offence
An indictable offence is a relatively minor offence
An indictable offence a civil offence
An indictable offence is one requiring a warrant
An indictable offence is one that must be tried in the Magistrates' Court

explanation.en: A is correct. Indictable-only offences include the most serious crimes, such as murder, rape, manslaughter, grievous bodily harm and robbery.

stem: A defendant was acquitted of a crime in the Crown Court. The prosecution wishes to make an appeal from the Crown Court on a point of law because it claims that the judged erred in a direction she gave to the jury.
ask: Where would you advise the prosecution, if at all, to appeal the defendant's acquittal?

options.en: I would advise the prosecution that there is no right of appeal for an acquittal
I would advise the prosecution that there is no right of appeal for an acquittal on a point of law
I would advise the prosecution to appeal the defendant's acquittal to the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court
I would advise the prosecution to appeal the defendant's acquittal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division)
I would advise the prosecution to appeal the defendant's acquittal on a point of law to the Supreme Court

explanation.en: D is correct. If the defendant is acquitted, in the Crown Court, the prosecution can appeal on a point of law; (the defendant will stay acquitted, but the Court of Appeal will, nonetheless, rule on the point of law).

stem: The ancient right to jury trial is preserved in some civil cases. In such cases the jury not only decides the outcome; it also decides on any amount of damages that it thinks should be awarded.
ask: Which one of the following statements most accurately describes when there is a right to trial by jury in a civil action case?

options.en: There is a qualified right to trial by jury in civil action cases of blackmail
There is a qualified right to trial by jury in civil action cases of false imprisonment
There is a qualified right to trial by jury in personal injury civil action cases of over £150,000
There is a qualified right to trial by jury in contractual dispute civil action cases of over £50,000
There is a qualified right to trial by jury in civil action cases of kidnap

explanation.en: B is correct. The Supreme Court Act 1981 gives right to trial by jury in civil action cases of malicious prosecution, false imprisonment and fraud. The Defamation Act 2013 removed the presumption of a trial by jury in a claim in respect of libel or slander. Statute; rule; constitution: Supreme Court Act 1981.

stem: In a controversial case concerning the life and death of two babies, the High Court of Justice is dealing with a case in which a hospital seeks to separate conjoined twins without the parents' consent. The case is of great public importance and the application will be heard by a bench of the High Court and will be chaired by the Head of the Division.
ask: Which one of the following statements most accurately describes the official title of the Head of the relevant Division?

options.en: The official title of the Head of the relevant Division is the Chancellor of the High Court
The official title of the Head of the relevant Division is the President of the Queen's Bench Division
The official title of the Head of the relevant Division is the Master of the Rolls
The official title of the Head of the relevant Division is the Lord Chief Justice
The official title of the Head of the relevant Division is the President of the Family Division

explanation.en: E is correct. The Family Division, which deals with family law and probate cases, consists of about 19 judges, headed by the President of the Family Division.

stem: Stephen is the defendant in a negligence case. It is alleged that he was responsible for causing a car accident which resulted in the driver suffering neck and back injuries. He denies that he was at fault but proceedings have been served against him and trial track allocated.
ask: What is the burden of proof required in Stephen's case?

options.en: The burden of proof required in Stephen's case is on a balance of reasonable doubt
The burden of proof required in Stephen's case is proof beyond reasonable doubt
The burden of proof required in Stephen's case is proof on a balance of probabilities
The burden of proof required in Stephen's case is proof on a balance of possibilities
The burden of proof required in Stephen's case is for proof beyond a balance of possibilities

explanation.en: C is correct. The standard or burden of proof in civil cases the claimant is required to prove his case 'on the balance of probabilities'. Once a claimant has set out his case, it is the turn of the counsel for the defence to produce evidence to refute it. The claimant need not prove his case beyond reasonable doubt, as in criminal cases, but must what he alleges is probably the right version, i.e., proof on a balance of probabilities.

stem: There were proceedings before a District Judge concerning a child's welfare at Rutland County Court. After hearing evidence, the District Judge refused the Local Authority's application for an interim care order and granted the parents' application for leave to instruct an independent social worker. The Local Authority immediately sought permission to appeal the interim order.
ask: Which judge should hear the local authorities appeal?

options.en: The local authority's appeal with permission should go from the District Judge to a Justice of the High Court
The local authority's appeal with permission should go from the District Judge to a Lord Justice of Appeal
The local authority's appeal with permission should go from the District Judge to a Circuit Judge
The local authority's appeal with permission should go from the District Judge to the Chancellor of the Family Division
The local authority's appeal with permission should go from the District Judge to the President of the Family Division

explanation.en: C is correct. An appeal on an interim matter from a decision of a district judge is to a circuit judge in chambers with permission.

stem: A vet had been suspended after two isolated acts of false certification were found by the Disciplinary Committee of the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons (RCVS) to amount to disgraceful conduct in a professional respect. The vet decided to appeal against his removal from the register of veterinary surgeons by the RCVS.
ask: Which of the following is the best advice to which body the vet should appeal his removal from veterinary register?

options.en: The vet should appeal his removal from veterinary register to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council
The vet should appeal his removal from veterinary register to the Court of Appeal's Civil Division
The vet should appeal his removal from veterinary register to a Circuit Judge
The vet should appeal his removal from veterinary register to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) in Strasbourg
The vet should appeal his removal from veterinary register to the Court of Justice of the European Union

explanation.en: A is correct. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council hears domestic appeals to Her Majesty in Council from the Disciplinary Committee of the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons.

stem: A Scottish mother commenced proceedings in Scotland arising from a case where a local Scottish authority had been found to have lawfully removed her child at birth. Her appeal of that decision was made to the Court of Session Inner House in Scotland, but in a final judgement her appeal was denied.
ask: Which of the following statements is the best advice if the mother wishes to pursue her case further?

options.en: The mother has no further avenue of appeal, because Scottish courts are not bound by decisions of the United Kingdom Supreme Court on matters of civil liability
The mother has no further avenue of appeal, because the Court of Session Inner House in Scotland is the highest court within that particular jurisdiction
The mother may have a further avenue of appeal to the United Kingdom Supreme Court
The mother may have a further avenue of appeal to the Family Division of the High Court in London
The mother may have a further avenue of appeal to the Court of Appeal's Civil Division in London

explanation.en: C is correct. Any appeal determined in the Inner House is to the UK Supreme Court. Such an appeal is allowed where it is from a final judgement of the Court of Session which disposes of the whole of the action (as opposed to a court ruling disposing of only part of the action).

stem: Your client has been criminally charged with false imprisonment. He is also being pursued through the civil courts for the same reason. He is uncertain as to the possible outcomes of either the civil case or the criminal cases.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes a basic distinction between civil and criminal cases?

options.en: A defendant in a civil case is either found by the court guilty or not guilty, and is required to pay damages to the claimant or to obey other orders or injunctions of the court, whereas a defendant in a criminal case is either found liable or not liable, and may be punished by law

A claimant in a civil case is either found by the court liable or not liable, and is required to pay damages to the claimant or to obey other orders or injunctions of the court, whereas a defendant in a criminal case is either found guilty or not guilty, and may be punished by law

A defendant in a civil case is either found by the court liable or not liable, and is required to pay damages to the claimant of the court, whereas a defendant in a criminal case is either found guilty or not guilty, and may be punished by law or instructed to obey other orders or injunctions

A defendant in a civil case is either found by the court liable or not liable, and is required to pay damages to the claimant or to obey other orders or injunctions of the court, whereas a defendant in a criminal case is either found guilty or not guilty, and may be punished by law

A defendant in a civil case is either found by the court liable or not liable, whereas a defendant in a criminal case is either found guilty or not guilty, and may be punished by law or is required to pay damages to the claimant or to obey other orders or injunctions of the court

explanation.en: D is correct. A defendant in a civil case is either found by the court liable or not liable, and is required to pay damages to the claimant or to obey other orders or injunctions of the court, whereas a defendant in a criminal case is either found guilty or not guilty, and may be punished by law.

stem: The defendants in a case are prostitutes, who claim that a balcony they were standing on and enticing customers from was not on the street, so their solicitation for sexual favours could not constitute a breach of the Street Offences Act 1969. The court held that the Act's purpose was to prevent harassment, and that this was still occurring as a result of the defendants' acts.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario?

options.en: The rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario is the Plain Meaning Rule
The rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario is the Golden Rule
The rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario is the Mischief Rule
The rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario is the Purposive Approach
The rule of statutory interpretation applied by the court in the scenario is the unified common approach

explanation.en: C is correct. In this scenario, the court applied the Mischief Rule, by holding that the Street Offences Act 1969's purpose was to prevent harassment, and that this was still occurring as a result of the defendants' acts. Lead case: Smith v Hughes (1960).

stem: A consumer purchased a car from a dealer by arrangement with a finance company to facilitate hire purchase terms. The consumer has fallen behind with the monthly instalment payments on the car. The finance company has sent the consumer a letter before action by post, in which the finance company has requested the balance of the purchase price. Since the consumer has not responded within the given period of time, the finance company is now commencing legal action. The financial value of the claim is £17,000 and any hearing is likely to take no longer than a day.
ask: Which is the most appropriate venue for the finance company to commence proceedings against the consumer?

options.en: The most appropriate venue for the finance company to commence proceedings against the consumer is in the Crown Court - civil division
The most appropriate venue for the finance company to commence proceedings against the consumer is in the County Court - small claims track
The most appropriate venue for the finance company to commence proceedings against the consumer is in the Magistrates' court - small claims-track
The most appropriate venue for the finance company to commence proceedings against the consumer is in the County Court - fast track
The most appropriate venue for the finance company to commence proceedings against the consumer is in the County Court - multi-track

explanation.en: D is the best answer. Contract/debt claims worth less than £100,000 must be started in the County Court. This would likely be a fast track matter. Virtually all specified money claims within the fast track threshold of under £25,000 are heard at the county court. A specified money claim generally discloses a contractual dispute about debts said to be due by from the defendant to the claimant.

stem: A man was arrested for sexually assaulting two sisters 35 years ago. The sisters decided to come forward after years of silence, and have only now decided to complain to the police. After a 'no comment' police interview, the duty officer informed the man that he was being charged with sexual assault.
ask: Who decides whether it would be in the public interest to prosecute the man?

options.en: A custody officer
The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS)
A police authority
A magistrate
A clerk of the magistrates' court

explanation.en: B Is correct. A prosecution is brought by the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) usually following police investigation and arrest.

stem: Your client was injured in a car accident, which affected his mental and physical condition. You estimate that his claim will amount to £60,000 for physical and mental damages.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?

options.en: The action should be commenced in the County Court
The action should be commenced in the High Court
The action should be commenced in the County Court only if the physical damage portion is at least £50,000
The action should be commenced in the High Court only if the physical damage portion is at least £50,000
The action may be commenced in either the County Court or the High Court

explanation.en: E is the best answer. The action may be commenced in either the County Court or the High Court. Proceedings which include a claim for damages in respect of personal injuries, other than those relating to clinical malpractice, may only be commenced in the High Court if the financial value of the claim is £50,000 or more. Personal injuries include disease, impairment of physical or mental condition, and death. However, the County Court retains parallel jurisdiction with the High Court, unless the Claimant believes that the claim ought to be dealt with by a High Court judge, by reason of the financial value of the claim, the complexity of the case, or its importance to the public in general. In this case, as the claim is for £60,000 in damages (mental and physical), and there is no reason to suggest the case is complex or of public importance, the claim may be commenced in either the County Court or the High Court.

stem: A client has made a gift of an antique vase during the tax year. He simply gave it to a friend who had always liked the vase. He had bought it several years ago for £5,000. It was valued for insurance purposes at £20,000. Someone had offered him £40,000 for it last year because they really liked it, but its actual market value is thought to be £15,000.
ask: What is the gain for the purposes of capital gains tax calculation?

options.en: £0 - it was a gift.

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The gain on a gift is the market value at the time of the gift, minus the purchase price, so this is £15,000 - £5,000. Insurance costs, etc. are irrelevant: it is the market value that is used.

stem: Your client is aware that not all disposals give rise to capital gains, either because of the type of asset involved or the type of transfer.
ask: Which of the following would fall into the category of potentially being a chargeable gain?

options.en: Disposal of land that is co-owned with another
Cash disposals
Disposals to a spouse
Disposals to a charity
Disposal of the estate of a deceased testator

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Land when co-owned may still be a chargeable gain, whereas cash, disposals to spouses and charities would not be. E is incorrect. If a settlement is created on death (either by will or by operation of the intestacy rules), no capital gains tax liability will arise, as no disposal is deemed to take place on death for capital gains tax purposes. The deceased's personal representatives will be deemed to acquire the assets concerned at their market value at the date of death. Note: The question is about capital gains tax liability, not inheritance tax.

stem: A person enters your office and explains the following sequence of events. Shares were purchased by her father several years ago for £20,000. Her father died last year and at the point of his death, the shares were worth £35,000. Earlier this year, after the shares were in her ownership as per his will, the client sold the shares for £40,000. She wants to know
ask: What figure would be allocated as the gain on the shares for her CGT liability?

options.en: Nothing

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. £5,000. The value of the shares is re-set at the point of her father's death and the amount of the gain up to that point is wiped out. Therefore, it is only the gain from the point of death to the point of disposal that counts.

stem: Bob has held assets for several decades and comes to you for advice on the capital gains implications of selling these assets. One of the assets was bought back in 1962 for £5,000. It has been re-valued every decade as follows: 1972: £8,000; 1982: £10,000; 1992: £14,000; 2002: £18,000; and it is sold in 2012 for £22,000.
ask: What is the capital gain figure that should be used?

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992 provides that capital gains tax was 'rebased' to 31 March 1982, so that tax is normally charged only on gains which are attributable to the period since then. Therefore, any gain prior to then can be wiped out. The gain would therefore be £22,000 - £10,000.

stem: Charlie tells you that he has disposed of several assets in the last few years and asks for advice in terms of dealing with them in the current year. Last year, Charlie disposed of an asset but made a £5,000 loss. This year he has sold one asset at a gain of £10,000 and another asset at a loss of £2,000.
ask: What is the gain for the purposes of capital gains calculations?

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. £3,000. The loss of £5,000 can be carried forward to be applied against the gain this year. The £2,000 loss can be set off against the £10,000 gain, making an £8,000 gain this year and when the loss that has been carried forward is applied, this gives an overall gain this year of £3,000.

stem: Personal representatives have several special rules which they have to consider when transferring assets.
ask: Which of the following best describes the obligations of a personal representative?

options.en: Personal representatives should transfer all assets at whatever cost and leave it to the beneficiaries to deal with the tax implications
Disposals that are made in the year of death are only subject to the allowance available in that year, but not for the next two years after death
When making the decision as to how to deal with assets that have come into their control as personal representatives, they should also consider inheritance tax implications
Where shares are sold within four years, or land within 12 months, at a value which is less than the market value, this lower figure can be used for inheritance tax purposes

If a loss is made during the disposal by a personal representative, this can be set off against any gains irrespective of whether it is in the same period relating to the actions of the personal representatives or not

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Personal representatives have several tax planning opportunities and should work to maximise these. Although in many cases transferring the assets will happen quickly, there is no immediate requirement for this and consideration should be given to all of the needs of the beneficiaries.

stem: Frank has transferred quite a few assets to his wife as he knows that there is no CGT when assets are transferred to his spouse.
ask: Which of the following best describes Frank's potential tax liability?

options.en: He still has to pay CGT at market value
The gain will be rolled over so, if his spouse sells, she will then have to pay CGT, based on the original value when he acquired the asset
It makes no difference that he has transferred to his spouse
This may cause difficulties for inheritance tax purposes
This may cause difficulties for income tax purposes

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. It works in the same way as holdover relief, so that when the spouse sells the asset, the initial value is deemed to be that at the point when the original spouse acquired the asset.

stem: George is selling his house which he has lived in himself since he purchased it 20 years ago. He has a holiday home as well which he will not be selling. There are three acres of land with his home. He has had an offer to sell the land at an above average rate because someone wants it for their horse to graze on.
ask: Which of the following best describes the potential CGT issues that need to be considered?

options.en: As he has two properties, the sale of his house and land will be subject to CGT
It doesn't make any difference how he sells the land and house; they are all exempt from CGT
He should not move out until the actual day of transfer as, if he does, he may lose some of his allowances
The garden should be sold either simultaneously or first as, if it is sold after, it may have a CGT liability attached to it
The fact that he works from home in the property is irrelevant

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Although there is a primary residence exemption, there are some factors that could jeopardise this; for example, working from home, so that part of the property is deemed to be a business, or where the house is sold separately and the land is sold later, as the land is no longer attached to the residence.

stem: Marcus and Lorraine are discussing capital gains tax. Marcus maintains that there is a fixed rate of capital gains tax which is applicable to every individual.
ask: Lorraine Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: Capital gains tax does not apply to individuals
The rate of capital gains tax varies depending on the individual's taxable income
There is a fixed rate of capital gains tax applicable to everyone
There is a fixed rate capital gains charge rather than a tax rate
Capital gains are no longer taxed

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. The rate at which a person pays capital gains tax will depend on their income.

stem: Esme owes £4,800 in capital gains tax during the 2017-2018 financial year. During the same financial year she sold an asset for less than she bought it for, incurring a loss of £1,200. Esme wants to know if she can deduct this amount from the amount of capital gains tax she owes.
ask: Which of the following best describes the effect of the loss on the capital gains tax liability?

options.en: A loss will not reduce the capital gains tax owed
A percentage of the loss can be deducted from the capital gains tax owed
The loss can be deducted from the tax owed providing it does not equate to 25% or more of the tax owed
The loss can be deducted from the capital gains tax owed
The loss can be deducted from the gains

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The loss from the sale of an asset can be deducted from the gains, thus reducing the capital gains tax owed. Note that option D is incorrect as the loss is not deducted from the capital gains tax owed. The loss reduces the gains, the same way an expense reduces the profit. The relevant tax rate is then applied on the taxable gain.

stem: Dave purchased some antique jewellery for £2,000. At the time of his death the jewellery was worth £45,000. The beneficiaries want to know if this will be subject to capital gains tax.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: Death is considered a 'sale' of the assets so capital gains tax is payable
When death causes the 'sale' of the assets, capital gains tax is payable on 50% of the gain
Capital gains tax is not due on the gain made between acquiring an asset and death
Capital gains tax is payable at a reduced rate
Whether or not capital gains tax is charged upon death depends on the taxable income of the deceased for the five years prior to death

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. When valuing an estate the items which make up the estate are valued immediately before the death of the individual, thus effectively wiping out any gain which arose during the time between acquisition of the asset and death.

stem: Kathy decides to sell a piece of furniture via auction. She makes a capital gain of £10,000 but spent £1,000 in auction fees in order to sell the item. Kathy wants to know if this can be deducted from the capital gain.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: The cost of selling the item can be deducted from the capital gain
Part of the cost of selling the item can be deducted from the capital gain
Half the cost of selling the item can be deducted from the capital gain
The cost of selling an item can only be deducted from the capital gain if the capital gain is over £10,000
The cost of selling an item cannot be deducted from the capital gain

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. The cost of selling the item can be deducted from the capital gain so Kathy can reduce her capital gain to £9,000.

stem: Ann has one property in which she lives. She bought it 20 years ago and recently sold it, making a gain of £100,000. She has been told that she is liable to pay capital gains tax on this gain.
ask: Which of the following best describes the CGT status of the property?

options.en: Capital gains tax is not payable on a person's only or principle private dwelling house
Capital gains tax is never payable on property
Capital gains tax is never payable on property or land
The first £50,000 of a gain on property is ignored but any gain exceeding this is liable for capital gains tax
Capital gains tax is payable on the full gain

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Individuals are not required to pay capital gains tax on any gains arising from the sale of their only or principle private dwelling house.

stem: Scott runs a private limited company which bought land in 2007. The company disposed of the land in 2016, making a gain of £40,000. Scott has been told that the company will be liable for capital gains tax due to the gain.
ask: Which of the following best describes Scott's capital gains tax liability?

options.en: The company is liable for capital gains tax
The company is liable for capital gains tax at a reduced rate
The gain is too small to be considered a capital gain
Scott is liable for the capital gain
Companies do not pay capital gains tax

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Companies do not pay capital gains tax.

stem: George runs a company which purchased property in 2008 and sold it in 2016, making a gain of £200,000. As companies are not liable for capital gains tax, George believes this gain won't be subject to tax in any way.
ask: Which of the following best describes George's tax liability arising from the sale?

options.en: The gain won't be subject to tax
George will pay income tax on the gain
The company will be required to pay capital gains tax
It is a chargeable gain and will be counted as taxable income and subject to corporation tax
It will be subject to corporation tax and capital gains tax

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Although companies do not pay capital gains tax, the gain is considered a chargeable gain. This is added to the company's taxable income and is, therefore, subject to corporation tax.

stem: Sharon believes that if you pay capital gains throughout your life your estate does not qualify for inheritance tax when you die.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: Capital gains tax is not payable by individuals
Individuals can be liable for capital gains tax during their life and have inheritance tax due on their estate
Individuals will only ever be subject to either capital gains tax or inheritance tax
Inheritance tax is not payable by individuals
Capital gains tax will not apply after 2012

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Individuals do not negate the liability for inheritance tax on their estate by paying capital gains tax throughout their lives. Although death is not considered disposal for capital gains tax purposes, both taxes are potentially payable.

stem: In 2015 Phil made a capital gain of £5,100 and in 2016 a capital gain of £15,000. Phil believes he can carry over the unused portion of his 2015-2016 allowance in order to reduce the capital gain made in 2016-2017.
ask: Advise Phil regarding the current law in this area?

options.en: Phil can carry over the unused part of his annual allowance
Only £1,000 of the annual allowance can be carried over
The annual allowance can only be carried over if it has not been used at all
A maximum of 10% of the annual allowance can be carried over
The annual allowance cannot be carried over

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Regardless of whether or not it has been used, the annual allowance cannot be carried over.

stem: A woman sold an asset in 2010 at a loss of £4,000. She made no other capital gains or losses until 2015 when she made a gain of £5,000. The woman would like to know if she can deduct the £4,000 loss from the gain.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: The loss can be deducted
The loss cannot be deducted as it equates to over half the gain
Only a loss made in the same or previous year can be deducted from a capital gain
Only a loss made within three years of the capital gain can be deducted
Only a loss made after a capital gain can be deducted

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Excess losses (such as the woman's loss of £4,000) can be carried forward without limit and deducted from future capital gains.

stem: In 2013 your client bought a car for £2,000 and sold it in 2016 for £5,000. He has been told that this is a capital gain and that he could be liable for capital gains tax if he exceeds his annual allowance.
ask: Which of the following best describe the current legal position?

options.en: The gain would qualify as a capital gain
Gains under £5,000 do not qualify as capital gains
If an asset is acquired for less than £2,500 it will not qualify for capital gains tax regardless of any gain made
Only businesses are liable for capital gains tax so your client won't have to pay any capital gains tax
The car is likely to be deemed a wasting asset so there won't be any capital gains tax payable

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Assets which are tangible and movable and have a life expectancy of less than 50 years are generally considered wasting assets and do not attract capital gains tax.

stem: Your client is looking to sell a wide range of his assets. She is asking for advice on possible capital gains liability.
ask: Which of the following assets would you advise are all part of Capital Gains Tax?

options.en: A large field; a collection of wines; the family home; a second home; an art collection
An art collection; the family home; a second home
A collection of fine wines; the family home; an art collection
A second home; the family home; an art collection; a collection of fine wines
A large field; an art collection; a collection of fine wines; a second home

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. A large field; an art collection; a collection of fine wines; a second home. The family home is not part of chargeable gains assets, regardless of whether or not the assets were purchased with a view to making a profit.

stem: A gift of an asset has been made between husband and wife.
ask: Which of the following is true about the capital gains charge?

options.en: There is no Capital Gains Tax and the gain made by the donor is wiped out
There is no immediate tax payment, but the total gain by both husband and wife will, ultimately, be taxed
Capital gains are the same, regardless of the fact that it is between husband and wife
The capital gains are reduced by 50%
If the donee keeps the property for at least a year, there are no capital gains repercussions

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Capital gains are not payable at the time of transfer, although when the donee sells, they will pay the total capital gains for both parties.

stem: A woman has been looking at disposing of some assets and is concerned about Capital Gains Tax. She is aware that some of her assets are likely to make a loss.
ask: Which option offers the best advice to the woman?

options.en: Losses can be off set against the gains in the year that the transactions are made
Losses can be carried forward to the next year, but cannot be used against gains in the same or previous years
Losses cannot be off set against gains, at any point
Losses can be off set against the previous years' gains
Losses can be off set against gains in the same or later years

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. The losses can be used in that year, or in subsequent years, against any other gains.

stem: The personal representatives of a deceased person are trying to work out the gain on property and whether or not they would be potentially liable for Capital Gains Tax.
ask: What would you advise the personal representatives as to their Capital Gains Tax liability?

options.en: Personal representatives never pay Capital Gains Tax
Personal representatives pay full Capital Gains Tax, based on the value of the asset and the purchase price
The value of the property is the value at the time of death; no gain before that point counts
Generally, personal representatives will not pay Capital Gains Tax, although, if they have held the property for a long time, this may not be the case
Capital Gains Tax will always be paid alongside Inheritance Tax

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The value of the property is rebased at the point of death; so, provided the estate is dealt with efficiently, no capital gains are likely to arise.

stem: In 1960 a person bought shares for £20,000, which increased in value to £75,000 on the 31ST of March 1982, and today sells them for £100,000.
ask: What is the chargeable gain for CGT purposes!?

explanation.en: The best answer is A. The 1982 market value (£75,000) will be taken when calculating CGT liability. The gain is £25,000. B is not correct because the 1982 market value applies. C is not correct because it is the current sale price that the purchase price is deducted from, not the 1982 market value, and the purchase price is the 1982 value. D is not correct because the initial purchase price is not added to the 1982 value. E is not correct because the purchase price used is not the difference between the 1982 value and the original purchase price, it is simply the 1982 value.

stem: A person buys an asset for £3,000. On death, it is valued for probate purposes at £5,000. The PRs complete the administration of the deceased's estate and transfer the asset. The asset is now worth £9,000 to the beneficiary.
ask: What is the PRs' chargeable gain for CGT purposes?

explanation.en: The best answer is B. As the PRs completed the administration of the estate, no CGT will be payable and the beneficiary will be deemed to acquire the asset at its probate value of £5,000. A is not correct, because the PRs completed the administration of the estate and transferred the asset. They did not sell it. C is not correct as this is the purchase price, and in any event the PRs completed the administration of the estate and transferred the asset. They did not sell it. D is not correct. If the PRs sell the item, it is deemed to have been acquired at the probate value, and the beneficiary is deemed to have acquired the item at this value, but as the PRs completed the administration of the estate and transferred the asset, there is no CGT liability. E is not correct as this is the increase in value of the item for the beneficiary. As the PRs completed the administration of the estate and transferred the asset, there is no CGT liability. If the beneficiary sold the item for £9,000, this might be the capital gain, if no personal exemption applies.

stem: A solicitor acts for Mr. Portnoy in divorce proceedings. Ancillary relief proceedings are issued by Mrs. Portnoy, as she wishes to have the matrimonial home transferred into her sole name. The solicitor becomes aware that the house was purchased by Mr. Portnoy with the proceeds of crime.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the effect of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 ("the Act") in this situation?

options.en: Transferring the house from Mr. Portnoy to Mrs. Portnoy would involve the solicitor in an arrangement which he knows facilitates the acquisition of criminal property
Transferring the house from Mr. Portnoy to Mrs. Portnoy would require the solicitor to make an authorised disclosure to the firm's nominated officer
Transferring the house from Mr. Portnoy to Mrs. Portnoy would constitute an arrangement under the Act because Mrs. Portnoy is committing an offence by receiving stolen property
Transferring the house from Mr. Portnoy to Mrs. Portnoy would not constitute a forbidden arrangement under the Act
Transferring the house from Mr. Portnoy to Mrs. Portnoy would not constitute a forbidden arrangement under the Act, provided the litigation is not a sham created for the purposes of money laundering

explanation.en: The best answer is (E). The case of Bowman v Fels settled the issue as to whether steps in litigation could be construed as 'arranging' under s. 328 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002. The Court of Appeal concluded that taking steps in litigation and the resolution of issues in a litigious context, including dividing assets in accordance with a court judgment, would not involve a solicitor in a breach of s. 328, albeit that careful consideration would need to be made of whether the client was committing an offence by receiving stolen property. Moreover, the solicitor would be unable to take advantage of this exclusion if the litigation was a sham created for the purposes of money laundering.

stem: Mr. Fox instructs his solicitor to sell his house. The solicitor suspects that the house was purchased with the proceeds of tax evasion and discloses to the NCA under s. 328 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002. Mr. Fox calls and speaks to the solicitor's trainee, demanding to know why his house sale has not been completed.
ask: Under which circumstances can the client be informed that an authorised disclosure be made?

options.en: The trainee may inform Mr. Fox that an authorised disclosure has been made in any event, because such disclosure will not prejudice any investigation that follows such a report
The trainee may inform Mr. Fox that an authorised disclosure has been made, if the client tells the trainee that he will not frustrate any action taken by the law enforcement authorities
The trainee may inform Mr. Fox that an authorised disclosure has been made, if the purpose is to dissuade him from engaging in the alleged money laundering
The trainee may inform Mr. Fox that an authorised disclosure has been made in any event, because the disclosure was made as soon as possible prior to the transaction taking place
The trainee may not inform Mr. Fox that an authorised disclosure has been made to the NCA in any circumstances

explanation.en: The best answer is C. Under s. 333A(1) of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002, it is an offence to disclose to any person that a suspicious activity report on money laundering has been made, where such disclosure is likely to prejudice any investigation that follows such a report. So, the trainee would appear to be in breach of section 333A of the Act. However, there are a number of defences to 'tipping off'. One such defence is that the disclosure is made to the client for the purpose of dissuading the client from engaging in the alleged money laundering under section 333D(2) of the Act. Therefore, the most accurate answer is C.

stem: You are a conveyancing solicitor. Your client asks you for an explanation for the delay in a property transaction. You suspect that a suspicious activity report has been made in respect of the other party to the transaction. The client also tells you that his bank account has been frozen and he asks you for legal advice.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the effect of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 in this situation?

options.en: The solicitor may tell his client of his suspicions for the delay in the property transaction, and may also give him legal advice as to why his account has been frozen, because the solicitor's suspicion has not come to him in the course of a business in the regulated sector

The solicitor may tell his client of his suspicions for the delay in the property transaction, and may also give him legal advice as to why his account has been frozen, because the solicitor is clearly seeking to dissuade his client from committing an offence
The solicitor may tell his client of his suspicions for the delay in the property transaction, but may not give him legal advice as to why his account has been frozen
The solicitor may give his client legal advice as to why his account has been frozen, but may not tell his client of his suspicions for the delay in the property transaction
The solicitor may not tell his client of his suspicions for the delay in the property transaction, and may not give him legal advice as to why his account has been frozen

explanation.en: While no applicable exception applies under section 333D(2) POCA 2002 (disclosures made by professional legal advisers to their clients for the purpose of dissuading them from engaging in criminal conduct), no tipping off offence can be committed in a case where a customer's bank account is frozen and he asks you for legal advice. This is because the solicitor's suspicion or knowledge of a suspicious activity report or an investigation will not have come to him in the course of a business in the regulated sector. Hence, in cases of litigation advice there is no scope for a section 333A offence. By contrast, where a client asks his conveyancing solicitor for an explanation for the delay in a property transaction, and the solicitor suspects that a suspicious activity report has been made in respect of the other party to the transaction, it is definitely questionable as to whether the solicitor would be able to avail himself of the exception to the offence of tipping off contained in s. 333D(2) POCA 2002, as the solicitor is hardly seeking to dissuade his client from committing an offence. Therefore, the best answer to this question is (D).

stem: A bank manager refers a company (registered in Jersey) to a firm of solicitor for advice on a corporate matter (involving the electronic bank transfer of a sum of 8,000 euros) for which the firm will receive a fee of 800 euros. The bank manager has known the two directors of the company for many years and they hold the company's shares equally.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the effect of the Money Laundering Regulations 2017 in this situation?

options.en: The solicitor's firm must obtain client identification because the work is within the regulated sector and within the requirements to undertake CDD
The solicitor's firm must obtain client identification because the company is registered outside of the UK
The solicitor's firm must obtain client identification because the client is no different from a private individual
The solicitor's firm must obtain client identification because it is not clear that the bank manager has undertaken such identification
The solicitor's firm does not need to obtain client identification

explanation.en: The correct answer is (A). While the transaction is one off in nature and the firm will only receive a fee of 800 euros, the transaction itself amounts to a transfer of funds exceeding 1,000 euros. Therefore, the correct answer is (A).

stem: (1) Arranging for the sale of a client's shareholdings upon his retirement. (2) Advising clients to take out an insurance policy after you investigate title to a property which they intend to purchase, and discover that a restrictive covenant has been breached. (3) Drafting a standard will for your client. (4) Providing general legal advice to your client which does not relate to a transaction involving a transfer of funds in excess of €1,000.
ask: Which of the following activities will involve you in the carrying on of relevant business under the Money Laundering Regulations 2017?

options.en: None of the above
(1) only
(1) and (2) only
(1), (2) and (3) only

explanation.en: (C) is the correct answer. Buying and selling of real property/business assets and the provision of financial services will all constitute relevant business under the MLR 2017. Will drafting services (3) and the provision of general legal advice (4) are not regulated activities, being neither a financial service nor a real property transaction (unless of course they become such, e.g. through the provision of advice about the tax affairs of another person or involve the transfer of funds in excess of €1,000).

ask: In which of the following situations would you make further enquiries of a client?

options.en: A client's legal expenses are covered by an insurance policy
A client asks you to make a payment to a legitimate party involved in a transaction using funds held for the client in your firm's client bank account
A client wishing to borrow money from a mortgage lender states his net income is €3,500, when you know from previous dealings with him that his income is only €2,000
A client pays you £130 in £10 notes which he says is to enable you to undertake local searches in his conveyancing matter
Your client is a limited company and the director who meets you has brought his passport but has not brought any company documents

explanation.en: (C) is the correct answer. The risk is that your client may be attempting to mislead the lender to improperly inflate a mortgage advance, by misrepresenting the borrower's income. If you discover or suspect that a mortgage advance has already been improperly obtained, you should consider advising the mortgage lender. A client's fees being covered under a policy of insurance is a perfectly routine and acceptable form of litigation funding. You would want, however, written confirmation of this, usually in the form of a certificate of insurance. In (B), payment to a legitimate party involved in a transaction using funds held for the client in a client account is a routine and often expedient method of effecting payment between parties. In respect of (C), payments of relatively small sums would not normally be regarded as a sufficient basis for a reasonable suspicion of money laundering. In (E), you are required to identify the client based on documents, data or information obtained from a reliable and independent source. Where your client is a business, you can obtain this verification through Companies House, once you are satisfied that the director is who he says he is.

ask: In which of the following situations would you consider reporting a suspicion of money laundering to the firm's Money Laundering Reporting Officer?

options.en: Where the client delays providing ID evidence
Where the client asks you do work that is outside your normal area of activity
Where your client asks you to terminate a property transaction early at a loss
Where the client asks for a payment to a third party to be made out of his funds in the client account
Where the client initially refuses to provide ID, is secretive, refuses to meet you in person and pays you in cash

explanation.en: (E) is correct. It is impossible to give a definitive list of suspicious transactions, but a-d can often arise during routine and legitimate matters on which a client may instruct a solicitor, and do not in themselves and in isolation give rise to grounds to make a report to the firm's MLRO. Answer e, however, would likely, or ought to, arise such suspicion in you that you make a report of those suspicions.

stem: You are again acting for Gordon as per the previous question. A week after the previous transaction fell through, Gordon instructs you on the purchase of a new site, and again lets you have a cheque for the deposit and an extra £20,000.00 on account of costs. Several weeks later this project also falls through, and Gordon e-mails you to ask you to return his money, as before.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes what you should do?

options.en: There is nothing out of the ordinary about this transaction. You may proceed with the return of the money to Gordon
Report the matter to your MLRO as this is possibly money laundering. Do not return the money to Gordon at this stage
Report the matter to your MLRO and advise Gordon of the same
There may be an innocent explanation, but report the matter to your supervising partner out of caution. You may proceed with the return of the money to Gordon
Raise questions of Gordon as to why the transaction has fallen through, but do not proceed with Gordon's request

explanation.en: Answer B is correct. You now have a pattern of transactions that bear the hallmarks of money laundering. Therefore you objectively have reasonable grounds to know or suspect that the client is engaged in money laundering, and failure to disclose is an offence under s330. It doesn't matter whether you actually didn't know or suspect that criminal property was involved. Making a disclosure (without tipping off, and committing an offence under S333A) prevents the s330 offence arising. Subjectively, your suspicions would certainly meet and exceed the criteria set out in Shah. Further, if you do suspect money laundering and return the money, which is criminal property, you may be guilty of entering into or becoming concerned in an arrangement that you know or suspect facilitates money laundering (S328(1)). Making a disclosure affords a defence to this offence, as well as preventing the s330 offence (failure to report) arising.

stem: Your MLRO reported Gordon to the NCA. The NCA asks you for copies of e-mail correspondence with Gordon. You forwarded these to your MLRO at the time you made the disclosure. However, your secretary, who has no knowledge of the disclosure or investigation, permanently deleted both the e-mails and those you forwarded to your MLRO. You did not arrange for the e-mails to be retained.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes your legal position?

options.en: As you have made a disclosure to your MLRO and did not comply with Gordon's request, you have fully complied with your legal duties and have committed no offences
You have committed a criminal offence in not retaining the e-mails and have no defence

You have committed a criminal offence in causing the e-mails to be deleted, but have a defence because you did not intend to conceal any facts disclosed by the documents to those carrying out the investigation
Your secretary has committed a criminal offence in deleting the e-mails and has no defence

Both you and your secretary have committed criminal offences but you both have defences, because you did not intend to conceal any facts disclosed by the documents to those carrying out the investigation, and your secretary did not know or suspect that the documents were relevant to the investigation

explanation.en: The answer is E. A person commits an offence under s342(2)(b) if they falsify, conceal, destroy or otherwise dispose of, or cause or permit the falsification, concealment, destruction or disposal of, documents which are relevant to the investigation. This is an offence that carries a maximum penalty of 5 years and/or an unlimited fine. By not retaining those e-mails and not instructing them to be retained, you caused their destruction. However, S342(6) contains the defences that: (a) a person did not know or suspect that the documents are relevant to the investigation; and (b) that they do not intend to conceal any facts disclosed by the documents from any appropriate officer carrying out the investigation. The former defence would apply to your secretary, who does not know about the disclosure or investigation (especially as you did not instruct for those e-mails to be retained). The latter defence would apply to you, as by making the disclosure and forwarding the e-mails to your MLRO, you did not intend to conceal any facts disclosed by the documents to those carrying out the investigation, even though the original e-mails themselves were destroyed.

stem: You act for Simon who has just won judgment in default for recovery of the sum of £20,000.00. The debtor delivers a cheque for this sum to your firm. Due to conduct of the parties after the issue of proceedings, you strongly suspect money laundering and that the litigation was fabricated. You speak informally to your MLRO who strongly advises you not to pay in the money, which will subsequently be paid out to Simon.
ask: Which of the following best describes what you should do?

options.en: You should follow your MLRO's advice and not pay in the cheque
You should return the cheque and advise both the debtor and party that you suspect money laundering
You should ensure that your MLRO makes a report, and await consent from the NCA before proceeding
You should immediately cease acting for Simon and return the cheque
You should pay in the cheque and subsequently pay the money to Simon and will commit no offences in doing so

explanation.en: The best answer is A. You should follow your MLRO's advice and not pay in the cheque. While the Bowman v Fels exemption applies until the execution of a judgment or completion of a settlement, and until then, no POCA offences can be committed, the exemption will not apply in this case as the fact pattern describes a situation of 'sham litigation'. The Law Society does not consider 'sham litigation' to come within the Bowman v Fels exemption and it remains with the within the ambit of s.328. 'Sham litigation' can arise where an acquisitive criminal offence is committed and settlement negotiations or litigation are intentionally fabricated to launder the proceeds of that separate crime such as a debt recovery action being settled before you even send the letter of claim.

stem: You act for David who is purchasing a car parking space for £14,000.00. David instructs you a few weeks later to handle the acquisition of another parking space, this time in another city - for £8,000.00.
ask: Which of the following best describes what you should do in respect of customer due diligence?

options.en: No due diligence is required as each transaction is less than €10,000.00

No evidence of identity is required as each transaction is less than €10,000.00, but you should obtain information to confirm the client's identity as a matter of good practice, and complete the rest of the customer due diligence requirements
You are required to conduct simplified due diligence
You are required to conduct standard due diligence
You are required to conduct enhanced due diligence

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Each transaction amounts to a transfer of funds exceeding €1,000 Euros (or equivalent) in value and therefore fall within the requirements of the Money Laundering Regulations 2017 for due diligence to be carried out on David under Regulation 27. David would require standard due diligence as he does not fit the categories for either simplified or enhanced due diligence on the facts.

stem: You are instructed to provide tax advice for a FTSE 250 company.
ask: Which of the following best describes what you should do with respect to customer due diligence measures?

options.en: No customer due diligence is required as the listed company trades on a regulated market
Simplified customer due diligence on a risk-based approach is required as the listed company trades on a regulated market
Regular customer due diligence on a risk-based approach is required as the listed company trades on a regulated market
Enhanced customer due diligence on a risk-based approach is required as the listed company trades on a regulated market
You cannot act for this client

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. You would perform simplified due diligence on a client if they are a company whose securities are listed on a regulated market (Regulation 37(3)). You will simply need to obtain evidence that the client is eligible for simplified due diligence, so A is not strictly correct. However you should also bear in mind the Regulation 27 requirements for customer due diligence to be conducted on a risk-based approach and that there is no automatic exemption from standard or enhanced due diligence. If the company had previously been investigated or prosecuted for money laundering, you would likely need to apply a higher standard of customer due diligence.

stem: You act for a well-known limited company on highly-publicised asset purchase. During the transaction, your senior partner suspects money laundering and makes a disclosure to your MLRO, advising all fee earners working on the deal that this disclosure has taken place. Your friend in another law firm asks for details. He is very interested in the transaction but neither he nor his firm has ever acted for the client.
ask: Which of the following best describes how you should proceed?

options.en: You may give your friend the information as you are covered by the exemption/defence of making a disclosure to another professional of the same industry
You must not provide the information to your friend as it is not for the purposes of preventing a money laundering transaction
You must wait for permission from your MLRO/the NCA before giving your friend the information
You may advise your friend that there are concerns, but not that a disclosure has been made
You should refer your friend to your senior partner

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. The exemption in s333C for making a disclosure to another legal professional does not apply here, as it does not concern a mutual client or transaction nor is it for the purposes of preventing money laundering. Any disclosure would therefore constitute tipping off. Consent from the NCA relates to actions that would be an offence in respect of the handling of criminal property, as opposed to tipping off.

stem: Whilst in your local pub on the weekend, you hear rumour that a well-known footballer is engaged in money laundering. This person is not nor ever has been a client of the firm, nor are they involved in any transaction with which your firm is involved.
ask: Which of the following best describes how you should proceed?

options.en: You must make a report to your MLRO otherwise you will be guilty of an offence of failing to disclose
You must make a report to the NCA directly otherwise you will be guilty of an offence of failing to disclose
You are not mandated to take any action
You should spread the rumour
You must make a report to the local police else you will be guilty of an offence of failing to disclose

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. An offence of failing to disclose requires that the information came to you in the course of a business in the regulated sector (s330(3)). In this case, the information did not come to you in those conditions. You are therefore not mandated to take any action. Nonetheless, spreading the rumour is not constructive, and you may risk breaching your professional duty to act with integrity and not to bring the profession into disrepute.

stem: You are acting for Trinity Investment Capital Limited in a property transaction, which is part of an investment group. You are provided with documentation to advise on, which, on review, causes you suspicion that the transaction is being used to facilitate money laundering. When you ask the client representative about the source of funds, he tells you "Don't worry about where the money comes from. It doesn't matter anyway, as all communications and documentation are privileged and I won't let you waive it".
ask: Which of the following best describes how you should proceed?

options.en: You must cease acting for the client but cannot make a disclosure due to legal professional privilege
You may continue to act for the client but cannot make a disclosure due to legal professional privilege
You must continue to act for the client but must make a disclosure to the NCA and wait for consent to proceed
You must advise the client that you are making a disclosure to the NCA
You can withdraw from the transaction and should consider also making a disclosure to the NCA

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Where you suspect, as in this case, that you are being used to facilitate criminal activity, the crime/fraud exception applies. This means that the information that caused you suspicion - which was given to you in 'privileged circumstances', as it was communicated to you by a person seeking legal advice (S330(10)) - is not protected by the normal 'privileged circumstances' requirement or legal professional privilege that would ordinarily prevent a disclosure. You can therefore consider withdrawing from the transaction, as if you proceed you are likely to commit a money laundering offence of 'arranging'. If you do withdraw, you should still consider making a disclosure so as to ensure that you are not committing a 'failure to disclose' offence (S330). You also should not tip off the client (S333A), which may occur if you continue to act but delay acting on instructions whilst waiting for consent from the NCA.

stem: You have been asked to act for Danielle Lyons in relation to a property transaction. Before commencing work on the matter, you undertake standard customer due diligence. You are unable to verify Danielle's identity as she has no identity documents to hand, and it is clear she will not be in a position to provide any at this stage, nor can she provide any letters from other parties to confirm her identity.
ask: Which of the following best describes how you should proceed?

options.en: You may continue to act for Danielle as long as you complete verification as soon as possible
You cannot act for Danielle but need not consider making a disclosure to the NCA
You must not act for Danielle and must consider making a disclosure to the NCA
You may forego customer due diligence but must carefully monitor the transaction on an ongoing basis
You must await permission from the NCA before acting for Danielle

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Under MLR Regulation 31(1), where you cannot complete customer due diligence measures, you must not carry out a transaction and must terminate any existing business relationship with the customer. You must also consider whether you are required to make a disclosure to the NCA.

stem: You have been approached by two men who have gone into partnership together last month. They are not registered professionals. They ask you to advise on drafting a partnership deed.
ask: Which of the following best describes how you should proceed with respect to customer due diligence?

options.en: As it is a partnership you need only verify their name, registered address, trading address and nature of business
You can complete customer due diligence using information on the partnership available at Companies House
You should complete customer due diligence on one of the partners only
You should complete customer due diligence on both of the partners
You do not need to complete any due diligence

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. A partnership is not a legal entity, so you must obtain information on the constituent individuals. As the individuals are not registered professionals, you should identify them as if they were individual clients to your firm, using standard customer due diligence. Note that the Law Society's Practice Note on Anti-money Laundering recommends that when partnerships are reputable with a lot of information available, Answer A would be correct. Answer B only applies to Limited Liability Partnerships, which are incorporated entities.

stem: You have been instructed by Nuts n Bolts Limited, an Isle of Man registered company, for UK tax advice. You are liaising with Mike Money, the Financial Director.
ask: Which of the following best describes what you should do with regards to customer due diligence?

options.en: You must apply enhanced customer due diligence on a risk-sensitive basis
You may apply standard due diligence, and must confirm the company's identity and beneficial owner(s) with documents that satisfy the customer due diligence requirements on a risk-sensitive basis
You may apply standard due diligence on a risk-sensitive basis, and must confirm the company's identity and beneficial owner(s) with documents from the Isle of Man Companies Registry only
You may apply standard due diligence on a risk-sensitive basis, and must confirm the company's identity and beneficial owner(s) with suitable documents that are certified copies only
You must apply standard due diligence, and a certificate of incorporation will be sufficient

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. The MLR do not mandate which documents should be obtained to verify the company's identity and beneficial owners when it is an overseas private listed company. The Law Society's Practice Note recommends a risk-based approach, looking at the risk of the client generally, the risk of the retainer and the risks presented as a result of the country in which the client is incorporated.

stem: You are instructed to act for Nick Stuff to provide tax advice. Your client care letter contained a paragraph concerning your obligations under anti-money laundering legislation. You become suspicious about Nick's financial transactions, and make a disclosure to your MLRO, which results in a suspicious activity report being made to the NCA, from whom you are awaiting a reply. You hold off on providing further advice as you suspect this may result in you committing an 'arranging' offence. Nick asks you the reason for the delay. You are concerned that a disclosure will cause him to flee the country.
ask: Which of the following best describes how you should proceed?

options.en: You may refer Nick to the money laundering paragraph in the client care letter specifically, without committing a tipping off offence
You may refer Nick to the terms and conditions of the letter generally, without committing a tipping off offence
You may not respond to Nick's query and must not communicate with him further
You must refer Nick to the NCA for them to respond to his query
You may tell Nick that you suspect money laundering but must not tell him that a suspicious activity report has been made

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. You can commit a 'tipping off' offence by either disclosing that a suspicious activity report has been made (S333A(1)), or that an investigation is being contemplated or carried out, if that disclosure is likely to prejudice the investigation (S333A(2)). In this case, drawing Nick's attention to the money laundering paragraph of the client care letter in particular (Answer A), as opposed to the terms generally may likely arouse his suspicions as you have been so specific as to the money laundering paragraph in particular. Answers C, D and E may also arouse his suspicions and may be considered 'tipping off', even though you have not specifically disclosed that there is or may be an investigation. You will not be able to rely on the professional adviser exemption under S333D(2) as you are not dissuading Nick from engaging in criminal conduct by making either a deliberate or inadvertent disclosure. You arguably would not be committing an offence under S342(1) as you do not know or suspect that the investigation is being conducted (as it is not at this stage) or that it is about to be carried out (as you have not yet received a reply from the NCA).

stem: You have a new client who has recently started their own business. They don't really understand much about their tax liabilities and have asked you what they need to know about VAT.
ask: Which of the following statements would you tell them?

options.en: VAT is a charge on certain business transactions
VAT applies only in the UK
You don't have to worry about VAT as you are a new business
VAT is paid by consumers not businesses, so don't worry
All products sold should have VAT charged which you need to pay to HMRC

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. VAT is charged on certain business transactions; it applies across the EU and can be relevant to a new business as it depends on turnover. Businesses have a responsibility to collect VAT, but it is not payable on all transactions.

stem: Bob is confused as to which of the payments he has made can be considered to be VAT-able disbursements.
ask: He has a list of disbursements that he has paid out and asks you which ones attract VAT?

options.en: Land registry fees
Stamp duty
Accountancy fees
Court fees
None of the above.

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Accountancy fees are VAT-able disbursements; official payments such as stamp duty and court fees do not attract VAT.

stem: You overhear a debate in the pub about what VAT actually is and how it works. One of your friends says that it is a consumption tax and another friend asks you to explain what he meant by this.
ask: What is the appropriate answer?

options.en: It is only paid on luxury items such as alcohol
It is only paid by those who consume a certain amount of goods
It is only paid by the wealthy
It is ultimately paid by the end consumers
It is only paid by certain households

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. VAT is referred to as a 'consumption tax' as it is ultimately borne by the final consumer. It is related to what is purchased, but it is based on the item and not on the wealth of the purchaser.

stem: A client asks you what the fundamental difference is between a VAT registrable business and a non-VAT registrable business.
ask: Which of the following statements would you use as part of your explanation?

options.en: All businesses charge VAT, but only those that are registered have to pay it over to HMRC
Non-registered VAT businesses do not pay or charge VAT
Registered businesses are able to gain tax credits against corporation tax for any VAT that they pay
There is no real difference; it just depends on the type of business
A non-registered business will still pay VAT, but will not charge VAT. A registered business will charge VAT and can take off any VAT that it pays from this amount

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. A registered company can reclaim VAT that it pays out, whereas a non-registered business cannot; however, a non-registered business would not have to charge VAT.

stem: A man is aware that VAT is charged when a taxable person makes a supply of goods. He does not know whether he is classified as a taxable person making a taxable supply.
ask: Which of the following is relevant in determining whether the man is a taxable person making a taxable supply?

options.en: The type of product being sold
Whether the supply is in the course of business
Whether the man has a turnover of more than the VAT registration threshold
Whether the man has chosen to become registered
The nature of the products and the transaction and whether the man has chosen to become VAT registered

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Several issues are relevant when it comes to determining whether or not a taxable person made a taxable supply for VAT purposes, including the nature of the products, the nature of the transaction and the choice / requirement to become VAT registered.

stem: David is confused about the various different levels of VAT rate. He has heard that it is possible for goods or services to attract no VAT, yet have an applicable VAT rate.
ask: How do you explain this?

options.en: It is the same thing and you can ignore these VAT-able supplies of services or goods
Zero rated goods or services are still VAT-able; they don't have a monetary value, but they still need to be recorded
There is no such thing as zero rated; all VAT is 20%
Zero rated VAT does not apply to UK goods
None of the above

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Zero rated is still recordable, but it does not have a value as such; this could change in the future to attract a VAT level that is higher than 0%. The transaction must be recorded in VAT accounts and on VAT Returns. The business may be able to claim back the VAT on related purchases.

stem: Matthew has a VAT registered business. In one quarter, he sells £6,000 worth of goods that attract the 20% VAT rate. He also purchased items which attract VAT at 20% that were €2,000 in value.
ask: What is Matthew's VAT position?

options.en: Matthew owes £1,200 VAT to HMRC
No VAT is payable
HMRC owes Matthew £400
Matthew owes £4,000 in VAT
