Matthew owes £800 in VAT

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Matthew has paid out £400 in VAT and collected £1,200 in VAT; therefore, the return would require Matthew to pay over £800 in VAT to HMRC.

ask: Having realised that some items are zero rated, David now wants to know which of these items he should be recording as being zero rated?

options.en: Food from stores
Children's books
Public transport
Newspapers
Food, children's books, public transport and newspapers

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Food, children's books, public transport and newspapers are potentially zero rated and need to be recorded.

stem: One of the trainees in your department is busy working out the VAT for several clients and decides to create categories to put the various different expenses into.
ask: She asks you which of these categories should be used?

options.en: Exempt, Zero rated and Additional rate
Zero rated, Reduced rate and Additional rate
Standard rate, Reduced and Zero rated
Standard rate, Additional rate and Zero rated
Reduced rate, Standard rate and Additional rated

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Additional rate does not exist. Standard rate is 20%, reduced rate is 5%, zero rated is 0% and exempt has no VAT.

stem: One of your colleagues is confused about the terminology associated with VAT and asks you about the concepts associated with input and output records.
ask: Which of these would be part of the explanation you give to your colleague?

options.en: It's the terminology associated with how an organisation keeps the records, based on how much overseas VAT they receive and how much they have paid out
It refers to the internal accounting processes used to record the amount of VAT payable to HMRC
Output tax refers to VAT paid by the company on goods being brought into the business
Input tax refers to VAT that the company charges on the goods and services it sells
It refers to purchases and sales made outside of the UK

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. It has no reference to foreign purchases, but deals rather with the internal accounting processes used to record the amount of VAT payable to HMRC. Input tax refers to VAT paid by the company on goods being brought into the business. Output tax refers to VAT that the company charges on the goods and services it sells.

stem: You are scheduling holidays within the tax department and are mindful that certain periods of the year are busier and therefore there should be a full complement of staff available.
ask: To what extent do you need to consider VAT returns?

options.en: At the same time as other returns, in the first week of April
September
As VAT returns are quarterly for each business, activity will vary
As VAT returns are annual based on each business' accounting year, activity will vary
January

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. VAT returns are due quarterly. Activity levels vary. Practically, this wouldn't be factored into holiday decisions.

stem: Toys All the Way Ltd is VAT registered. It has made sales of £15,000 at the 20% VAT rate and has sold £5,000 worth of car seats (at the 5% VAT rate). It has purchased several items to the total value of £8,000 all at the 20% VAT rate. Assume that all sales figures given above are exclusive of VAT.
ask: How much VAT would need to be paid to HMRC (if at all)?

options.en: No VAT would be due
£1,650 to HMRC
£1,650 owed back from HMRC
£2,400 to HMRC
£2,400 owed back from HMRC

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. The company's output tax is (15,000*0.2) + (5,000*.05) = £3,250. Their input tax is £1,600 (8,000*0.2), which is subtracted from the output tax. They are required to pay £1,650 to HMRC.

stem: You are asked by a client about VAT exempt items. How do you explain these items and the reason behind having exempt items?
ask: Which of the following is the most accurate explanation?

options.en: Some items are exempt from VAT and no VAT can be charged
Zero rated items are considered to be exempt
Items that cannot be considered for input tax purposes are exempt
Items that cannot be considered for output tax purposes are exempt
None of the above

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. The government places restrictions on the items that can have VAT charged on them and these items are considered to be VAT exempt.

stem: One of your clients, who is a training provider, is worried that they have been charging VAT on exempt items and gives you a list of items that they have been charging VAT on.
ask: Which of these items would you inform your client may be exempt and may not attract VAT?

options.en: Office stationery
Books to be sent out to clients
Training courses
Coffee and tea facilities
They're all OK to be charged VAT

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Provided certain conditions are met, training courses do not attract VAT; therefore, although it is not guaranteed that these would be exempt, further investigation is necessary.

stem: Although many of your clients are required to register for VAT, it is also possible for them to register voluntarily. However, several of your clients have asked why they would bother to register voluntarily.
ask: Which of the following would you state as an advantage of voluntary registration?

options.en: Administration charges will increase for the company
You will have to charge customers VAT
You will be able to recover any VAT you pay out
All prices would have to change
There are no benefits

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. By registering voluntarily, all VAT that has been paid out could be reclaimed, meaning that a company that buys more than it charges out in any given year - i.e. makes an expenditure - may be better off becoming VAT registered

stem: Unusually, one of your clients is a charity and is also VAT registered. You are not used to dealing with this type of client and decide to look up the types of VAT rates that are relevant. You find that almost all charitable activities are rated at 0%.
ask: Which of these is exempt from VAT?

options.en: Charity shops selling donated goods
Charitable advertising
Construction of buildings for charitable purposes
Goods sold at charitable events
Sponsored charitable events

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Sponsored events are exempt from VAT; all others are rated at 0% and could potentially be changed to have a charge to VAT.

stem: Several clients are now experiencing financial difficulties and have found that an increasing number of their clients are not paying invoices. As the invoices have now been issued, your clients have paid the VAT for these invoices. They are aware that they may be able to claim some of the VAT that is associated with bad debts.
ask: Which of the following is a condition of the processes for claiming back VAT associated with bad debts?

options.en: The debt must be at least six months old and less than four years and six months old
The debts could have been passed on to a factoring company
The debt must be older than three years and six months old
The debts must not have been recognised as bad or transferred to a bad debt account
The selling price on the items must be more than their normal selling price

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. If the debts have been passed on to third parties for recovery, then they cannot be used to claim back the VAT associated with the bad debts. The debt must be at least six months old, but cannot be older than four years and six months old. The debts must have been recognised as bad and transferred to a bad debt account. The selling price on the goods must have been no more than the normal selling price.

stem: A heated discussion has broken out about the merits of having certain items that are deemed to be exempt from VAT.
ask: Which of these is seen as a particular disadvantage of having exempt status available?

options.en: The system becomes more complicated
Less VAT is being paid
It encourages mis-labelling of products so they can be considered exempt
It varies from country to country, making it hard to track
It makes the administration much more complex

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Manufacturers and resellers may be encouraged to change labelling, which does not necessarily assist consumers, in a bid to gain exempt status.

stem: A man is taking his car for a Ministry of Transportation (MOT) test. When he receives the invoice, he realises a VAT was charged on the MOT test. He queries this as he believes that MOT tests are not subject to VAT.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: MOT tests are subject to VAT
MOT tests are subject to reduced rate of VAT
Whether or not MOT tests are subject to VAT depends on the class of vehicle
MOT tests are not subject to VAT
MOT tests are subject to a higher rate of VAT than other items

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. MOT tests are not subject to VAT. The MOT test is an annual test of automobile safety, roadworthiness aspects and exhaust emissions required for most vehicles over three years old used on public roads in the UK. Statutory fees and services, such as MOT testing, congestion charge, tolls for bridges, tunnels and roads operated by public authorities, are outside the scope of UK VAT.

stem: Michaela recently paid the congestion charge as she was travelling in London. When making payment she was charged VAT. Later she queried this as she was told that the congestion charge is not subject to VAT.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: The congestion charge is a statutory fee and not subject to VAT
The congestion charge is always subject to VAT
Whether or not the consumer pays VAT on the congestion charge depends on where it is purchased
VAT on the congestion charge is charged at a special rate
The congestion charge is exempt from VAT if the person paying lives in the Greater London area

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. As a statutory fee, the congestion charge is outside the scope of the UK VAT system.

stem: A sole trader collects antiques as a hobby and decides to sell some of her pieces. Her friend tells her that by doing so she is carrying out business activities and buyers should be paying VAT.
ask: Advise the sole trader regarding the current legal position?

options.en: VAT should be paid on all sales, regardless if it is a business activity or the sale or a personal item
The sale of a personal item should include VAT if it is sold for over £5,000
VAT does not need to be paid on the sale of personal items
The sale of a personal item should include VAT if it is sold for over £10,000
VAT is not applicable to the sale of second-hand goods, regardless of whether it is a business or personal sale

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. If an item is sold and it is a non-business activity, then VAT does not need to be paid. The sale of such items falls outside the scope of the VAT system in the UK.

stem: A man has just registered his company for VAT. He understands that he is required to pay VAT on sales but wants to know if the company can claim VAT back for purchases.
ask: Advise the man as to whether and how a company can claim back VAT for purchases?

options.en: A company can start charging VAT but not claim it back
A company can start claiming VAT back once they have charged at least £50,000 in VAT
A company can only start claiming back VAT once they have been registered for at least 24 months
A company can start claiming back and charging VAT once registered
A company can start claiming back VAT once they have been registered for at least 12 months

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Once registered, a company can add VAT to its 'outputs' (e.g. sales) and claim back the VAT it has spent on its 'inputs' (e.g. goods into the business). The difference between the inputs and outputs can then be paid to the HMRC (or claimed from the HMRC if the company has overpaid the amount due).

stem: A man operates his business as a sole trader and is about to register the business for VAT purposes. He believes that once registered, he will have the discretion whether or not to charge VAT to sales.
ask: Advise the man regarding the current legal position?

options.en: Once a sole trader is registered for VAT purposes, VAT must be charged on every sale
Once a sole trader is registered for VAT purposes, VAT must be charged on every sale which is in excess of £100
Sole traders must charge VAT regardless of whether they are registered or not for VAT purposes
Once a sole trader is registered for VAT purposes, VAT must be charged on every sale which is in excess of £950
Sole traders must charge VAT on every sale; there are no exemption available

explanation.en: The best answer is A. A sole trader registered for VAT must charge it on every sale (subject to services and goods that are exempt from VAT or with a zero tax rate).

stem: Your client is aware that only a taxable person needs to be registered for Value Added Tax VAT. He asks whether he would need to register for VAT if he completed all his work through a partnership or a corporation, as it would not then be a person.
ask: Which of the following is the most accurate response?

options.en: A taxable person is the same as a legal entity; therefore VAT applies to people as well as companies
A taxable person can include all businesses such as sole traders, partnerships and corporations
A taxable person is the person that registers i.e. the director, the partner, or the person operating as a sole trader
A taxable person is only in reference to a limited company
A taxable person only applies to registered businesses

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. A taxable person can include all businesses such as sole traders, partnerships and corporations. The notion of a taxable person is broad when it comes to VAT and refers to sole traders, partnerships, limited companies and public companies alike. The word 'person' is misleading; it is the entity that needs to be registered.

stem: You are preparing VAT (Value Added Tax) returns for a client and need to gather all of the details relating to taxable supplies.
ask: Which option best states the most suitable option?

options.en: Taxable supplies are any supply of goods and services at standard, reduced or at 5% rate
Taxable supplies are any supplies of goods and services at standard or reduced rate
Taxable supplies are any supplies of goods and services at standard rate
Taxable supplies are any supply of goods and services at standard, reduced or zero rate
Taxable supplies are any supply of goods and services at standard, reduced, zero or exempt rate

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Taxable supplies are any supplies that attract standard, reduced and zero rated VAT, but not exempt supplies. Zero rated supplies are still taxable, although the rate is currently set at 0%.

stem: Your client provides a range of products relating to children and believes all her items are zero rated.
ask: Which of the following is subject to the reduced VAT rated?

options.en: Children's shoes
Children's clothes
Children's books
Children's car seats
Children's food

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Children's car seats are a reduced rate taxable supply, all others are zero rated.

stem: A registered trader buys goods for £100 and in the same VAT quarter sells them for £400. The standard VAT rate applies.
ask: What is the VAT liability to HMRC?

explanation.en: The best answer is D. The goods were purchased for £100, which with 20% VAT amounts to £120.00. They were sold for £400, which would incur VAT of £80. The trader will have to account to HMRC for £60.00 (£80 output tax received from the customer on the sale LESS £20.00 input tax paid by the trader on the purchase). A is not correct as this is 20% of the purchase price, the input tax. B is not correct as this is 20% of the sale price, the output tax. C is not correct as the output tax exceeds the input tax and the VAT liability is output tax - input tax. E is not correct as the standard VAT rate is 20%, not 5%.

stem: A VAT registered company made sales of €1,000 of goods (at the 20% VAT rate) and provided £1,500,000 insurance and £500,000 credit. The company spent £150,000 in running a fantasy football league game for staff as a hobby, £5,000 for congestion charge fees and £5,000 for MoTs for company vehicles.
ask: How much VAT would need to be paid to HMRC (if any)?

options.en: £300,200 to HMRC
£100,200 to HMRC
£29,800 owed back from HMRC
£200 to HMRC
£1,800 owed back from HMRC

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Insurance and providing credit are exempt from VAT. Education and training, if certain conditions are met, are exempt from VAT. Non-business activities such as a hobby are outside the scope of VAT. Fees that are fixed by law - statutory fees - are also outside the scope of VAT, including the congestion charge or vehicle MoT tests. £1,000 X 0.2 = £200. A is not correct because insurance is exempt from VAT. B is not correct because providing credit is exempt from VAT. C is not correct as hobbies are outside the scope of VAT. E is not correct as fixed, statutory charges are outside the scope of VAT.

stem: A VAT registered charity raised £10,000 through fundraising events and £5,000 through membership subscriptions. The company spent £1,000 on newspapers, and £4,000 on food (not including any restaurant meals or hot takeaway food).
ask: How much VAT would need to be paid to HMRC (if any)?

options.en: £2,000 to HMRC
£1,000 to HMRC
£800 to HMRC
£1,200 to HMRC

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Fundraising events by charities, and membership subscriptions, if certain conditions are met, are VAT exempt. Newspapers and food (not including any restaurant meals or hot takeaway food) are zero rated A is not correct as fundraising events by charities are VAT exempt if certain conditions are met. B is not correct as membership subscriptions are VAT exempt if certain conditions are met. D is not correct as membership subscriptions are VAT exempt if certain conditions are met and newspapers are zero rated E is not correct as fundraising events by charities are VAT exempt if certain conditions are met and food is zero rated.

stem: One of your clients has been given the sad news that he is likely to have a shortened life span and is unlikely to survive for more than another three years. He is planning to give away all of his assets in the near future to reduce his Inheritance Tax (IHT) liability on death.
ask: What do you tell him?

options.en: Giving away his assets will be a great way to reduce IHT liability
He will also need to consider income tax liability if he gives away assets
He may also be liable for a capital gains liability if he gives away assets
IHT is not paid by him and is always paid by the recipients of the gifts or the inheritors of his estate
IHT is never payable when gifts are made in anticipation of death

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Care should be taken when looking to give away assets as a way of reducing IHT, as giving an asset away at this point could give rise to a capital gains liability.

stem: A client is giving away his assets after being informed that he has a terminal illness and a short life expectancy. Despite giving away most of his property, he is still concerned that some of his gifts may be subject to Inheritance Tax (IHT).
ask: Which of the following statements is true?

options.en: If a gift is made within seven years of the death of the individual, then it may be included in the calculation for IHT purposes
If the gift is of a family heirloom, then it will not be subject to IHT
Land will never attract IHT
Gifts to blood relatives won't be caught
Gifts under £15,000 are excluded in any case

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is A. If a gift is made within seven years of the death of the individual, then it may be included in the calculation for IHT purposes. When a gift is made and the individual dies within seven years, the gifts (subject to certain limits) still form part of the estate for IHT purposes.

ask: One of your colleagues has said that they have heard of Inheritance Tax (IHT) being called something else and wonder which one of the following it may be?

options.en: Rich person's tax
Anti-living tax
Parents' tax
Voluntary tax
Left over asset tax

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is D. IHT has often been referred to as a voluntary tax as there is the argument that, if an individual organises their affairs suitably during their lifetime, they can avoid paying the tax at all.

stem: You are asked to explain the underlying concept of Inheritance Tax (IHT) to a new trainee.
ask: Which of the following explanations would be appropriate?

options.en: IHT is based on the value of all of the assets that an individual owns at the time of death
IHT is based on the value of the estate of the individual which may include lifetime gifts prior to death
The contents of the will are irrelevant when calculating IHT
The types of property are irrelevant when calculating IHT
The recipient of the estate is irrelevant when calculating IHT

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is B. IHT is based on the value of the estate, which may include gifts during the lifetime of the individual. There may be reliefs available, but it is the value of the estate that is the starting point for the calculation.

stem: A man comes in to your office to deal with the estate of his father. The entire amount of his estate is £500,000 and it is all being split between him and his sister.
ask: What is the Inheritance Tax (IHT) liability (assuming there are no reliefs, etc., available and no relevant lifetime gifts)?

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is E. £70,000. The rate for IHT is normally 40% for all amounts over £325,000 (based on 2017-2018 rates). £500,000 - £325,000 = £175,000, which is taxed at 40%, yielding an IT liability of £70,000.

stem: A private company limited by shares has 10,000 shares in issue. Your client owns 7,000 of the shares, worth £50 each, and will give his son 3,000 shares. The value of your client's remaining shares will be reduced to £40, as he loses his majority shareholding.
ask: What is the reduction in the value of his estate by this action?

options.en: The reduction in value has no bearing on your client's estate, as he is likely to be living for several decades more

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is B. £190,000. The value of the shares before the transfer was £350,000 (£7,000 * £50 = £350,000). The value of the shares after the transfer is £160,000 (£4,000 * £40 = £160,000); a difference of £190,000. The losses associated with not having the majority rights will form part of the estate reduction.

stem: A married woman has a complicated will and a large estate. She has created a wide range of provisions and made several transfers in anticipation of her death. She is 92.
ask: Which of the following items would be relevant to her estate calculations?

options.en: Gifts of £250 each to her eight grandchildren
A house that the woman gave to her daughter 10 years ago
Her husband's life insurance policy, payable to her upon death, if he outlives her
A £200 gift to her good friend
Property that the woman gave to her sister eight years ago

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is C. An individual can make as many gifts of under £250 each to individuals as they choose and this will be outside of the estate for IHT purposes. Transfers of wealth which took place more than 7 years prior to her death are also discounted from the IHT accounts. As the husband's life insurance policy is written in trust for her benefit, she owns the beneficial interest in the policy, and the value of the policy therefore forms part of her estate.

stem: An unmarried couple died in the same car accident; both pronounced dead at the same time by the paramedics. Their daughter wants to know how this is dealt with for the purposes of determining succession and Inheritance Tax.
ask: Which of the following is part of your advice to the daughter?

options.en: The younger is deemed to have died first, but the daughter can still choose whose estate should be dealt with first
The older is deemed to have died first and their will is dealt with accordingly, followed by the younger
The younger is deemed to have died first
It doesn't make any difference; the combined impact of the wills would be taken into account and it would be these that the daughter needs to deal with
The daughter can choose which will to follow in any event

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is B. The position in relation to simultaneous deaths between non- spouses is that the older is presumed to die first and their will is dealt with first, followed by the younger partner's will.

stem: A woman is having difficulties valuing the estate of her deceased mother. She has been told that several of the assets may be subject to revaluation.
ask: Which of these would potentially need to be re-valued?

options.en: Two vases that are to be separated under the will but are worth just as much individually as they are as a pair
A life assurance policy that has equal values on maturity and on pay-out on death
Shares in a company which have voting rights that are not affected as a result of the deceased's death
Land that did not have to be separated by will to be allocated to different people
Two vases that are to be separated under the will but are worth more as a pair

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Two vases that are to be separated under the will but are worth more as a pair. When valuing assets for an estate, the actual death of an individual may have an impact on their value and this needs to be borne in mind when valuing the assets.

stem: When sorting out the affairs of her mother, your client finds that her mother's finances are in a bit of a mess. Her mother had an outstanding mortgage of £20,000 which no-one knew about. Her mother also has an income tax bill of £3,000, although none of it has been paid. She has an outstanding credit card bill of £500. The costs of her funeral were £1,500 and £500 for the solicitors to sort out the will in the initial aftermath of death.
ask: Which of these items can be deducted from the value of the estate to calculate Inheritance Tax (IHT)?

options.en: Solicitors' costs, credit card, funeral costs and income tax bill
Credit card, solicitors' costs, mortgage and funeral costs
Mortgage, credit card, funeral costs and income tax bill
Funeral costs, income tax bill, mortgage and solicitors' costs
Income tax bill, funeral costs and solicitors' costs

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Mortgage, credit card, funeral costs and income tax bill. Solicitors' costs in the course of the administering the estate are not an allowable expense against IHT, whereas all of the other 'debts' can reduce the value of the estate.

stem: Your client knows that there are certain lifetime transfers that would not be part of his estate if he dies in the next seven years.
ask: He has drawn up a list of the expenditures and gifts that he is making this year and asks you which of these would be exempt from Inheritance Tax (IHT)?

options.en: The total amount of gifts of £325 to each of his 10 grandchildren
A gift of £3,250 to his daughter
A gift of £3,000 to his son
A gift of £5,000 to his other daughter who is not yet married
A gift of £500 to his gardener above and beyond payment for his work on the garden, with the first £250 attracting the small gift exemption

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is C. A gift of £3,000 to his son. The annual exemption allows you to give away up to £3,000 per tax year free of IHT. On top of the annual exemption is a small gifts exemption, but the two cannot be combined to create a total gift of £3,250 to one person (Answer B). Answer C uses the full annual exemption. Answer D is wrong because each parent can give their child up to £5,000 when they get married or enter into a civil partnership. The daughter is not yet married. The small gift exemption allows you to gift up to £250 each to any number of recipients each tax year, although not to anyone who received a gift from your £3,000 annual exemption. You can't give more than £250 and claim the first £250 is a small gift (Answer E). If you give an amount greater than £250, the exemption is lost altogether and the amount would eat into the annual exemption (so not all of the 10 gifts to the grandchildren would be exempt since they would exceed the small gift exemption each and the total annual allowance when combined).

stem: Several individuals have come into your office as they are involved in the estate relating to a woman. They are not sure who is ultimately responsible for paying the Inheritance Tax (IHT) and ask for your advice.
ask: Which of these do you say is responsible for paying IHT on an estate?

options.en: The spouse
The personal representatives
You are as their solicitor
The main beneficiary
Whoever they want

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is B. The responsibility for IHT rests with personal representatives. However, it may well be that the solicitor or other individuals are involved, for ease of gathering the information.

stem: Several beneficiaries who have received assets from an estate come to see you as it transpires that they have not, in fact, paid any Inheritance Tax (IHT).
ask: What happens now?

options.en: The beneficiaries will be fined
The personal representative is now personally responsible
Nothing, it's too late
The beneficiaries are responsible in equal shares
The beneficiaries are responsible for the IHT associated with their assets

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is E. It is the beneficiaries who will ultimately be liable for the IHT associated with their assets, but the personal representative should have ensured it was paid initially.

stem: Your client is concerned that he cannot afford to pay all of his Inheritance Tax (IHT) liability at once. He asks about paying in instalments.
ask: On which of these assets would IHT be able to be paid in instalments?

options.en: Land and assets over £250,000
Quoted shares and unquoted shares
Quoted shares but not unquoted shares
Unquoted shares but not quoted shares
Partnership shares but not quoted or unquoted shares

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The best answer is B. IHT on land, quoted, unquoted and partnership shares may all be paid in instalments. IHT on assets generally cannot be paid in instalments. Value is immaterial although, in reality, most large assets will fall into one of the other categories, but value itself is not the deciding factor.

stem: client wants to know, where an Inheritance Tax (IHT) instalment payment is opted for, what the payment schedule is.
ask: Which option best advises your client?

options.en: Your client can choose her own payment schedule
The schedule starts one month after the date of death and carries on for two years, on a monthly basis
The schedule is spread over five years, in five equal instalments
The schedule starts six months after death and is paid in 10 equal instalments
Instalments are not allowed for IHT

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The instalment plan is set and is not open for negotiations with HMRC under normal circumstances.

stem: A woman gives her house to her son on the understanding that she will continue to live in the house until her death. She believes this will avoid liability for Inheritance Tax (IHT).
ask: Advise the woman regarding this provision under current law?

options.en: Such a transaction will avoid inheritance tax
The house will still be treated as part of the woman's estate
If the house is not in the woman's name, it will not be considered part of her estate
Such a transaction will avoid IHT if it's done two years before her death
Such a transaction will avoid IHT if it's done five years before her death

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is B. As the woman still has a beneficial interest in the house, the value of it when she dies will be included in her estate.

stem: A woman wants to leave a sum of money to a man in her will, but also wants to stipulate what should happen to the money if the man does not survive her by longer than 15 days. She was previously advised by another firm that it's not possible to state what happens to the money once it has passed to the man.
ask: Advise the woman regarding her requirements?

options.en: The woman cannot stipulate what should happen to the money if the man does not survive her
The woman can stipulate what should happen to the money but only if the man does not survive her by 14 days
The woman can stipulate what should happen to the money but only if the man does not survive her by 28 days
The woman can stipulate what should happen to the money if the man does not survive her
Only the man can stipulate what happens to the money when it passes to him, regardless of how long he outlives the woman

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The woman can stipulate what should happen to the money if the man does not survive her. The law allows a substitutional gift to be made if the beneficiary dies shortly after the testator. For example, the woman could leave the money to the man, but specify that the money passes to another person if the man does not outlive her by 30 days.

stem: In his will, your client left an antique vase to a woman. There has been some confusion regarding the value of the vase and further confusion over how to assess the probate value.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: Probate value is the cost of the vase when it was purchased
Probate value is the value at which the beneficiary values the item
If probate value is unknown, then the mean value between the cost of purchase and its current value must be taken
If probate value is unknown, a valuer can be used to determine the value of the item immediately before the death of the deceased
If there is no value stated before death then the item cannot be passed to a beneficiary

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is D. If the probate value of an item is unknown or unclear a valuer can be used in order to determine the value.

stem: Your client had an outstanding income tax bill of £22,000 when he died. His family believe that this will not be deducted from his estate for Inheritance Tax purposes.
ask: Advise the family regarding this issue according to the current law?

options.en: Outstanding income tax can be deducted from a person's estate
Outstanding income tax cannot be deducted from a person's estate
Outstanding income tax can only be deducted from a person's estate if the value of the estate is £450,000 or more prior to the deduction
Only 20% of an outstanding tax bill can be deducted from a person's estate
An outstanding tax bill is void when the person who owes the debt dies

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is A. An outstanding tax bill can be deducted from the person's estate.

stem: Before his death, a man was taken to court by a woman. The man was ordered to pay the woman £20,000 as damages for a tort. The man made payments every month, but there was still £15,000 outstanding when he died. The man's estate will pass to his wife, who is arguing that the £15,000 cannot be deducted from his estate and that the outstanding amount owed is void upon death.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: The outstanding amount owed is void upon death
The outstanding amount owed is not legally void but still cannot be claimed
The outstanding amount can be deducted from the man's estate
A percentage of the outstanding amount can be deducted from the man's estate
The outstanding amount can be deducted from the estate but only if the man died in 2010 or later

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The outstanding amount can be deducted from the man's estate.

stem: Before a woman died, she discovered that she had been overpaying her income tax. She was due to reclaim £17,000, but died before she had the chance to do so. Her relatives would like to know if this money can be claimed back and added to her estate.
ask: Advise the relatives regarding the current legal position?

options.en: Overpayment of income tax can be claimed back and added to the woman's estate
Overpayment of income tax cannot be reclaimed once the person is deceased
Overpayment of income tax cannot be reclaimed, regardless of whether the individual is alive or deceased

Overpayment of income tax cannot be claimed back. Generally, the amount of overpayment is reduced from the next year's tax bill. There is no alternative so if a person dies they lose this benefit as they will obviously not have any future liability for income tax
A percentage of the overpayment amount can be claimed back and added to the estate

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is A. If there has been an overpayment of income tax it can be claimed back and added to the estate.

stem: A man is organising a funeral and wants to know if the funeral expenses can be deducted from the deceased's estate.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: Funeral expenses cannot be deducted from the estate
£1,000 towards the cost of funeral expenses can be deducted from the estate
Funeral expenses can be deducted providing they account for no more than 2% of the estate
Reasonable funeral expenses can be deducted from the estate
Any amount of funeral expenses can be deducted from the estate

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Reasonable funeral expenses can be deducted from the estate.

stem: A couple have been married for 30 years. When the husband died, he left his house to his wife, as he wasn't sure if it would immediately pass to her. The wife has been told that, as he made this specification in the will, it will be subject to Inheritance Tax (IHT), despite the spousal exemption.
ask: Advise the wife regarding the current legal position?

options.en: Any specific distribution clauses mean that IHT will need to be paid
The spousal exemption will still apply
There is no spousal exemption applicable, so IHT will be paid
IHT is not paid on property, regardless of whether there is a spousal exemption
IHT is never paid if the beneficiary is of the same generation as the deceased

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Despite making a specific provision, the spousal exemption will still apply.

stem: A woman leaves £100,000 to a charity in her will. Her other beneficiaries have been informed that this will be subject to Inheritance Tax (IHT), regardless of the fact that it's a gift to charity.
ask: Advise them regarding the current law?

options.en: The woman's gift to charity is exempt from IHT
The woman's gift to charity would only be exempt from IHT if it was less than £1,000
The woman's gift to charity would only be exempt from IHT if it was less than £5,000
The woman's gift to charity would only be exempt from IHT if the charity is run by the Government
The woman's gift to charity is not exempt from IHT

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Gifts made to charity are exempt from IHT.

stem: A man owns two pieces of machinery which have always been used solely by the partnership of which he is one of four partners. Upon his death, there is confusion regarding whether Inheritance Tax (IHT) will be due on the two pieces of machinery.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: The machinery will be subject to inheritance tax in the same way as any other property owned by the man
The machinery will be deemed to be owned by the partnership
No IHT will be paid on the machinery
IHT will be due but will be subject to a 50% business rate relief
IHT will be due but will be subject to a 75% business rate relief

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is D. If the machinery is used mainly for the purposes of the business immediately before the death of the partner then there will be a 50% business rate relief on the value of the machinery.

stem: A man leaves a monetary gift to the Labour party in his will. His family are of the view that this is exempt from Inheritance Tax (IHT), but they are subsequently informed that IHT should be paid on the donation.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: There are no exemptions for donations to political parties
There are no exemptions for gifts or donations of any kind
An exemption can be made providing the donation is less than £100
An exemption can be made as long as the donation does not exceed 5% of the estate
There is an exemption for donations to major political parties

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is E. There is an exemption for donations to major political parties.

stem: Two years before his death, a man gave away £2,500 in gifts each year in the four years before his death. When his estate was calculated for the purpose of Inheritance Tax (IHT), these amounts were included. The recipients of these gifts claim that they should not be included as they are exempt from IHT.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: There is no exemption for gifts
There is only an exemption for gifts not exceeding £1,000 per year
The exemption for gifts only applies if the gift is to one recipient per year
The gifts will be exempt from IHT
A percentage of the gifts will be exempt from IHT

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is D. There is an annual exemption for gifts of up to £3,000 per year.

stem: In the 2016-2017 tax year, your client did not use any of his annual exemption for gifts. However, in the 2017-2018 tax year he would like to give away £5,000 in gifts. Your client would like to know if he can use last year's annual exemption in addition to the current year's exemption.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: The annual exemption for Inheritance Tax (IHT) purposes can be carried over from one year to the next
The annual exemption for IHT purposes cannot be carried over from one year to the next
50% of the previous year's annual exemption can be carried over into the next year
25% of the previous year's annual exemption can be carried over into the next year
The annual exemption can only be carried over if the gift is to be given to one recipient

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is A. The annual exemption for IHT purposes can be carried over from one year to another.

stem: In her will, a woman left a donation to a large national art gallery. Her family are seeking clarification regarding whether the donation will be subject to Inheritance Tax.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: There is no exemption for such donations
There is an exemption for donations to national art galleries
There is an exemption providing the gift is no more than £500
There is an exemption providing the estate is worth at least £500,000
There is an exemption providing the estate is worth at least £750,000

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is B. There is an exemption for donations to national art galleries.

stem: A couple have been married for 25 years. They each gave away £2,500 during 2010. They were then informed that this exceeds the annual exemption for Inheritance Tax (IHT) purposes, which, they are told, is £3,000 per married couple or civil partnership.
ask: Advise the couple regarding the current legal position?

options.en: The annual exemption is per individual, not per couple
The annual exemption is per married couple or civil partnership
Although the annual exemption is based on the individual, it is reduced by 25% for married couples and civil partners
The annual exemption is reduced for people who are or have been married or who are or have been in a civil partnership
The annual exemption is reduced by 10% if you are married or in a civil partnership

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is A. The annual exemption for IHT purposes is per individual, even those in a marriage or civil partnership.

stem: A man comes from a large family and wishes to give a gift of £100 to each of his cousins and second cousins. This equates to giving 54 gifts of £100. His advisers have warned the man against doing this as it would exceed his annual gift exemption for Inheritance Tax (IHT) purposes, but the man disagrees, as each gift is less than £250.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: The gifts will exceed the annual gift exemption so could be liable for IHT
IHT would be applicable to the gifts which take Max over the annual exemption
The small gifts exemption would apply to all the gifts
The small gifts exemption would apply to some of the gifts
All gifts are exempt from IHT

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The small gifts exemption means that a person can make an unlimited amount of gifts per year providing each gift is under £250.

stem: A man wishes to give away some monetary gifts which would not be liable for Inheritance Tax (IHT) should he die soon. He would like to give a friend £3,200 and believes he can do so by using his £3,000 annual exemption and giving the other £200 separately under the small gift exemption.
ask: Advise the man as to whether he can do this under current law?

options.en: The man can give the £3,200 as one gift and the total would not attract IHT
Providing the £3,000 and £200 are given as separate gifts, they would not be liable for IHT
The man cannot use the £3,000 exemption and the small gifts exemption in the same year
The annual exemption and small gifts exemption cannot be combined to give one person a gift larger than £3,000
The small gifts exemption is a maximum of £100, so the man could not give £3,200 and avoid IHT liability

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The annual exemption and small gifts exemption cannot be combined to give one person a gift exceeding £3,000.

stem: A man wants to give a woman a gift of £600. He does so and states that the first £250 is given under the small gifts exemption. The man assumes that if he dies soon, only the remaining £350 would be liable for Inheritance Tax (IHT).
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: The first £250 of any monetary gift is always assumed to be given under the small gifts exemption
The man can give the first £250 under the small gifts exemption providing he informs the recipient of this at the time of the gift
The man can give the first £250 under the small gifts exemption providing he puts this in writing
The man can give the first £300 under the small gifts exemption
The man cannot give the first £250 under the small gifts exemption. The gift is given as a whole and, therefore, does not fit into the small gifts exemption

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Part of a larger gift cannot attract the small gifts exemption. In instances such as this, the full amount would be subject to IHT, should the person giving the gift die within the statutory time frame.

stem: A man wishes to give his daughter a wedding gift of £5,000. He is concerned that, should he die soon, the sum would be liable for Inheritance Tax (IHT).
ask: Advise the man regarding the current legal position?

options.en: The £5,000 would be subject to IHT
The amount in excess of the £3,000 annual gift limit would be subject to IHT
The man could give £3,000 and £250 under the annual gift limit and the small gifts exemption but the remaining amount would be subject to IHT
The entire £5,000 would not be liable for IHT
The annual gift limit cannot be incorporated into the £5,000, so the man could only give the first £250 without potential liability for IHT under the small gifts exemption

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The exemption for parents giving wedding gifts is £5,000, so none of the money would be liable for IHT.

stem: A woman would like to give her daughter £7,000 as a wedding gift but is worried that the amount could be liable for Inheritance Tax (IHT) if she dies soon.
ask: Advise the woman regarding the current legal position?

options.en: The £7,000 would be subject to IHT
The amount in excess of the £3,000 annual gift exemption limit would be subjected to IHT
The amount in excess of the parent's wedding gift exemption limit would be subject to IHT
The woman could combine the parent's wedding gift exemption and the small gifts exemption but anything over this would be subject to IHT
The woman could combine the parent's wedding gift exemption and the annual gift exemption to avoid liability for IHT on the gift

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is E. If the woman wishes to do so, she can combine the parent's wedding gift exemption and the annual gift exemption to give up to £8,000 as a wedding gift to a child without it being liable for IHT.

stem: A man wishes to give his grandson £5,000 as a wedding gift and thinks that this matches the limit for the wedding gift exemption in relation to Inheritance Tax.
ask: Advise the man regarding the current law in this area?

options.en: £5,000 is the wedding gift exemption limit for any family member
£5,000 is the wedding gift limit for parents, brothers/sisters and/or grandparents
The exemption limit for wedding gifts from grandparents is £2,500
The exemption limit for wedding gifts from grandparents is £1,000
The exemption limit for wedding gifts from grandparents is £500

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The exemption limit for wedding gifts from parents is £5,000 but this is reduced to £2,500 when the gift is given by a grandparent.

stem: A man wishes to give a woman a gift of £50,000. He knows that if he dies within a certain amount of time the gift could be liable for Inheritance Tax, but isn't sure exactly what the time limit is.
ask: Advise the man regarding the current time limit according to current law for potentially exempt transfers?

options.en: As long as the person making the transfer doesn't die within two years of the transfer being made then it will not be liable for IHT
As long as the person making the transfer doesn't die within five years of the transfer being made then it will not be liable for IHT
As long as the person making the transfer doesn't die within seven years of the transfer being made then it will not be liable for IHT
As long as the person making the transfer doesn't die within 10 years of the transfer being made then it will not be liable for IHT
As long as the person making the transfer doesn't die within 12 years of the transfer being made then it will not be liable for IHT

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is C. A potentially exempt transfer becomes exempt from IHT once the person giving the gift has lived for more than seven years after the gift was made.

stem: A man gives his daughter £100,000 and is aware that it is a potentially exempt transfer for the purposes of Inheritance Tax (IHT). He believes that she must pay the IHT now and then claim it back should it become exempt in seven years.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: IHT is not paid on a potentially exempt transfer unless it fails to become an exempt transfer and the person who makes the transfer dies. At this point, the IHT is due
IHT is paid at the time of the transfer and claimed back if it becomes exempt
IHT is paid at the time of the transfer and claimed back with interest if it becomes exempt
A potentially exempt transfer cannot be accessed until the transfer has either become exempt or the individual that made the transfer dies, meaning that IHT is due
Potentially exempt transfers are not liable for IHT at any point

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is A. IHT is only due if the person who makes the transfer dies within seven years of the transfer being made.

stem: In 2011 your client used his annual gift exemption. In 2012, he decided to give his friend £100,000 as a potentially exempt transfer and in 2013 he gave £230,000 to his cousin as another potentially exempt transfer. When your client died in 2015, his estate was valued at £ 200,000. His family assumes that there would be no liability for Inheritance Tax (IHT), as his estate did not exceed the threshold.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: The 2011, 2012, 2013 gifts and transfers will be liable for IHT
The 2011, 2012, 2013 gifts and transfers and the estate your client left at the time of his death will be liable for IHT
The 2012 and 2013 transfers become chargeable and will be taken into account when the liability for IHT is decided
There will be no IHT due, as your client's estate does not meet the threshold
There will be a 10% rate of inheritance tax due on your client's estate

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is C. These potentially exempt transfers are not exempt, as your client died within seven years of making them. They will, therefore, form part of his estate, meaning IHT will be payable.

stem: In 2012, your client used her annual gift exemption. In 2014, she gave £150,000 to her niece and in 2015 she gave £250,000 to her nephew. When she died in 2016 she had an estate of £250,000. Her niece and nephew are now unsure which of them, if any, is liable to pay Inheritance Tax (IHT).
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: IHT is not due
IHT is due on the estate only
Your client's niece will avoid paying IHT, but her nephew will be liable
Your client' nephew will avoid paying IHT, but her niece will be liable
Both your client's niece and nephew will avoid paying IHT

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The potentially exempt transfers to your client's niece and nephew are not exempt because your client died within seven years of the transfer. For each transfer the £3,000 annual gift rate can apply, which reduces each transfer to £147,000 and £247,000. The first transfer made in 2014 to your client's niece takes up £147,000 of the nil rate band and your client avoids paying IHT. £178,000 of the nil rate band remains. This can be deducted from your client's nephew's transfer and means he will pay IHT on £69,000. Your client's estate will also be subject to IHT.

stem: In 2013, your client used his annual gift exemption. In 2014 he gave £200,000 to a woman and in 2015 he gave £200,000 to a friend. Your client died in 2016.
ask: How much Inheritance Tax (IHT) will the woman be required to pay?

options.en: The woman will pay no IHT

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is A. The transfer to the woman used up £200,000 of the nil rate band allowance, so IHT would not be due on the transfer to the woman.

stem: Your client lives in a large house surrounded by woodland which he owns. Prior to his death, your client made a few enquiries as to the value of selling the timber but decided against selling. His estate is now being calculated and some argue that the value of the timber should be included in the estate when calculating Inheritance Tax (IHT) liability.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: The value of the timber will not be included in your client's estate
The value of the timber will be included in your client's estate
The value of the timber will be included in your client's estate, because he had made enquiries as to its value
The value of the timber will only be included in your client's estate if the beneficiary intends to sell the timber separately in the future
An average value of the timber will be added to the value of the estate

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is A. The value of the timber will not be included in your client's estate. Unless the timber is given away or sold while your client was alive, then it will not be added to the value of his estate. Per HMRC, when a person dies, the beneficiaries of his or her woodland can ask that the value of the timber - but not the land - be excluded from the deceased's estate. However, when the timber is sold, the beneficiaries may have to pay IHT on the value of the sale, unless it also qualifies for relief.

stem: A man inherited a large amount from his sister, but sadly he died 3.5 years later.
ask: On calculating the Inheritance Tax (IHT) now due on the man's death, you are aware of quick succession relief and wonder by how much this will reduce the IHT liability?

options.en: Nothing; they are not spouses

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is C - If the death takes place between three and four years, 40% of the IHT paid by the man in relation to his sister's estate will be taken off his current tax bill.

stem: You have just read a will for the estate of an old client of yours and one of the beneficiaries does not wish to have the assets they have been bequeathed.
ask: What do you tell them?

options.en: You can complete a diversion to send the assets to another person of the beneficiary's choice
You can simply allocate the assets to another beneficiary
The beneficiary must take the assets but can just sell them as they see fit
A disclaimer can be made, but the beneficiary will then lose control of the assets
The other beneficiaries can each take a greater share of the estate, inclusive of the assets concerned

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Where a beneficiary does not wish to take the asset that has been left to them, they are able to make a disclaimer, but they will then lose control of the asset.

stem: Two of your clients are personal representatives for a deceased individual and they are concerned about the practicalities of administering the estate.
ask: Which of the following is the most accurate?

options.en: Your client will need to turn all assets into cash, to work out the true value of the estate
Your client will have to ensure that the Inheritance Tax (IHT) is paid in relation to the estate
The beneficiaries need to ensure that they keep an accurate check on deadlines
Items cannot be ring-fenced to prevent them from being used for IHT
Debts will not need to be satisfied from the estate

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is B. The personal representatives (PRs) have to ensure that the IHT is paid in relation to the estate. The assets do not all have to be sold, although it may be possible to liquidate some of them to pay off debts. Some assets can be ring-fenced. Timing is important, particularly with assets that are changing in value. The PRs are on tight timelines and need to ensure that they keep an accurate check on deadlines.

stem: You have just read a will for the estate of an old client of yours. One of the beneficiaries does not wish to have the property they have been bequeathed and does not want to lose control of the assets. He is looking for alternative ways of dealing with the situation. He suggests a variation.
ask: What do you tell him?

options.en: A variation does not allow him to retain control of the assets, so is of no use
Those taking the benefit of the assets would have to be beneficiaries under the will
No Inheritance Tax (IHT) liability will follow from a variation, regardless of the way in which the variation is undertaken
The variation could be viewed as a potentially exempt transfer, which may result in IHT being payable, if the individual dies within seven years
The variation will be viewed as a potentially exempt transfer, which may result in IHT being payable, if the individual dies within seven years

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The variation could be a potentially exempt transfer, but it is not necessarily a potentially exempt transfer; the way the variation is categorised depends on the circumstances.

stem: A professor acts as a consultant and owns 40% of shares in a private company. The professor is recognised as a leader in his field and in developing new software as part of his role as a consultant. When the professor dies, his son inherits his estate. The shares are valued at their open market value immediately before the professor's death. However, once the professor died the value of the shares plummeted by 70% due to the fact that he will no longer be working for the company. The son argues that it's unfair to value the shares at their market value prior to the professor's death.
ask: Which of the following best describe the current legal position?

options.en: Shares cannot be inherited, so the value is irrelevant
The shares must be valued at their open market value immediately before the professor died
The shares will be valued at their open market value six months after the professor's death if all beneficiaries are willing to delay probate
The change in value of the shares may be taken into account
The change in value of the shares will only be taken into account if the company were a public limited company

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is D. There are occasions where the change in the value of an asset may be taken into account. It could be deemed acceptable to take into account the devaluation of the shares which will mean that they will be valued at having a lower value than the open market value immediately before the professor's death.

stem: A woman is dealing with the estate of her father who recently died. She is concerned that she will be responsible for paying Inheritance Tax (IHT). His estate is valued at £300,000.
ask: Advise the woman regarding the amount of IHT to be paid according to current law?

options.en: IHT must be paid at 10%
IHT must be paid at 20%
IHT must be paid at 40%
The value of the estate means it is under the threshold for paying IHT
Estates valued under £500,000 are exempt from paying IHT

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is D. As the estate has been valued under £325,000 it comes under the nil rate band and no IHT will be owed.

stem: A man takes out a life insurance policy written in trust for a named beneficiary, believing that this policy will not be part of his estate upon his death. A woman tells him this is incorrect and that life insurance policies are counted as part of a person's estate for Inheritance Tax purposes.
ask: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.en: Life insurance policies are always included in a person's estate
Life insurance policies that are written in trust for a named beneficiary are not included in a person's estate
Life insurance policies that are written in trust for a named beneficiary are included in a person's estate
Life insurance policies are never included in a person's estate
Life insurance policies that are written in trust for a named beneficiary are the only type of policies to be included in a person's estate

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Generally, life insurance policies are included in a person's estate. However, when the policy is written in trust for a named beneficiary, it is not part of the estate.

stem: You are creating a memo for the use of more junior colleagues about Inheritance Tax (IHT).
ask: What is the rule for determining which assets should be considered part of the estate for IHT purposes?

options.en: The deceased needed to be legally entitled to the assets, immediately before death
The deceased needed to be legally entitled to the assets, immediately after death
The deceased needed to be beneficially entitled to the assets, immediately before death
The deceased needed to be beneficially entitled to the assets immediately after death
The deceased needed to be both legally and beneficially entitled to the assets, immediately before death

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is C. The deceased needs to be beneficially entitled to the assets, immediately before death, for them to be included in the estate. Note: The ownership of land is dealt with in two ways: (i) the legal ownership (ii) the economic benefit, commonly referred to as the beneficial ownership. The legal ownership is separate from the beneficial ownership and the legal owner does not necessarily need to be the same as the beneficial owner. The legal owner is said to hold the beneficial interest in the property on trust for the beneficial owner, who has a right to the income from the property or a share in it, and a right to the proceeds of sale of the property or part of the proceeds.

stem: A man left his property worth £500,000 to his son, for life, with the remainder being left to his daughter. The son has died and you are trying to quantify the extent of Inheritance Tax (IHT) liability on the man's estate.
ask: Which of the following best explains the extent of the IHT liability, if any, in this case?

options.en: The estate will be treated as if the whole £500,000 was being transferred from the son to the daughter
It will depend on the number of years that the man was living in the property
There would be no IHT liability, at this point
IHT would be payable on half of the value
IHT would be payable on the current value of the property

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is A. The property will be treated as if it had been transferred in its entirety from the son to the daughter.

stem: A person dies in January 2017 leaving assets valued at £500,000 and liabilities of £150,000.
ask: What is the Inheritance Tax liability payable by the personal representatives (PRs)?

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is A. £10,000. Value of estate: Assets 500,000. Less: Liabilities 150,000. Net value: 350,000. Rates of tax: £325,000 @ 0%; £25,000 @ 40% = 10,000. Tax payable by PRs: 10,000.

stem: A person dies, leaving an estate comprising a house worth £300,000; shares worth £500,000; and various bank accounts worth a total of £155,000. The deceased owed £70,000 to creditors. The house passes to the spouse of the deceased under a will and the entire residuary estate is to go to the children. The cumulative total of chargeable transfers in the seven years before death is £190,000.
ask: What is the Inheritance Tax (IHT) liability?

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The best answer is D. £180,000. The value of the estate assets (house + shares + cash) on death is £955,000. Liabilities (debts of £70,000) are deducted, giving the value of the estate transferred (£885,000). The house is covered by the spouse exemption, leaving a chargeable estate of £585,000. The cumulative total of transfers made in the previous seven years is £190,000. This is deducted first from the nil rate band, leaving £135,000. £135,000 × 0% £450,000 X 40% = £180,000 payable in IHT.

stem: A husband and wife each have property worth £310,000. The husband dies on the 1st of March 2015, leaving all of his estate to his wife. The wife dies on the 15th of April 2016, leaving all of her estate (which is now worth £620,000) to the children.
ask: What is the Inheritance Tax (IHT) liability?

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The best answer is A. £0. Because the first spouse left all of his estate to the surviving spouse, the spouse exemption will apply and no IHT will be payable. Further, if a deceased spouse or civil partner hasn't used any of his or her nil rate band, this can be used to increase the IHT threshold of the surviving spouse or civil partner when he or she dies. His or her estate can be worth up to £650,000 in 2016-2017 before IHT is owed.

stem: Person A and person B are in a civil partnership. Person A dies on 4 May 2014, leaving their entire estate of £290,000 to person B. Person B dies on 19 August 2016, leaving all of their estate to person B's children, which is now worth £635,000.
ask: Which of the following answers best describes how much inheritance tax is due on person B's estate?

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is A; no inheritance tax ('IHT") is payable on person B's estate. From 9 October 2007, the balance of the nil-rate band (£325,000 per person) is transferable between spouses or civil partners. Therefore, in this scenario, IHT will only be payable if the estate is worth more than both partner's nil-rate band combined i.e. £650,000.

stem: Person A gifts a house worth £420,000 to person B on 1 October 2012. Person A dies on 15 September 2016 and leaves an estate of £1,250,000. Person A never used their annual gift exemption.
ask: Which of the following answers best describes how much IHT is payable on the gift?

explanation.topic: Wills and the Administration of Estates
explanation.en: The correct answer is A; £28,480 will be payable as IHT on the gift of the house, calculated as follows: Being a lifetime transfer, person A is able to use their annual exemptions from 2011 (carried forward) and 2012 = £6,000. £420,000 less £6,000 = £414,000. Person A also has a nil-rate band of £325,000, £414,000 less £325,000 = £89,000. £89,000 taxed at 40% = £35,600. Because the transfer was made within 3-4 years before death, taper relief applies and only 80% of the charge to IHT is payable; 80% of £35,600 = £28,480.

stem: A woman is a sole trader. During the years 2014, 2015 and 2016, she made approximately £2,000 per year. However, in 2017, she made £14,000. The woman believes that she is allowed to 'carry over' the remainder of the personal allowance she didn't use in years 2014, 2015 and 2016.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: The personal allowance can be carried over indefinitely
The personal allowance can be carried over but only for one year
Only £1,000 of the personal allowance can be carried over
Only 50% of the personal allowance can be carried over
The personal allowance cannot be carried over

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. No part of the personal allowance can be carried over into the subsequent tax year.

stem: An individual receives income from the following sources: they are employed part-time; they work freelance some of the time on a job by job basis; they also have property which they have sold at a profit.
ask: When they are looking at their tax liability, which of their income sources should they consider when it comes to paying income tax?

options.en: The property gain
The part-time employment
The freelance employment
The property gain and part-time employment
The part-time employment and freelance employment

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Although income tax is likely to be deducted as part of the part-time employment, there is still an income tax liability; freelance employment will also fall into the category of income tax.

stem: Consider an individual who is a partner in a firm and receives partnership profits. They have an accountant who produces the annual expenses and income report for the partnership.
ask: Who is responsible for the income tax calculations and preparation of the required forms?

options.en: Each individual partner needs to complete their own income tax form, based on profits only
The accountant can prepare and send off all documents without gaining the approval of the individuals
The partnership will pay corporation tax and the individuals are not involved
Each individual partner needs to complete their own income tax form, based on profits, and a partnership return is required
A partnership does not pay tax at all

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Individuals will have to pay income tax based on their profits and a partnership return will also be required; the accountant can be involved, but the individuals will have to sign their own forms.

stem: An employee who works full-time recently gave up his job in the middle of the tax year and became self-employed.
ask: At the end of the year, which of the following is most likely to be true of the employee's income tax position?

options.en: PAYE would be paid by the employer after their departure
The individual would only be required to complete self-assessment from the commencement of self-employment
Business expenses cannot be deducted during the self-employed period
A readjustment based on PAYE that has been taken from the self-employed period may be necessary against the employed period
A readjustment based on PAYE that has been taken from the employed period may be necessary against the self-employed period

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Changing status in the middle of the year requires the individual to draw on a wide range of income tax issues and types. Several different tax situations can exist in the same tax year.

stem: Your client asks for your advice on his income tax liability for the current tax year. He is required to fill in a self-assessment form. He has complicated financial affairs, having taken out several loans to facilitate various transactions.
ask: Which of the following best describes a loan in which your client would be able to deduct interest payments as against his income tax liability?

options.en: A loan to buy a car for his wife who does some administration for him
A loan to buy a new printing press for the business
A personal loan so that he can pay his own mortgage during a difficult period
A mortgage on his home
A loan to pay inheritance tax, as he has to pay personally not as a personal representative

explanation.en: The best answer is B. The interest on a loan that is associated purely with business expenses is tax deductible. Interest on a loan taken in order to pay inheritance tax as a personal representative is also deductible. However, such interest is not deductible if taken to pay his own personal tax liability.

ask: With respect to the 2017-18 tax year, which of the following statement best describes the legal position pertaining to tax deduction at source on savings and dividend income?

options.en: Bank and building societies must deduct 20% of any interest accumulated of their depositors. Companies distributing dividends do not deduct 10% tax from source before making dividend distributions
Bank and building societies must deduct 20% of any interest accumulated of their depositors. Companies distributing dividends deduct 10% tax from source before making dividend distributions
Bank and building societies do not deduct any interest accumulated of their depositors. Companies distributing dividends deduct 10% tax from source before making dividend distributions
Bank and building societies do not deduct any interest accumulated of their depositors. Companies distributing dividends do not deduct any tax from source before making dividend distributions

Bank and building societies do not deduct any interest accumulated of their depositors. Companies distributing dividends do not deduct any tax from source before making dividend distributions, unless the amount of the dividend is over £100,000

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Bank and building societies do not deduct any interest accumulated of their depositors. Companies distributing dividends do not deduct any tax from source before making dividend distributions. The Personal Savings Allowance means that basic and higher rates taxpayers will not have to pay tax on certain amounts of their savings income they receive from banks and building societies. As a result, most people will no longer pay tax on savings interest and banks and building societies will stop deducting tax at source from interest accumulated in their customers' accounts. Due to the Dividend Allowance, companies distributing dividends do no longer deduct tax from source before making distributions, and dividend income are received by taxpayers in full.

stem: Carl wants to know why, when he looks at his payslip, the amount that he actually takes home is less than he expects. He understands that he pays income tax but is still confused.
ask: Which of the following best describes a likely reason?

options.en: Carl has to pay income tax on his student loan repayments
Carl's employers forgot to charge NI in the past, and he has NI back payments to pay
Carl is liable to income tax on pension contributions
PAYE is calculated weekly, so some weeks it will appear higher relative to hours worked
PAYE is calculated across the year, so some weeks it will appear higher relative to hours worked

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. There are many other factors that may result in less take home pay than just income tax.

stem: A partnership is preparing its accounts for the end of the year and is also giving the income details to the individual partners, so that they can produce their own accounts on self- assessment. Several changes have happened in the partnership, including new partners entering and some going part-time.
ask: Which of the following best describes how the % split of profits should be dealt with?
