You could only provide generic mortgage advice

explanation.en: The best answer is A. It is not normally in a client's best interests to be referred by the solicitor to a tied agent (i.e. an agent which sells the products of one particular company or provider only). Instead, a referral should be made to an independent financial adviser. 06.1 and IB6.1 prevents a solicitor from entering into any restrictive arrangements in connection with regulated activities that could constrain the advice you give to clients or the referrals that you make. On the other hand, a solicitor is permitted to regularly refer a client interested in taking out a mortgage to a particular mortgage provider, provided this is in the client's best interests and the solicitor explains to the client that the agent offers products from only one mortgage provider (see IB6.2). B is not the correct answer. A solicitor is permitted to regularly refer a client interested in taking out a mortgage to a particular mortgage provider, provided this is in the client's best interests and the solicitor explains to the client that the agent offers products from only one mortgage provider (see IB6.2). C is not the best answer. A referral can, and probably should in this case be made to an independent financial adviser. 06.1 and IB6.1 prevents a solicitor from entering into any restrictive arrangements in connection with regulated activities that could constrain the advice you give to clients or the referrals that you make. On the other hand, a solicitor is permitted to regularly refer a client interested in taking out a mortgage to a particular mortgage provider, provided this is in the client's best interests and the solicitor explains to the client that the agent offers products from only one mortgage provider (see IB6.2). D is not the best answer. A solicitor is permitted to regularly refer a client interested in taking out a mortgage to a particular mortgage provider, provided this is in the client's best interests and the solicitor explains to the client that the agent offers products from only one mortgage provider (see IB6.2). It is not normally in a client's best interests to be referred by the solicitor to a tied agent (i.e. an agent which sells the products of one particular company or provider only). Instead, a referral should be made to an independent financial adviser. E is not the best answer. As you are authorised by the FCA there is no restriction on providing mortgage advice. In any event, solicitors are allowed to recommend independent financial advisers as part of the professional practice without FCA approval. They can also recommend tied agents if this is in the client's best interests.

stem: You have been acting for Alex in the sale of his house. The net proceeds are £1,200,000. He asks you to invest in a mixed portfolio consisting of shares in premier league clubs and entertainment organisations. He asks you to make the necessary arrangements. You are not authorised by the FCA and have no significant investment experience.
ask: Which of the following best describes the advice you can give Alex?

options.en: You can only give generic investment advice
You can give the client advice about preferential investments, but cannot make arrangements
The client should be referred to an independent financial adviser. Arrangements should be made with or through an authorised third party
The client does not need to be referred to an independent financial adviser. Arrangements must be made through an authorised third party
You can give investment advice since you intend to make arrangements through an authorised third party

explanation.en: D is the best answer. The first point to consider is whether you have enough expertise even to provide generic advice to Alex about investments (mandatory principles and 01.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct). If not - then you can either refer him to an independent financial advisor from the very outset, or use the ATP route. If you do have enough expertise generally - then you can use the ATP route in order to obtain specific advice. Once the advice has been given, you will be able to make arrangements in consequence of the advice without such arrangements being caught by the Act - provided these are carried out with or through an authorised person. The incidental exemption does not seem to apply - as the investment aspect seems to be a completely separate investment. A is not the best answer. You can go beyond generic advice using an independent adviser or authorised third party. B is not correct. The first point to consider is whether you have enough expertise even to advise Alex generally about investment (mandatory principles and 01.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct). If not - then you can either refer him to an independent financial advisor from the very outset, or use the ATP route. If you do have enough expertise generally - then you can use the ATP route in order to obtain specific advice. Once the advice has been given, you will be able to make arrangements in consequence of the advice without such arrangements being caught by the Act - provided these are carried out with or through an authorised person. However, you are neither authorised nor qualified to provide specific investment advice to the client. C is not correct. It suggests that you would have no alternative but to refer the client to an IFA for obtaining specific advice. This is incorrect, as the ATP route may be used for obtaining advice for the client, without having to refer to an IFA. The first point to consider is whether you have enough expertise even to advise Alex generally about investment (mandatory principles and 01.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct). If not - then you can either refer him to an independent financial advisor from the very outset, or use the ATP route. E is not the best answer. You must consider whether you have enough expertise even to advise Alex generally about investment (mandatory principles and 01.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct). If not - then you should refer him to an independent financial advisor from the very outset or obtain advice about the options available to Alex from an ATP.

stem: You act for Jackie Onasis, the widow of a former client. She is the executrix of her deceased husband's will. The estate includes the family home (which the executrix wants to sell) and a substantial portfolio of stocks and shares. Some of the shares will be transferred directly to individual beneficiaries under the will, while others will need to be sold.
ask: Which of the following best represents the services that you can offer the widow?

options.en: You can only give generic advice
You can use the exemption for professions (Part XX FSMA)
You must use the ATP exemption
You cannot advise the client
The investment advice is unlikely to be necessary in distributing the assets of the estate in accordance with the will

explanation.en: B is the best answer. You can use the exemption for professions (Part XX FSMA). The house is not an investment - though when it is sold, the proceeds may have to be invested. The stocks and shares will, however, be investments within the FSMA. Possible regulated activities under the FSMA include advising your client, arranging in relation to the sale of the shares and safeguarding the shares. You could use the exclusion for activities reasonably necessary in the course of administering the estate (except for managing), provided any remuneration for the advising / arranging / safeguarding was not charged 'separately.' Even if the above exclusion does not apply, you could still argue that all of the above activities are 'incidental' to the main purpose for which you were instructed, viz. to administer the estate - in which case you could use the exemption for members of a profession. Advising and arranging (as well as taking a non-routine discretionary management decision regarding) the sale of retail investment products are all permitted (provided, of course, that you have sufficient expertise - 01.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct, such that you could do these without using an ATP. The same, of course, applies to safeguarding. In order for the exemption to apply, you would need to ensure that all commission was properly accounted for to the client. A is not the best answer. You can rely on the incidental exemption (Section XX) to give more specific advice. C is not the best answer. You should use an ATP if you are not sufficiently experienced to give advice. Only those activities incidental to the administration of the estate itself would be exempted under the incidental exemption (Section XX). If the widow wanted assistance with what to do with her share of the estate after the administration was finished, this exemption would not be available, and an ATP would have to be used. D is not the best answer. You can give generic advice and advise and arrange under the incidental exemption or under the ATP exemption. E is not correct. The investment advice may be necessary in order to distribute the assets of the estate.

stem: You are a partner in a boutique media law firm. The firm have many high net worth individuals who require financial advice. The firm hires a financial adviser with a good track record and the results for clients are highly successful. Despite the economic trend, the clients get good returns on their investments. A rival, realizing that neither the adviser, nor the firm, are authorised by the FCA, reports the firm to the FCA.
ask: Which of the following best represents the firm's potential liability?

options.en: The firm could face a very substantial fine from the FCA and anybody involved could face imprisonment
The firm could face a very substantial fine from the Court. The adviser would not be separately culpable
The firm could face a very substantial fine from the SRA and anybody involved could face imprisonment
If convicted, the adviser and any other person involved could be sentenced to imprisonment for a maximum of two years and a fine
If convicted, the adviser and any other person involved could be sentenced to imprisonment for a maximum of six months and a fine

explanation.en: The best answer is D. Under section 23 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (ESMA) any person convicted of carrying out a regulated activity without authorisation can be sentenced to imprisonment for a maximum of two years and a fine. A is not the best answer. The firm could be fined and the individuals could face imprisonment, but as section 23 FSMA provides criminal sanctions, it is likely to be the Crown Court that imposes the sanctions. B is not the best answer. Under section 23 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) any person convicted of carrying out a regulated activity without authorisation can be sentenced to imprisonment for a maximum of two years and a fine. C is not the best answer. It is the FCA in the first instance that regulated unauthorized regulated activities. The SRA may impose sanctions for failure to comply with the FCA requirements which would be a breach of principle 1 - the duty to uphold the rule of law, principle 6, to uphold the reputation of the profession, and 7, to comply with regulatory and legal requirements. E is not the best answer. Under section 23 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) any person convicted of carrying out a regulated activity without authorisation can be sentenced to imprisonment for a maximum of two years and a fine.

stem: You are a member of a very reputable city firm with many household name clients. The firm outsource compliance to an agency which has a reputation for reliability and a good track record. You advertise that the firm is authorised by the FCA to give investment advice. You are surprised to receive a summons for a breach of section 24 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) for making false claims to be authorised or exempt.
ask: Which of the following best describes a possible defence?

options.en: You outsource your advertising and are not responsible for what advertising material may claim
You did not realise that authorisation was required and will, in future, ensure that you personally obtain authorisation from the FCA
Nobody suffered any loss as a result of the oversight
You were never given any warnings by the SRA or the FCA. You did everything that you were told you have to do
You took all reasonable precautions and exercised all due diligence to avoid committing the offence

explanation.en: E best describes a potential defence to prosecution under section 24 of the FSMA. Firms are required to take all reasonable precautions and exercise all due diligence to comply with the requirements of the Act, but there is a defence of due diligence. A is not the best answer. The firm are obligated to take all reasonable precautions and exercise due diligence to ensure that advertising is correct. The firm are responsible for what their advertising material contains and outsourcing advertising does not detract from this obligation. B is not correct. As with any statute, ignorance of the law is no defence. Firms are required to make themselves aware of the requirement, although the sanction imposed may be more lenient where the breach was inadvertent and there is a high likelihood of future compliance. C is not correct. As the FSMA creates criminal offences of non-compliance such as section 24, the firm in breach can be held criminally liable irrespective of whether anybody suffered any loss. The sanction imposed may take this into account as a mitigating factor. D is not the best answer. The SRA are not directly involved in regulation under the FSMA. They only become involved where the firm seeks to rely on the exemption for professionals. There is no prerequisite of a warning by the FCA (or the SRA). The firm are under a duty to ensure compliance. However, due diligence may be a defence to prosecution under section 24 ESMA.

stem: Your firm are approached by Alphonse Capone in respect of tax advice. Mr Capone is entitled to a tax rebate and you secure this for him. Mr Capone suggests that you should diversify and offer financial advice. He enters into a contract to pay you a generous commission on any profits made as a result of your advice. The portfolio you suggest is highly successful. Mr Capone refuses to pay the commission as he discovers you were not authorised by the FCA.
ask: Which of the following best represents your redress against Capone?

options.en: You can enforce the contract against Capone, although you may face sanctions from the FCA
You cannot enforce the contract against Capone and you are likely to face sanctions
You cannot enforce the contract against Capone, but as the investments were successful you are unlikely to face any sanctions
You can recover from Capone on grounds of unjust enrichment as a matter of restitution
You can enforce the contract against Capone and as the investments were successful, you are unlikely to face any sanctions

explanation.en: The best answer is B. Contracts entered into in breach of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 are unenforceable (section 26(1) FSMA), including against the client. Sanctions, including imprisonment, a fine or loss of any existing authorisation from the FCA or the SRA are possible, even though no loss was incurred. A is not correct. Contracts entered into in breach of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 are unenforceable (section 26(1) FSMA), including against the client. C is not the best answer. Sanctions, including imprisonment, or a fine are possible, even though no loss was incurred, as the offences under sections 21, 23 and 24 are criminal and not dependent on loss. Section 26(2) addresses recovery of losses where the client suffers a monetary loss. D is not the best answer. You cannot recover under the agreement (section 26(1)) FSMA and it is unlikely that the court will look favourably on a restitution claim, particularly as UK common law has a restricted concept of restitution or quasi-tortious claims. E is not correct. Contracts entered into in breach of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 are unenforceable (section 26(1) FSMA), including against the client. Sanctions, including imprisonment, or a fine are possible, even though no loss was incurred, as the offences under sections 21, 23 and 24 are criminal and not dependent on loss. Section 26(2) addresses recovery of losses where the client suffers a monetary loss.

stem: You represented Mrs Taylor in her divorce proceedings and in providing estate planning advice. You advised her to keep a valuable Emmings modern art painting which was subsequently sold by her heirs at auction at a loss. You are not authorised by the FCA and did not rely on an exemption.
ask: Which of the following best describes your position?

options.en: Art works are generally not regulated investments and so your advice would probably not require FCA authorisation
Matrimonial advice and estate planning are exempt from the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 requirements and never need authorisation
All matrimonial advice requires FCA authorisation or exemption where valuable property is involved
All estate planning advice requires authorisation or exemption where valuable property is involved
Generally matrimonial and estate planning do not require FCA authorisation, unless valuable property is involved

explanation.en: The best answer is A. Art works are generally not regulated investments and advice in relation to them does not require FCA authorisation. Matrimonial and estate planning may well involve regulated investments such as shares and debentures, unit trusts, government and public securities. Advising as well as safeguarding such assets are regulated activities and would require authorisation or exemption. B is not correct. Matrimonial and estate planning may well involve regulated investments such as shares and debentures, unit trusts, government and public securities. Advising as well as safeguarding such assets are regulated activities and would require authorisation or exemption. C is not correct. Matrimonial advice would only require authorisation or exemption if a regulated activity if regulated investments such as shares and debentures, unit trusts, government and public securities were at issue, and if you carry out a regulated activity such as dealing in investments as an agent, arranging, safeguarding, administering a client's assets or advising D is not correct. Estate planning would only require authorisation or exemption if regulated investments such as shares and debentures, unit trusts, government and public securities were at issue, and if you carry out a regulated activity such as dealing in (the sale of) investments as principal or agent, arranging assignment of life policies, managing, safeguarding and administering client's assets or advising. E is not the best answer. Matrimonial and estate planning require authorisation or exemption if regulated investments such as shares and debentures, unit trusts, government and public securities are at issue, or if you carry out a regulated activity such as dealing in (the sale of) investments as principal or agent, arranging assignment of life policies, managing, safeguarding and administering client's assets or advising. The value of the investments is only a factor in determining, for example, whether the incidental exception applies, but authorisation is required even for investments of little value or those that involve a loss.

stem: You are asked to act as the personal representative of Mr F Mercury who leaves his property to his fellow band members and a former partner. In the course of administering the estate, you are required to handle a portfolio of shares, debentures and arrange the allocation and reinvestment of a return on an occupational pension scheme.
ask: Which of the following best represents your regulatory obligations?

options.en: You need FCA authorisation as regulated investments are involved and you are safeguarding, arranging and possibly advising in relation to particular investments
You would need FCA authorisation unless you provide purely generic advice
You would not need FCA authorisation as you would only be providing generic advice, provided that you get no commission and there is no separate bill
You could rely on the exemption for solicitors acting as personal representatives, provided that you get no commission and there is no separate bill
You could rely on the exemption for solicitors acting as personal representatives, provided that you only give generic advice

explanation.en: The best answer is D. You are likely to be involved in a regulated activity. Solicitors acting as personal representatives (PRs) can rely on the exemption for trustees and PRs in Article 66 of the Regulated Activities Order 2001 (RAO), provided that you get no commission and do not bill the client separately for investment advice. A is not the best answer. You are likely to be involved in a regulated activity. However personal representatives (PRs) can rely on the exemption for trustees and PRs in Article 66 of the Regulated Activities Order 2001 (RAO), provided that you get no commission and do not bill the client separately for investment advice. B is not the best answer. You are likely to be involved in a regulated activity. However personal representatives (PRs) can rely on the exemption for trustees and PRs in Article 66 of the Regulated Activities Order 2001 (RAO), provided that you get no commission and do not bill the client separately for investment advice. C is not the best answer. Personal representatives (PRs) can rely on the exemption for trustees and PRs in Article 66 of the Regulated Activities Order 2001 (RAO), provided that you get no commission and do not bill the client separately for investment advice. If that is the case, there is no reason to restrict the advice and assistance to purely generic advice. E is not the best answer. Personal representatives (PRs) can rely on the exemption for trustees and PRs in Article 66 of the Regulated Activities Order 2001 (RAO), provided that you get no commission and do not bill the client separately for investment advice. If that is the case, there is no reason to restrict the advice and assistance to purely generic advice.

stem: You represent Ms Herb, and member of the band Girlz Own in a copyright dispute regarding royalties in respect of certain popular, successful songs. In the course of your work, you advise her regarding offshore trusts on behalf of her children. You are not authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), but you are careful to follow the SRA Financial Services (Conduct of Business) Rules 2001 and to stay within the SRA Financial Services (Scope) Rules 2001.
ask: Which of the following best describes your position?

options.en: You can rely on the exemption for members of a profession
You cannot rely on the exemption for members of a profession if the advice is not complementary to your legal advice
You can rely on the exemption for members of a profession provided that less than 50% of the work was investment advice
You can rely on the exemption for members of a profession provided that you only gave generic advice
You cannot rely on the exemption for members of a profession if you provide advice about overseas trusts or assistance

explanation.en: The best answer is B. You cannot rely on the exemption for members of a profession in part XX of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) if the investment advice was not complementary to legal advice. If you were advising in a legal capacity about the offshore trust, you may be able to rely on the exemption if the advice is incidental, i.e. less than 50% of the advice. A is not the best answer. You cannot rely on the exemption for members of a profession in part XX of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) if the investment advice was not complementary to legal advice. If you were advising in a legal capacity about the offshore trust, you may be able to rely on the exemption. C is not the best answer. You cannot rely on the exemption for members of a profession in part XX of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) if the investment advice was not complementary to legal advice. If it was complementary to the legal advice, the advice would need to be incidental, i.e. less than 50% of the firm's work. D You cannot rely on the exemption for members of a profession in part XX of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) if the investment advice was not complementary to legal advice. If it was complementary to the legal advice, the advice would need to be incidental, i.e. less than 50% of the firm's work. If you can rely on the exemption you can perform regulated activities and are not restricted to generic advice. E You cannot rely on the exemption for members of a profession in part XX of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) if the investment advice was not complementary to legal advice. If it was complementary to the legal advice, the advice would need to be incidental, i.e. less than 50% of the firm's work. If you can rely on the exemption you can give advice in relation to overseas trusts and assist, provided that you have the knowledge and expertise to do so.

stem: Your corporate commercial firm also represents existing clients in matrimonial disputes and estate planning. The firm advertise themselves as a commercial firm and the clients are corporate executives seeking corporate legal advice involving investment advice. Matrimonial and estate planning work takes more billable hours than investment advice. However, the investment aspects of the corporate work nets tens of millions of pounds per year, while the matrimonial and estate planning makes just one million pounds on average per year.
ask: Which of the following best represents the firms' entitlement to rely on an exemption?

options.en: If legal advice exceeds 50% of the firm's work, the firm may be entitled to rely on the exemption for members of a profession
If legal advice exceeds 50% of the firm's work, the firm can always rely on the exemption for members of a profession

If regulated activities are less than 50% of the firm's, the firm may rely on the exemption for members of a profession, even if they hold these services out to be separate from legal services or the work is very significant to the firm

If regulated activities are more than 50% of the firm's, the firm may still be entitled to rely on the exemption for members of a profession if they do not hold these services out to be separate from legal services or profession and if the scale of the regulated activities is not significant to the firm's work

Even if regulated activities are less than 50% of the firm's, the firm may not be entitled to rely on the exemption for members of a profession if the scale of the regulated activities is very significant to the firm's work

explanation.en: The best answer is E. The exemption for members of a profession in part XX of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) requires that the regulated activity is incidental to the professional advice, i.e. legal advice in respect of lawyers. This means that the work is less than 50% of the firm's work. However, if the work is of a scale that is very significant to the firm, as it is here, or if the regulated activity is held out by the firm as separate services, the exemption will not apply. A is not the best answer. Even though professional advice must exceed the regulated financial advice, if the work is of a scale that is very significant to the firm, as it is here, or if the regulated activity is held out by the firm as separate services, the exemption for members of a profession in part XX FSMA will not apply. B is not the best answer. Even though professional advice must exceed the regulated financial advice, if the work is of a scale that is very significant to the firm, as it is here, or if the regulated activity is held out by the firm as separate services, the exemption for members of a profession in part XX FSMA will not apply. There are also other factors that must be satisfied, such as that the advice complements the professional services. C is not the best answer. Even though professional advice must exceed the regulated financial advice, if the work is of a scale that is very significant to the firm, as it is here, or if the regulated activity is held out by the firm as separate services, the exemption for members of a profession in part XX FSMA will not apply. D is not the best answer. In order to rely on the exemption for members of a profession, the professional advice must exceed the regulated financial advice. However, even if it does exceed 50% of the firm's work, if the regulated activity is of a scale that is very significant to the firm, as it is here, or if the regulated activity is held out by the firm as separate services, the exemption for members of a profession in part XX FSMA will not apply.

stem: You arrange life insurance for Mr Stringfellow as an incidental part of estate planning advice, relying on the exemption for members of a profession. The policy was connected to the advice given. Your firm receives commission. The client signed a blanket waiver of commission at the start of the retainer. You write to the client offering him the opportunity to refuse to accept your offer to set off the commission against legal costs.
ask: Which of the following best represents the firm's entitlement?

options.en: You can never set off commission against unpaid fees
You are entitled to set off commission against unpaid fees as you have the client's consent
You do not need written consent to set off commission against unpaid fees
You cannot set off commission against unpaid fees without positive written consent
You may set off commission against unpaid fees provided that you confirm the amount of commission to the client in writing

explanation.en: D is the best answer. Solicitors relying on the exemption for members of a profession under Part XX Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) are not permitted to retain commission or set it off against fees without positive, informed written consent from the client for the specific amount of commission. A blanket consent or negative consent are not sufficient. A is not correct. Even solicitors relying on the exemption for members of a profession under Part XX FSMA may set off commission against unpaid fees provided that they have positive, informed written consent from the client for the specific amount of commission. Blanket consent or negative consent is not sufficient. B is not the best answer. Solicitors relying on the exemption for members of a profession under Part XX Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) are not permitted to retain commission or set it off against fees without positive, informed written consent from the client for the specific amount of commission. Blanket consent or negative consent is not sufficient. C is not correct. Solicitors relying on the exemption for members of a profession under Part XX Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) are not permitted to retain commission or set it off against fees without positive, informed written consent from the client for the specific amount of commission. Blanket consent or negative consent is not sufficient. E is not the best answer. The client must be informed of the amount of commission, but solicitors relying on the exemption for members of a profession under Part XX FSMA are not permitted to retain commission or set it off against fees without positive, informed written consent from the client for the specific amount of commission. Informing the client that you will set off the commission unless the client instructs you otherwise, negative consent, is not sufficient. Blanket consent, such as at the beginning of the retainer, is not sufficient.

stem: You are a small village solicitor and perform most of the conveyancing, probate and tax work for the village's residents and for farmers in the area. You have limited knowledge of investment and rely on the exemption for members of a profession when you are approached about investment matters from time to time. You refer all clients to Safedude financial advisers, a tied agent.
ask: Which of the following best represents whether you have met you regulatory requirements?

options.en: You are not permitted to refer clients to financial advisers
You are free to refer clients to any adviser, provided that you comply with the SRA Conduct of Business rules
You must ensure that each individual client is referred to the most appropriate financial adviser and should not refer all clients to one provider or a tied agent
The SRA Code of Conduct permits you to choose a financial adviser, and so you may refer all clients to one adviser whom you know to be a tied agent
You can refer every client to the nearest financial adviser, geographically, even if they are a tied agent

explanation.en: The best answer is C. When solicitors suggest to a client that the client should seek advice from a financial expert they must do nothing to compromise their integrity or independence (principles 2 and 3 of the Code of Conduct), and must act in the client's best interests (principle 4). As a general rule, it follows that solicitors should not, therefore, refer a client for investment advice to one specific product provider or to an appointed representative ('tied agent'), who sells them (see IB6.4 and 012.6). A is not correct. Since solicitors do not always have the expertise required to provide investment advice, it is sometimes necessary and often advisable to refer the client to a suitable expert. However, when solicitors suggest to a client that the client should seek advice from a financial expert they must do nothing to compromise his integrity or independence (principles 2 and 3 of the Code of Conduct), and must act in the client's best interests (principle 4). B is not the best answer. Solicitors are required to comply with the SRA Code of Conduct as well as the SRA Financial Services (Conduct of Business) Rules 2001. When solicitors suggest to a client that the client should seek advice from a financial expert they must do nothing to compromise their integrity or independence (principles 2 and 3 of the Code of Conduct), and must act in the client's best interests (principle 4). As a general rule, it follows that solicitors should not, therefore, refer a client for investment advice to one specific product provider or to an appointed representative ('tied agent'), who sells them (see IB6.4 and 012.6). D is not the best answer. When solicitors suggest to a client that the client should seek advice from a financial expert they must do nothing to compromise their integrity or independence (principles 2 and 3 of the Code of Conduct), and must act in the client's best interests (principle 4). As a general rule, it follows that solicitors should not, therefore, refer a client for investment advice to one specific product provider or to an appointed representative ('tied agent'), who sells them (see IB6.4 and 012.6). E is not correct. When solicitors suggest to a client that the client should seek advice from a financial expert they must do nothing to compromise their integrity or independence (principles 2 and 3 of the Code of Conduct), and must act in the client's best interests (principle 4). As a general rule, it follows that solicitors should not, therefore, refer a client for investment advice to one specific product provider or to an appointed representative ('tied agent'), who sells them (see IB6.4 and 012.6). You can certainly include the details of local providers, even if they are tied agents. If the client specifically requests a local provider, you could recommend the local provider even if they are a tied agent, provided that you inform the client fully of the implications of instructing a tied agent, ie. that they will not suggest any other options that may be better value or give a better return.

stem: After many years of providing incidental investment advice, your personal injury claims firm decided to open a separate financial advice division named "DoubleYourMoney". The new division has separate marketing material and separate contact details. When referring clients to the financial advice division, you are careful to inform them that it is distinct, and that they are free to obtain advice elsewhere.
ask: Which of the following best represents the obligations of the firm?

options.en: The firm may continue to rely on the exemption for members of a profession if less than 50% of the firm's overall workload is investment advice
Solicitors are not permitted to establish a separate business. There is nothing to stop the individuals leaving the firm to start a new business that is independent of the firm
As the financial advice division is not part of the legal advice division of the firm, there are no professional conduct implications other than those applying to all referrals to or from the firm
The separate financial advice business is required to advertise that they are regulated by the SRA
The separate financial advice business will probably need to be authorised by the FCA

explanation.en: The best answer is E. As the separate business will be dedicated to financial advice, it will most probably require FCA authorisation. It cannot rely on the fact that the firm overall mostly gives legal advice, as the separate business is considered distinct from the firm. The financial advice division must identify that it is separate and not regulated by the SRA. Separate businesses must comply with Chapter 12 of the Code of Conduct, which envisages and permits their existence. A is not correct. As the separate business will be dedicated to financial advice, it will most probably require FCA authorisation. It cannot rely on the fact that the firm overall mostly gives legal advice, as the separate business is considered distinct from the firm. B is not the best answer. Chapter 12 of the Code of Conduct envisages and permits the existence of separate businesses operated by law firms. C is not correct. Separate businesses must comply with Chapter 12 of the Code of Conduct. The separate business must identify that it is separate from the firm and not regulated by the SRA. Confidential information cannot be shared between the firm and the separate business. D is not correct. The separate business must identify that it is separate from the firm and not regulated by the SRA. As the separate business will be dedicated to financial advice, it will most probably require FCA authorisation.

stem: You are approached by William Kid who instructs you to sell and purchase several properties in succession over the course of six months. The client is not in the property business and says that these are residential or holiday homes. The client is always on time paying bills and has accounts with large international banks. You perform the requisite identity checks.
ask: Which of the following best describes your potential anti-money laundering liability?

options.en: As you performed identity checks, you cannot be found guilty of any anti-money laundering offences
If you suspect that the properties represent the proceeds of crime you could be guilty of an offence unless you report the concern to the National Crime Authority (NCA)
If a proper price was paid for the properties, you do not have to worry that the purchase or sale could facilitate money laundering
You should notify the client if you suspect that they may be guilty of money laundering and ask the client to explain the source of their income and their reasons for the property purchases
You are not entitled to notify the National Crime Authority (NCA) on a mere suspicion as this would constitute a breach of confidentiality

explanation.en: The best answer is B. You could be guilty of concealing, disguising, converting, transferring or removal from the UK of criminal property (section 327 Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 (POCA)); acquiring, using or having possession of criminal property (section 329); or entering into or becoming concerned in an arrangement which a person knows or even suspects facilitates the acquisition, retention, use or control of criminal property (section 328) if you suspect that the property may represent the proceeds of crime. You do not have to know that the property does represent the proceeds of crime. You are required to report your suspicions to the National Crime Authority (NCA) (section 330) and you must not inform the client as this could constitute an offence of "tipping off" (section 333A). A is not the best answer. You could be guilty of concealing, disguising, converting, transferring or removal from the UK of criminal property (section 327 Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 (POCA)); acquiring, using or having possession of criminal property (section 329); or entering into or becoming concerned in an arrangement which a person knows or even suspects facilitates the acquisition, retention, use or control of criminal property (section 328) if you suspect that the property may represent the proceeds of crime. You are required to report your suspicions to the NCA (section 330). C is not correct. Although it is a defence to POCA offences if the full price is paid for property, this does not apply if the sale or acquisition would aid the concealment of the money as being the proceeds of crime. The Law Society's Practice Note on anti-money laundering at paragraph 5.5.2 explains that if you suspect that money is criminal property, you must make an authorised disclosure to the NCA and obtain consent to deal with the money before you accept it in payment of your fees. D is not correct. You are required to report your suspicions to the NCA (section 330) and you must not inform the client without the consent of the NCA, as this could constitute an offence of "tipping off" (section 333A). E is not correct. You are required to notify the NCA promptly if you suspect that property might represent the proceeds of crime. Failure to do so is an offence under POCA section 330. There is no requirement for the suspicion to be clear, on reasonable grounds or firmly grounded on specific facts, but there must be a degree of satisfaction, not necessarily amounting to belief, but at least extending beyond speculation ('more than fanciful'). The test for whether you hold a suspicion is a subjective one. If you think a transaction is suspicious, you are not expected to know the exact nature of the criminal offence or that particular funds were definitely those arising from the crime. Disclosure to the NCA is permitted and mandatory. You cannot seek the client's consent to disclose as this could constitute tipping off (section 333A) although at the beginning of the retainer it is advisable to inform the client that there are circumstances in which confidentiality is superseded, such as in the event of fraud or crime.

ask: You are planning a seminar to deal with various tax issues associated with corporation tax and your secretary asks you to identify which of the following should be on the invitee list?

options.en: Sylvia Smith, a freelance designer
Joe Bloggs LLP
Davies and Davies Partnership
Fresh Foods Limited
Donfield Charity

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Corporation tax applies to limited companies.

stem: George is trying to get the affairs of his company in order and therefore wants to know
ask: What type of payment schedule it is likely to be subject to. He has overheard several of his friends talking about corporation tax payments and asks you which of the following best describes his company's tax obligations. George's company has a profit of £2 million a year?

options.en: Tax is due nine months after the end of the tax year
As it is a large company, it will need to be paid on a quarterly basis
It is all due within 30 days of the end of the tax year
He can negotiate with the revenue based on his own circumstances; there are no set rules
There is no corporation tax for a company of this size

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Companies with over £1.5 million profit pay on a quarterly basis and not in one lump sum at the end of the tax year.

stem: Charlie is a director of a successful software company. She has heard that corporation tax was based on the schedule system but asks you to explain what this means.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current position under the Corporation Tax Act 2009 (the Act) for Charlie?

options.en: Profits are only taxed if there is a specific provision bringing it within the charge to tax
This refers to the HMRC handbooks that need to be referred to
The forms that need to be completed have many schedules and this refers to the schedules that need to be completed
Schedules refer to the historic system and are no longer relevant
Schedules to the accounts are relevant and drawn upon for the purposes of corporation tax

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Strictly speaking, the Corporation Tax 2009 replaced the historic terminology such as "Schedule A", "Schedule D Case I" etc., with more descriptive terms but different rules still apply for utilising tax losses depending upon the nature of the income under which the losses arise. The source rule still applies which means that something is taxed only if there is a specific provision bringing it within the charge to tax. Accordingly, profits are only charged to corporation tax if they fall within the provisions of the Act, and are not otherwise exempted by an explicit provision of the Act.

stem: Several of your corporate clients are confused, as they understand that income tax and capital gains are taxed separately. However, they don't know how this works from a corporate point of view and have asked you to explain. Each client has net trading profits, as well as income derived from the sale of business assets such as offices, machinery, equipment and goodwill.
ask: Which of the following best describes their corporation tax liability?

options.en: Corporation tax simply includes operational profits, so they can ignore capital gains in the calculation
Corporation tax is based on both the income profits and the capital gains within the company, in any given period
Capital gains, only, are taxed as corporation tax; profits are paid as part of the income tax
All income and capital gains are shared among the directors to account for as their own
Corporation tax is only payable by public limited companies, so there is no need for private limited companies to worry about this

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Corporation tax is a blanket name for operational profit and capital gains within a corporation.

stem: Claude is in the middle of completing his corporation tax returns. He needs to work out his charges on income, but he does not fully understand
ask: What should fall within this heading. He asks you which of these best describes elements he should include in his calculations?

options.en: Gifts to directors
Payments to non-executive directors
A CEO's salary
Gift aid payments
Bonuses for the company secretary

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Charges on income are based on charitable and annuity payments, not on payments to directors or internally within the company.

stem: Ethel is aware that she can deduct some business expenses from her profits in order to reduce her corporation tax bill. She has brought in a list of expenses and asks you which ones she can deduct.
ask: Which best describes the deductible expenses?

options.en: Guarantee payment for a director's personal loan
Food for the directors at a hotel
Director's car which he uses for business occasionally
Advertising a new product in a particularly glitzy way
Advertising the sale of Ethel's family home

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. She can deduct an expense, if it is wholly and exclusively in the name of the business, regardless of whether or not it is excessive or 'glitzy'.

stem: Clueless Ltd has struggled with its finances on an annual basis and is always confused as to which financial payments it can deduct as an expense. The company has several loans and it does not deduct any of the expenses. The directors now believe that they could make some reductions to their corporation tax bill.
ask: Which of the following best describes an expense that could be set off against the corporation tax bill?

options.en: A special bonus to directors which is significantly above their typical salaries
Interest on a personal loan
Insurance for the Chief Executive
Employee fantasy football subscription
Directors' salaries

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Expenses are only potentially tax deductible if they are to do with the business. Directors' emoluments are allowed, so long as they appear reasonable.

stem: Three business partners are looking to go into business together and are considering the best structure for their needs. They have asked you about the key differences, from a tax point of view, between being in partnership and being a limited company. They have heard many rumours.
ask: Which of the following best describes the tax position?

options.en: The partnership pays partnership tax
Directors pay corporation tax on their salaries
In a partnership, the individual partners pay partnership tax on what they receive
A company is taxed on its profits
Companies pay more tax than partnerships

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. With a partnership, the partnership itself does not pay tax, rather the partners pay on what they receive. A limited company will pay corporation tax and the directors are treated as employees.

stem: When calculating capital allowances, one of your clients seems to have included some assets under the plant and machinery title that should not be present.
ask: Which of the following best describes items that would fall into the definition of plant and machinery?

options.en: Extension to the office building
A home office
A conference room
A printing press
A rented barn

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. The others are buildings and offices, rather than plant and machinery; fixtures in a rental property would fall into the category of plant and machinery.

stem: Your client has made an appointment to obtain help with their corporation tax forms. You are writing your client to tell them which records they need to bring with them to your office.
ask: Which of the following best describes the documents your client would require to complete a corporation tax form?

options.en: A record of the company directors' assets
A record of all payments made out of pocket by staff and directors on behalf of the company
A list of the stock that the company officers bought from the company
A record of all income of the company's officers in the year
A record of all the company's assets

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Completing corporation tax returns requires a wide amount of data and all financial movements of the company, but not the individuals in the company. A record of all the company's assets is going to be one of the documents that will be required in order to prepare the financial statements of the company and the corporation tax form.

stem: A company has total profits of £400,000 and pays out £200,000 to four directors as salary, with the rest being subject to corporation tax. Compare this with a partnership in which all £400,000 is paid out to the four partners. Assume no use of personal allowances and a corporation tax rate of 20%, with the directors / partners all being subject to a tax rate of 40%.
ask: How much less tax would the company scenario be liable for?

options.en: No difference

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. With the company, £200,000 would be subject to 40% and £200,000 subject to 20%, giving a total amount of tax payable of £120,000 (80,000 + 40,000). The partnership scenario would apply 40% to all £400,000, which would be a tax amount of £160,000. The difference is, therefore, £40,000.

stem: Botchit Ltd has failed to comply with the requirements in relation to its corporation tax liability. As such, it is likely to be facing penalties. In order to prepare itself for the likely penalty, a company representative has made an appointment to come and see you.
ask: Which of the following best describes information that would form part of your advice?

options.en: The actual corporation tax liability is not relevant when it comes to determining the penalty
The penalty could be 50% of the amount due, if it continues to conceal information from HMRC deliberately
Where it is deliberate, but no further concealing has taken place, the maximum penalty can be up to 80% of the tax due
Non-deliberate errors can still attract a penalty of 70%
If the company makes every effort to disclose all information, the amount of the penalty may be reduced

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. Penalties are calculated with reference to the corporation tax liability of the entity and vary, based on culpability.

stem: When one of your clients is trying to allocate various different incomes and gains, they find that certain income types could fall into multiple categories.
ask: Which of the following best describes how income should be handled in these circumstances?

options.en: The client should enter the income in every relevant category
The client should split the income across the various categories
They should ignore the categories and put them under the 'other' category
The most appropriate category should be selected, as it can only fall into the one category
The most appropriate two categories can be selected and the income divided between them

explanation.en: The correct answer is D. Income can only fall into one category and this is where the income should be put.

stem: One of your long-term clients has decided to set up a business and plans to register with HMRC for corporation tax.
ask: Which of the following best describes the information needed by HMRC for corporate tax purposes?

options.en: Salaries of directors
Registration details from Companies House
Details of the purpose of the business of the company being set up
Home addresses of the directors
VAT registration number

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Salaries are not needed in the first instance (they will form part of the corporation tax calculation at the end of the year). Business addresses will be needed for the directors, however not their home addresses.

stem: A person is in the process of setting up a limited company and is trying to understand what qualifies as an allowable expense. He believes that the wages of employees are an allowable expense, as opposed to National Insurance paid on behalf of employees, which he believes is a burden the company must absorb.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: National insurance contributions are an allowable expense
National Insurance contributions are an allowable expense if the company employs over five people
National Insurance contributions are an allowable expense if the company employs over 12 people
National Insurance contributions are only allowable if the business is a government organisation
National Insurance contributions are not an allowable expense

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. National Insurance contributions paid on behalf of employees are considered an allowable expense and the person will be able to consider them as an expense in addition to the employee's wages.

stem: A man has run a limited company for five years. He decides that the company shall make a number of charitable donations throughout the year and wants to know if Gift Aid is deductible from the company's gross income.
ask: Advise the man regarding the current legal position?

options.en: Gift Aid is not deductible
Gift Aid is deductible
10% of the Gift Aid donated is deductible
25% of the Gift Aid donated is deductible
Gift Aid is deductible providing the donation is less than £25,000

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Gift Aid donations are deemed to be 'non-trade' charges on income and can be deducted from a company's gross income.

stem: A man owns a limited company and wants to donate some of the profits to charity. His friend tells him that this will be considered an allowable expense, but he is unsure.
ask: Which of the following best describe the current legal position?

options.en: Charitable donations by corporations are not considered an allowable expense
Charitable donations by corporations are considered an allowable expense if the donation is over £10,000
Charitable donations by corporations are considered an allowable expense if the donation is over £25,000
Charitable donations by corporations are considered an allowable expense if the donation is over £50,000
Charitable donations by corporations are considered an allowable expense

explanation.en: The correct answer is E. If a corporation makes a charitable donation the sum is deducted from the company's gross profits as an allowable expense. Therefore, the company does not pay tax on the amount donated.

stem: Your client runs a limited company and wants to determine what constitutes a valid business expense.
ask: Advise your client regarding the current legal position?

options.en: A business expense must be solely for the purpose of the business
A business expense is valid if it is intended to benefit the business
A business expense is valid if it is intended to benefit the business or its employees
A business expense is valid if it is paid for out of the company's accounts
A business expense must be solely for the purpose of the business and be paid out of the company's accounts

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. In order to be classed as a business expense it must be solely for the purpose of the business.

stem: Your client is in the process of setting up a limited company. She is calculating figures and is concerned that she will not be able to make a profit whilst the company pays corporation tax, income tax and capital gains tax.
ask: Advise your client regarding the current legal position?

options.en: Corporations are liable to pay income tax, corporation tax and capital gains tax
Corporations are only liable to pay corporation tax
Corporations are only liable to pay corporation and income tax
Corporations are only liable to pay corporation and capital gains tax
Corporations are only liable to pay income tax and capital gains tax

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Rather than paying income and capital gains tax, corporations pay a different tax known as corporation tax.

stem: Two people run a members-only golf club. Rather than being a limited company, the business is run as an unincorporated association. They believe that they do not need to pay Corporation Tax, as unincorporated associations are not required to pay a levy on their income.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the current legal position?

options.en: Unincorporated associations must pay Corporation Tax
Unincorporated associations can choose to either pay Corporation Tax or income tax
Unincorporated associations are not required to pay tax
Unincorporated associations must pay Corporation Tax and Capital Gains Tax
The tax owed by unincorporated associations depends on the income of the people running the association

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Unincorporated associations are still required to pay corporation tax. The unincorporated association form is usually chosen when a number of individuals agree or 'contract' to come together for a common purpose - which may be of a social nature. Unincorporated associations have no separate legal personality.

stem: A director of a limited company is aware that the company is not liable for Capital Gains Tax and also believes that, as a director, he does not have personal liability for Capital Gains Tax.
ask: Which of the following best describes the current legal position?

options.en: Companies and their directors are not liable for Capital Gains Tax
Directors still have a personal liability for Capital Gains Tax
Directors have a personal liability for Capital Gains Tax, but at a reduced rate
Both companies and directors pay Capital Gains Tax
Only partnerships pay Capital Gains Tax

explanation.en: The correct answer is B. Although companies do not pay capital gains tax, directors are still able to incur personal Capital Gains Tax liabilities.

stem: It is the end of the tax year and you are in the process of sorting out the end of year accounts for several corporations. Your assistant is helping you and has asked about how they should ascertain the final profit figure that is chargeable to Corporation Tax. Your assistant knows that he needs to reduce this figure with certain charges on income.
ask: Which of the following options best states what may be used as a charge on income?

options.en: Wages, interest on loans and dividends
National Insurance (NI), accountancy fees and dividends
Interest on loans, NI and accountancy fees
Dividends, wages and accountancy fees
Accountancy fees, interest on loans and dividends

explanation.en: The correct answer is C. Interest on loans, NI and accountancy fees. Dividends are an appropriation of protits and theretore they are not an expense against protit, whereas the others are payments made against a profit. Answer C is the only option that does not include dividends.

stem: Your client is new to running his business. Although he is quite well versed on income tax procedures, he is new to corporate tax matters.
ask: Which part of your client's income is subject to Corporation Tax?

options.en: All the income and capital gains of the company are subject to Corporation Tax
All the income of the company is subject to Corporation Tax
All capital gains of the company are subject to Corporation Tax
All of the client's personal income from any source and that of the company are subject to Corporation Tax
All of the client's income from the company is subject to Corporation Tax

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. Corporation Tax is payable on income and capital gains accruing to the business only. The company is a separate legal entity and generates its own tax liability, which is distinct from the director's liabilities.

stem: In 2016-2017 a private limited company made a trading profit of £60,000 and chargeable gains of £10,000. The company also has charges on income of £10,000 for that accounting period (assume they have not been claimed yet). In 2017-2018 it makes a trading loss of £80,000 and chargeable gains of £10,000. The company carries on the same trade over these years.
ask: What is the company's total taxable profit in 2016-2017?

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. 2017-2018: Trading profit £80,000 (loss); Chargeable gains £10,000; Carry across relief £10,000 (£10,000 of trading loss of £80,000 should be used to offset the chargeable gains of £10,000 in 2017-2018, and therefore cannot be carried back against profits made in the preceding 12-month period). The remaining £70,000 (or in fact £60,000 of that amount) can be rolled back to offset the trading profits of £60,000 in 2016-2017. This brings the trading profits in 2016-2017 to zero. With the charges of income of £10,000 which offset the chargeable gains of £10,000, the taxable profit of the company is zero. 2016-2017: Trading profit £60,000; Less carry back relief £60,000; Chargeable gains £10,000; Less charges on income £10,000; Taxable profit £0.

stem: A private limited company has an accounting period from the 1st of January 2017 to the 31st of December 2017. For the accounting period it has trading receipts of £2,000,000. It made a gain from the sale of office furniture of £150,000 over the course of the accounting year. £10,000 was spent on raw materials, £240,000 on wages and £10,000 on general production costs.
ask: What is the company's taxable profit for the 2017-2018 tax year for corporation tax purposes?

explanation.en: The best answer is D. Assuming the raw materials, wages and general production costs were all exclusively for the purpose of the business and the wages were not excessive, these are deductible from gross trading profits as charges on income. £2,000,000 - £260,000 = £1,740,000 net trading profit. This must be added to the other income from the sale of office furniture of £150,000, giving £1,890,000. There are 365 days in the company's accounting period (from the 1st of January 2017 to the 31St of December 2017), of which 90 occur in the 2016-2017 financial year (from the 1st of January 2017 to the 31st of March 2017) and 275 days occur in the 2017-2018 financial year (from the 1st of April 2017 to the 31st of December 2017). To calculate the company's taxable profit for 2017-2018, we should use the fraction 275/365 X £1,890,000 = £1,423,973. A is not correct as the taxable profit for the tax year is the profit from the 1st of April to the 31st of December (275 days, not 12 months). B is not correct as it uses nine months to calculate the taxable profits instead of 275 days (although there is a slight difference, you should note that the calculation should be based on days, not months). C is not correct as raw materials, production costs and wages are deductible charges on income provided that they are reasonable and for the purpose of the business. E is not correct as other income must be included in the profits, assuming that they were not solely attributable to 2016 or 2017.

stem: A private limited company has trading receipts of £2,000,000 for the accounting period. It makes National Insurance payments on behalf of employees of £250,000, pays £250,000 for business insurance, pays £800,000 employees' wages and pays £200,000 interest on business loans. The company also makes Gift Aid donations of £300,000. Other income from the sale of real estate is £100,000. The company declares dividends of £100,000.
ask: What is the taxable amount for corporation tax purposes?

explanation.en: The correct answer is A. National Insurance payments on behalf of employees, business insurance, employees' wages and interest on business loans are deductible charges on income. Gift Aid donations can be deducted from any income. Dividends do not reduce the taxable amount or liability. B is not correct because the interest on business loans is a deductible charge on income. C is not correct because business insurance is a deductible charge on income. D is not correct because wages and National Insurance payments on behalf of employees are deductible expenses. E is not correct as dividends are not deductible.

stem: Candy Confectionary, in a promotion for its chocolate bars, gave away the pop CD, "Baby Blues", in exchange for three wrappers and 80 pence for postage. According to the law, Maiden Music, the publisher of the song, is entitled to 7.25 per cent of the selling price of each CD. It is now suing Candy Confectionary despite Candy Confectionary's claim that the chocolate bar wrappers are just thrown away and are of no direct value to them, so cannot form part of the consideration.
ask: Were the chocolate wrappers part of the consideration in the contract to buy the song?

options.en: Yes, the "selling price" on which Maiden Music's royalty should be based wasn't just the 80 pence but also included the value represented by the three wrapping papers
No, because the wrappers were thrown away by Candy Confectionary when they got them back from customers, so bore no economic relationship with "Baby Blues"
Yes, since according to the law, Maiden Music, the publisher of the "Baby Blues", was entitled to 7.25 per cent of the "selling price" of each song
No, because the only economic value in the wrappers was that they represented sales of chocolate bars
No, because the wrappers were of no direct value to Candy Confectionary, and they did not form part of the promotion

explanation.en: A is correct. The wrappers were part of the consideration in the contract to buy the song, despite the fact that they were thrown away by Candy Confectionary, and even though they were of no intrinsic value. Lead case: Chappell v Nestlé [1960] AC 87; [1959] 2 All ER 701.

stem: Last month Richard gave his penniless nephew his old car. The following week his nephew won £250,000 in the lottery and promised to pay Richard £5,000 out of his winnings as payment for the car. Since then Richard has seen neither his car nor hair of his nephew.
ask: Can Richard enforce his nephew's promise?

options.en: Richard can enforce this promise, because there is consideration on both sides of the agreement
Richard cannot enforce this promise, because the conduct of the parties shows that there wasn't any substantial agreement
Richard can enforce this promise, even though what is provided by way of consideration is both a benefit to him, and a detriment to his nephew
Richard can enforce this promise, because whether he agreed to give the car, or sell it for £1, the courts will treat it as a binding contract
Richard cannot enforce this promise as his consideration, giving his nephew the car, is past

explanation.en: E is correct. Past consideration is no consideration. The transfer of the car was undertaken and completed without any thought of payment, and before his nephew made his promise. Lead case: Roscorla v Thomas (1842) 3 QB 234.

stem: Edward had bought a car from Malcolm. Malcolm then promised that the car was 'sound and in good condition'. This turned out to be untrue.
ask: Is Malcolm's promise enforceable?

options.en: Yes, the promise is enforceable and Edward would be able to recover, because both parties must have contemplated that payment for the service would be made
Yes, because Malcolm's representation in fact contained an implied promise that the car was sound
No, since the consideration provided by Edward was already past when Malcolm's promise, that the car was sound, was made
No, because Malcolm was only promising to do what he was already obliged to do under their existing contract
Yes, if that had been a true representation of the facts, then it would have constituted a binding contract

explanation.en: C is correct. Edward is unable to sue on this promise, since he has provided no consideration for it. The sale was already complete before the promise was made. Lead case: Roscorla v Thomas (1842) 3 QB 234.

stem: Donfield United was recently promoted to the English Premier League. At the club's request, the police authority agreed to provide it with the more expensive 'special police services', whereby police officers would attend at matches both inside and outside the ground, rather than the less expensive 'regular' service the police authority had suggested, of only providing officers to attend matches inside the ground. The club now claims that since the police authority was obliged to do so in accordance with its duty to maintain law and order, it is not obliged to make any payment for the 'special police services' it provided.
ask: Does the police authority have a legitimate claim that it provided good consideration for the 'special police services'?

options.en: No, because such an agreement would be against public policy
Yes, since the club was liable to make any payment for police services unless they requested attendance by officers to fulfil roles other than police duty
No, because there was no consideration for the promise to pay for the special police services
Yes; while there is an obligation on the police to afford efficient protection, there was consideration made for the promise because the club requested the special police services
No; because there is an obligation on the police to afford efficient protection, and no consideration was made for the promise merely because the club requested the special police services

explanation.en: D is correct. There was sufficient consideration. The police authority provided more than its public duty required of it and was entitled to charge and claim for the monies owed to them in respect of the 'special police services'. The provision of policemen at a football ground to keep law and order is the provison of special services by the police. The police authority is under a duty to protect the public against crime or threatened crime for which no payment is due. The police, however, have no duty to protect the public against the mere fear of possible future crime. The police authority's claim for police services provided at Donfield's stadium would be legitimate. Lead case: Glasbrook Bros v Glamorgan CC [1925] AC 270. Comment: The facts bear similarity to Harris v Sheffield Utd FC [1987] 2 All ER 838.

stem: When half the crew of "the Bounty" deserted on arrival in Tahiti, Captain Blyth promised the remaining sailors that, due to the greater hazard of continuing the voyage back to England with insufficient crew, they would receive additional payment. When the Bounty docked in Southampton, however, the ship owners refused to honour the captain's promise, claiming that the sailors were already bound by the existing contract to sail back and to meet such emergencies of the voyage as necessary.
ask: Was the sailor's agreement to sail back valid consideration so as to enforce the captain's promise?

options.en: No, because the remaining crew members were only promising to do what they were already obliged to do under their existing contract

No; by agreeing to the remaining crew members' demands there would be an increased risk in this type of situation whereby crew members would blackmail ship owners and captains into promising extra wages to avoid being stranded
Yes, because the voyage had become so dangerous that it was unreasonable to require the crew to continue
Yes, as a result of his promise, the captain did not have to seek replacement crew, avoided delays, and made sure the existing crew continued to work
No, the desertion of part of the crew was just part of the normal hazards of the voyage

explanation.en: Cis correct. In this situation, the voyage had become so dangerous that it was unreasonable to require the crew to continue. A greater remuneration was promised to the sailors to steer the ship home as the number of deserters virtually rendered the vessel unseaworthy. The promise would therefore be binding because the sailors had gone beyond their call of duty in agreeing to sail an unseaworthy vessel. This discharged the remaining sailors from the original contract, allowing them to enter in to a new bargain. Lead case: Hartley v Ponsonby (1857) 7 E & B 872.

stem: Busy Builders subcontracted to pay Chippy Carpenters to refurbish 20 flats at a cost of £5,000 per flat. In order to avoid paying a penalty clause in the main contract with the general contractor, midway through the refurbishment, Busy Builders offered to pay Chippy Carpenters at a rate of £5,750 for each remaining non-refurbished flat. Chippy Carpenters completed the work on the remaining flats but Busy Builders defaulted on their promise of additional payments.
ask: Which option best states the legal position?

options.en: There is no consideration, because Chippy Carpenters' provided no consideration, since Busy Builders did not receive a benefit, or at the very least would avoid a detriment, through the completion of the work

There is no consideration, because there was an element of duress brought upon Busy Builders to pay the additional sum for what amounted to Chippy Carpenters' performance of existing contractual obligations

There is no consideration; Chippy Carpenters were only doing something they were already bound to do under the existing contract, so the promise by Busy Builders to pay the additional sum was gratuitous
There is consideration, because the promise was freely given by Busy Builders to pay Chippy Carpenters an additional sum for the performance of their obligations
There is consideration, because the principle that a contracting party can rely upon its own breach to establish consideration is entrenched in English law

explanation.en: D is correct. The promise to pay the additional sum was binding, because promises to perform existing obligations can amount to consideration, even between contracting parties. A party that agrees to make supplementary payment to secure the timely performance of a contract may provide sufficient consideration contractually to support the extra payment as long as the agreement to pay is not invoked by economic duress or fraud and where it guarantees the completion of the contract to the paying party's satisfaction and benefit (e.g. by avoiding the imposition of penalty clauses in a contract with a third-party). Lead case: Williams v Roffey Bros & Nicholls (Contractors) Ltd. [1990] 1 All ER 512

stem: An executor to an estate alleges that a son failed to honour a promissory note to pay off a debt which he gave to his father when his father was still alive. The son admits that he gave the promissory note to his father, but claims that his father promised him that he would not enforce it, provided that the son promised not to keep on complaining about being left out of his father's will.
ask: Which option best advises the parties?

options.en: The agreement is not enforceable; a promise to discharge a debt must equally be supported by consideration
The agreement is not enforceable; even though the son's consideration is capable of expression in terms of value, the father was under no moral duty to take notice of his son's complaint
The agreement is enforceable; the father was under a moral duty to take notice of his son's complaint
The agreement is enforceable, because the son's promise to refrain from complaining amounts to good consideration for a promise to discharge his debts
The agreement is enforceable; because the son's abstaining from doing what he had every right to do was sufficient consideration

explanation.en: Option A is the best answer. The traditional rule is that a promise to discharge a debt must equally be supported by consideration. The promise not to complain is not sufficient consideration to be released from the debt. Furthermore, consideration must be capable of expression in terms of value. Even furthermore, since the son had no right to complain about his disinheritance; he can't give up something for which he has no tangible rights in the first place. As Pollock CB explained in White v Bluett (1853) upon which the fact pattern is based: ".... Looking at the words merely, there is some foundation for the argument, and, following the words only, the conclusion may be arrived at. It is said, the son had a right to an equal distribution of his father's property, and did complain to his father because he had not an equal share, and said to him, I will cease to complain if you will not sue upon this note. Whereupon the father said if you will promise me not to complain I will give up the note. In reality, there was no consideration whatever... The son had no right to complain, for the father might make what distribution of his property he liked; and the son's abstaining from doing what he had no right to do can be no consideration."

stem: Henry started a county court action against Rufus to recover a debt, originally stated at £450.
