Rufus sent Henry a cheque for £150, and sent side letters to Henry and the court stating that the cheque was in settlement of his debt, and that he did not dispute that he owed him money but disputed the total amount claimed. Henry cashed the cheque but replied that he was continuing with the action until he received full payment.
ask: Which option best states the applicable law under these circumstances?

options.en: Rufus's payment of the lesser sum does not settle the claim; by accepting the £150, Henry has received no additional benefit by way of consideration

Rufus's payment of the lesser sum settles the claim; while Henry had not intended to accept the £150 in full settlement, nevertheless by doing so, he had compromised his claim by a binding accord and satisfaction
Rufus's payment of the lesser sum settles the claim; Henry had intended to accept the £150 in full settlement and by doing so, he had compromised his claim by a binding accord and satisfaction

Rufus's payment of the lesser sum does not settle the claim, because Henry's claim for the disputed amount was not settled by a compromise involving partial payment by Rufus and by Henry accepting the £150

Rufus's payment of the lesser sum does not settle the claim, because Henry's cashing of the cheque, constituted a clear and unequivocal acceptance that no further sum was due because the side letters imposed new terms

explanation.en: A is the best answer. There was no consideration here for Henry's alleged agreement to abandon his claim. Acceptance by Henry of a lesser sum from Rufus than the amount claimed could not constitute accord and satisfaction so as to compromise the action between them unless Henry received some additional benefit by way of consideration. Therefore there is in law no consideration because Henry had not compromised his claim by a binding accord and satisfaction. Furthermore, Rufus unequivocally admitted liability for the sum paid by cheque, and was not giving Henry any additional benefit on top of that. The sending of the cheque for £150 was an open admission of liability. A clear admission of money due is something quite different from an offer of a sum in compromise. Lead case: Foakes v Beer (1884) 9 App Cas 605. Comment: The facts of the case relate to Ferguson v Davies [1997] 1 All ER 315.

stem: Charlie's Autos placed a notice in a trade magazine that a car auction would take place outside Wednesbury recreation ground on Friday morning. Gaynor read the advert, took the day off work, and travelled the 20 miles from her home, only to find that the auction had been cancelled. She is thinking of bringing an action for breach of contract against Charlie's Autos to recover her expenses in attending the advertised event.
ask: Can she sue Charlie's Autos for her out of pocket expenses on the basis of breach of contract?

options.en: No, because The Sale of Goods Act 1979 is clear that in relation to a sale of goods by auction any bid does not constitute an offer until the bid is accepted
No, because the notice did not give rise to any contract that all the items mentioned would actually be put up for sale
Yes, because Charlie's Autos put the items up for sale and pledged itself to the sale
Yes, because it was a contract made with the highest bidder, and Charlie's Autos was therefore in breach of it
Yes, because a collateral contract arose upon Gaynor acting upon the notice

explanation.en: B is correct. An auctioneer's call for bids is regarded as an invitation to treat, which is a mere request for offers. Lead case: Harris v Nickerson.

stem: Alice rents a house from Aaron, who wrote to inform her that he might be willing to sell it to her, and she wrote back saying she wanted to go ahead with the acquisition. Aaron declined to sell the house after all, and informed Alice that the option to buy was no longer available. Alice claims a breach of contract because Aaron refuses to proceed with the sale.
ask: Was there was a binding contract, and can Alice therefore enforce the sale?

options.en: Yes, because the letter from Aaron was a firm intention to proceed with the sale, and once Alice returned the application form, Aaron was bound to proceed with the sale
Yes, because analysing the transaction in terms of offer and acceptance is superfluous when the conduct of the parties show that there was a material agreement
Yes, because the offer had been accepted as soon as the letter of acceptance had been posted
No, because the language of Aaron's letter to Alice was not sufficiently definite to amount to an offer; it was simply an invitation to treat
No, because the letter should be regarded as a mere advertising slogan which meant nothing in contractual terms

explanation.en: D is correct. The evidence does not suggest that Aaron ever made an offer to sell and hence there could be no valid acceptance. All that had occurred in this case were the first steps towards negotiations for a sale which never reached fruition. Lead case: Gibson v Manchester City Council.

stem: Stellar Brewery posted an offer to sell a hundred barrels of its finest premium ale to the Wetherforks pub chain and asked for a reply 'in course of post'. The letter containing the offer was misdirected and arrived later than would normally have been the case. Wetherforks replied immediately by post, as requested, stating that it wished to accept Stellars' offer, only to be informed by Stellar that, since it thought that Wetherforks was not going to accept its offer due to the delay, the barrels had already been sold to another pub chain.
ask: Which option best states whether there is a binding contract between the parties?

options.en: There is a binding contract between the parties in these circumstances because the court must apply the postal rule to stop Stellar escaping from what it might see as a bad bargain for the sale of the ale
There is no binding contract between the parties in these circumstances; by the time the letter of acceptance was posted, Stellar Brewery had sold the barrels to another pub chain
There is a binding contract between the parties in these circumstances; even though there was a misdirection of the offer, the offer was made when it actually reached Wetherforks
There is no binding contract between the parties in these circumstances; the fact of misdirection must have been so obvious to Wetherforks, it would have been put on notice that the offer had lapsed
There is no binding contract between the parties in these circumstances, because the letter has been misdirected in the post by Stellar Brewery

explanation.en: C is the best answer. An acceptance by means of the post is valid from the moment of posting, not merely from when the letter is received by the offeror. Where there has been a misdirection of the offer, as is the case here, the offer is deemed made when it actually reaches the offeree; not when it would have reached him in the ordinary course of post.

stem: A husband and wife agreed that because of the husband's physical aversion to the heat, he will not return with her when she goes back to Hong Kong, where she works for an international bank. The wife agreed to pay the husband £500 per month in maintenance while they were away from each other, but a few months later, the wife informed the husband that she wanted a permanent separation. The husband claims that his estranged wife has subsequently reneged on her promise to keep up the monthly payments and is considering legal action to enforce the agreement.
ask: Which option best advises the husband?

options.en: The presumption that domestic agreements are not intended to be legally binding is rebutted once the parties begin to haggle and the burden then shifts to the wife to show that they did not intend to create legal relations
The presumption that domestic agreements are not intended to be legally binding is ordinarily rebutted once the parties have officially separated
While the wife's promised financial support of her husband concerned a domestic agreement, the sanctity of marriage does not override the sanctity of the contract

There is a presumption, based on public policy considerations, that such domestic agreements are intended to be legally binding in order to protect the weaker or most vulnerable partner in a marriage or civil partnership, in this case the husband
The presumption that domestic agreements are not intended to create legal relations is ordinarily not rebuttable where the parties are living together in good relations at the time of the agreement

explanation.en: E is the best option. The presumption that domestic agreements are not intended to create legal relations is ordinarily not rebuttable where the parties are living together in good relations at the time of the agreement. It is therefore unlikely that the court will enforce the agreement. Domestic agreements between spouses are, in general terms, presumptively unenforceable, especially if the parties are still living together at the time of the agreement, so said the Court of Appeal in the case of Balfour v Balfour [1919]. Those spousal agreements which are intended to regulate the terms of the parties' separation, such as in the case of Merritt v Merritt [1970] 2 All ER 760, however, are usually regarded as binding on the parties, especially where the parties are estranged. Lord Denning MR distinguished the differing circumstances in the case of Merrit v Merrit, and said: "The parties [in Balfour v Balfour]... were living together in amity. In such cases their domestic arrangements are ordinarily not intended to create legal relations. It is altogether different when the parties are not living in amity but are separated, or about to separate. They then bargain keenly. They do not rely on honourable understandings. They want everything cut and dried. It may safely be presumed that they intend to create legal relations." Option B is not the best option in this case, because at the time of the agreement, the parties had not separated in the sense that the marriage was considered to be over. Lead case: Balfour v Balfour [1919] 2 KB 571

stem: Helen, her granddaughter Hermione and their lodger William, regularly entered the lottery together, and although all the tickets were always in Helen's name, they had agreed to share the cost of entry by using the same ticket. The ticket with Helen's name on it has won £1,500,000. Helen says she will share the winnings with Hermione, but she refuses to share any of the proceeds with William.
ask: Did the understanding between the parties sufficiently amount to the formation of a binding contract, so that William can sue Helen?

options.en: Yes, since this was in the nature of a formal syndicate, they should all reap the benefit of success
Yes, this was a joint enterprise to which each party had contributed in the expectation that if the ticket won, the proceeds would be shared equally
No, because this was the sort of rough and ready statement made in domestic circles which was not intended to be binding

No, because in the context of domestic agreements like these, the court cannot enforce such a contract unless the arrangement made at the time was one which was intended to give rise to legal consequences
No, because it runs counter to public policy that any domestic agreements are intended to be legally binding

explanation.en: B is correct. Where such parties make an outward sign that they intend the agreement to be legally binding, this will be effective. Lead case: Simpkins v Pays [1955] 3 AIl ER 10.

stem: Delia's mother persuaded her to come to England from Penang to study medicine, promising to let her to stay in her house. After several years and several unsuccessful attempts, however, Delia had still not passed her medical exams. Although they were previously on very good terms, mother and daughter have fallen out and Delia's mother is seeking possession of the house, but Delia insists there had been a contract between them.
ask: Which option best states the courts' approach in these circumstances?

options.en: There is a presumption that Delia and her mother did not intend to be legally bound because it was a domestic agreement between parent and child
There is a presumption that the parties intended to be legally bound in such domestic agreements, which the mother will have to rebut
The court will enforce a domestic agreement like this one, because it has all the elements of a contract, which was intended to give rise to legal consequences
There appears to be a contractual relationship between the parties, because a normal mother doesn't sue her daughter in court
The presumption that domestic agreements are not intended to be legally binding does not apply when the parties are not living in harmony but are separated

explanation.en: A is correct. The fact that the understanding between Delia and her mother had all the qualities of a domestic agreement means that the presumption would go against there being an intention to be legally bound, and thus make it easier for the mother to succeed in her argument. Lead case: Jones v Padavatton [1969] 2 All ER 616.

stem: The fast food chain, MacDavid's, made a special offer whereby any customer buying a family sized MacDavid's 'Lucky Meal' would receive a free sticker featuring an image of an England international footballer, which could be collected to make a set, but had virtually no intrinsic value. The question has arisen whether MacDavid's should pay Value Added Tax (VAT) regarding the stickers.
ask: Which option best states whether a contract of sale has arisen, if at all?

options.en: The fact that the stickers have virtually no intrinsic value is not enough to rebut the presumption of enforceability
The fact that the stickers have virtually no intrinsic value is enough to rebut any presumption of enforceability
The stickers have virtually no intrinsic value and the law presumes that business agreements are not intended to be legally binding
The giving away of free promotional material cannot form part of a general offer, or unilateral contract

The fact that the stickers have virtually no intrinsic value is not enough to rebut any presumption of enforceability because the presumption is that parties intend to create legal relations even if there is a clear and express statement to the contrary in the agreement

explanation.en: A is correct. There was a unilateral contract under which Mac David's was saying If you will buy our 'Lucky Meal', we will give you one of these stickers'. The decision of the House of Lords in Esso Petroleum Ltd v Commissioners of Customs and Excise [1976] shows the difficulty in rebutting the presumption that business agreements are intended to be legally binding. While the majority held that there had been no sale and Esso was not liable for VAT, it decided that the petrol station's price indications were invitations to treat. The giving away of promotional material ex gratia formed part of a general offer, or unilateral contract. This unilateral contract ran parallel with the main contract of sale (an amount of petrol for an agreed sum). There was, therefore, legal intent despite the coins having virtually no intrinsic value. Lead case: Esso Petroleum Ltd v Commissioners of Customs and Excise [1976] 1 All ER 117.

stem: Two companies began trading with a third company in an agency agreement. The three companies entered into an agreement concerning sales and purchases incorporating a clause that the agreement was to be 'in honour' only and not legally enforceable.
ask: Would this arrangement between two companies give rise to a binding contract?

options.en: No, because such an arrangement would not allow the companies involved to avoid their respective legal liabilities in connection with any transaction which they might enter into with a view to commercial advantage
No, because it isn't possible, even by using explicitly worded terms of an agreement, to rebut the presumption that the agreement was intended to be legally binding

No, because by using sufficiently explicit wording, companies may rebut the presumption that the agreement was intended to be legally binding, and in this situation, the 'in honour' clause had removed this essential feature of a valid contract

Yes, because there is a presumption regarding business agreements that commercial organisations intend to create legal relations and this includes the contract such as the one entered in to by the respective companies
No, because such an 'honour clause' would be repugnant to the intention of the rest of the document, and its enforceability contrary to public policy

explanation.en: C is correct. The arrangement would not create a binding contract because of the 'in honour' clause which would remove this essential feature of a valid contract. Lead case: Rose and Frank Co v Crompton Bros [1925] AC 445.

stem: Tamara wanted to inherit her mother's diamond ring and promised her mother to pay 5,000 if the mother would not sell it. When Tamara failed to pay the 5,000, her brother Tarquin sued her.
ask: Can Tarquin enforce Tamara's promise at common law?

options.en: Yes, because there were such ties of love and affection from the mother to both Tamara and Tarquin, that quite naturally, consideration and privity extends to both of them
No because there were insufficient ties of love and affection from the mother to Tamara and Tarquin for consideration and privity to extend to both of them
Yes, because a claimant in the position of Tamara is considered to be a creditor beneficiary
No, because Tamara's promise was made to the mother, so there is neither privity nor consideration between him and Tamara
Yes, because the mother in these circumstances was agent for Tarquin in making the contract and Tamara ought to be liable upon it

explanation.en: D is correct. The general rule is that someone not a party to a contract cannot be liable under it nor benefit from it. The doctrine linked to the rule that consideration must move from the promise. Lead case: Tweddle v Atkinson (1861) 1 B & S 393; 121 ER 762.

stem: Harrison & Co sell widgets to a dealer who then sells them to Dynamic DIY for high street sale. The dealer is restrained to selling the widgets at prices set by Harrison or to trade to customers at a discount of 12%, if the secondary customers then sell at Harrison's chosen price. Dynamic DIY have been selling the widgets at below the recommended list price.
ask: Under the common law rules of privity of contract, can Harrison & Co restrain Dynamic DIY from selling its widgets, on terms other than those specified in its agreement with the dealer?

options.en: Yes, on the grounds that the party to whom the benefit accrues may bring an action, so Harrison & Co could rely on the terms of their contract with the dealer, because Dynamic DIY were a party to this contract

No, because there was no consideration moving from Harrison & Co to Dynamic DIY since by selling the widgets to the dealer they became the property of the dealer who could choose to do with them as they pleased

Yes, because the law recognises that when the right acquired by a third party in a contract between others, arises by way of contract, such a right can be conferred on a stranger to a contract as a right to enforce the contract in personam
No, because in English law an undisclosed principal may not sue upon a contract, even if entered in to as agents
Yes, because consideration was freely given by Harrison & Co to the dealer or to Dynamic DIY at Harrison & Co's request

explanation.en: B is correct. Harrison & Co were not parties to the agreement between the dealer and Dynamic DIY. Lead case: Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co Ltd v Selfridge & Co Ltd [1915] AC 847.

stem: Ben took over his Aunt Jessica's business and promised to pay her a weekly allowance of £250 and promised her that he would also pay her husband, Joshua, a weekly allowance of £175. After his aunt died, Ben paid one instalment to Joshua and refused to pay any further.
ask: Is Joshua entitled to enforce payment of the allowance which Ben agreed to pay to him under the common law doctrine of privity of contract?

options.en: No, because Ben's agreement with Jessica to pay money to Joshua conferred no right on Joshua to enforce payment
Yes, Joshua may sue Ben on the promise he made to his wife for his benefit, because Joshua had an immediate interest in the benefit of the agreement, even though he may not have been named as a party
No, because in English law an undisclosed principal may not sue upon a contract, even if entered in to as agent

Yes, because the contract was made for the benefit of Joshua who has a legitimate interest to enforce it in the name of Jessica as contracting party or jointly with Ben, and since Ben refuses to join, Joshua may include him as a defendant
Yes, because in such a case as this, to uphold the doctrine of privity would be unjust and bring the law in to disrepute

explanation.en: A is the best answer. The doctrine of privity of contract does not allow third parties like Joshua to sue to enforce benefits under the contract between Ben and Jessica. Lead case: Beswick v Beswick [1968] AC 58. Note that option B is not the best answer. Indeed, under the Contracts Rights of Third Parties Act 1999, a third-party may enforce a term of a contract if: (a) the contract states so; or (b) a term of the contract confers a benefit on the third-party, as long as the contract identifies the third-party by name or as a member of a class. The question, however, asks whether the third-party can enforce the agreement under the common law doctrine of privity of contract. It is still necessary, therefore, to understand and be able to answer questions, regarding the common law doctrine and the various exceptions to it, such as: bailment; assignment and trust. Since s.1 (2) allows an exemption from the effects of s.1 (1)(b) if the contract specifies that a third-party should not be able to enforce the term, the common law is still clearly with us. In fact, in furtherance of s.1 (2), the majority of commercial contractors have revised their standard contracts to guarantee they no rights are conferred on third-parties.

stem: Lionel agreed to buy land from Daisy for a sum of £850,000 of which £150,000 was to be paid to Francesca. The contract specifically identified Francesca, and professed to confer a benefit on her. Lionel now refuses to pay Francesca.
ask: Is Lionel directly liable to Francesca for his breach of promise to pay her?

options.en: Yes, Lionel would be liable in damages for the breach of the promise to pay her the £150,000, since the contract intended to confer a legally enforceable benefit on her
No, Lionel would not be liable in damages for the breach of the promise to pay her the £150,000, since the contract did not intend to confer a legally enforceable benefit on her
No, because the doctrine of privity means that the law will deny the effectiveness of a contract for the benefit of a third party even where that is the expressed intention of the parties
Yes, but in the absence of evidence to suggest that Daisy suffered any detriment from a failure by Lionel to pay the £150,000 to Francesca, Francesca could establish no more than nominal damages
No, because there was no consideration moving from Francesca to Lionel since by agreeing to sell land to Daisy, it became Daisy's property, and she is entitled to do with it as she pleases

explanation.en: A is correct. Where the agreement was intended to confer a legally enforceable benefit, the third party can sue directly for the breach of the promise to pay. Daisy could only claim nominal damages if she sued Lionel, but Francesca could claim for the full £150,000 that Lionel had agreed to pay her, as she is named in the contract as a third party that benefits from the contract. Statute: Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 Lead case: Woodar v Wimpey [1980] 1 WLR 277.

stem: Paisley Paint Suppliers assured Fort Bridge that the industrial paint they supplied would last for at least five years. On the basis of this assurance, Fort Bridge entered in to a contract with Pete's Painters to paint Fort Bridge's Victorian iron rail bridge, and instructed Pete's Painters to use Paisley's paint. Pete's Painters bought the paint from Paisley, as instructed, but after the project was completed, Fort Bridge discovered that the paint was already beginning to peel after just a couple of months.
ask: Can Fort Bridge claim compensation directly from Paisley Paint Suppliers under these circumstances?

options.en: No, because Fort Bridge had provided no consideration for the promise given by Paisley Paint Suppliers
No, because the only contract which Paisley Paint Suppliers had made was to sell paint to Pete's Painters, and Fort Bridge was not a party to that agreement

Yes, because by Fort Bridge entering into a contract with Pete's Painter's, which required them to contract with Paisley Paint Suppliers for the particular paint, a collateral contract came in to existence, which meant that there was consideration for the assurance
No, because the doctrine of privity means that Fort Bridge, as a third-party, is denied the effectiveness of a contract, even where that is the expressed intention of the parties

Yes, but in the absence of evidence to suggest that Pete's Painters' suffered any detriment from a failure by Paisley Paint Suppliers to supply suitable paint, Fort Bridge could establish no more than nominal damages

explanation.en: C is correct. Fort Bridge could recover on the basis of a collateral contract. The consideration for the promise as to the paint's durability was the instruction by it to Pete's Painters to purchase the paint from the Paisley Paint Suppliers. Lead case: Shanklin Pier v Detel Products [1951] 2 KB 854; [1951] 2 All ER 471.

stem: Provident & Co, entered a tenancy agreement for Sky Inc to rent an office in its building, and Sky subsequently transferred the lease to Atlantic Inc. Sky's partners personally guaranteed Atlantic's lease to Provident, but Provident subsequently entered in to a supplemental deed with Atlantic which contained a limitation clause stating that 'in the event of a default in the lease, liability shall not extend to the personal assets of individual partners of Atlantic, (the tenant) or any previous tenant'. Atlantic has defaulted on the lease, but Sky's partners claim that although they were not parties to the supplemental deed, the reference to "any previous tenant" allowed them, as non-parties, to claim the benefit of the limitation clause, which thus protected them from personal liability.
ask: Which statement best sums up the law in relation to whether the partners of Sky Inc, as non-parties to the deed, are entitled to enforce the limitation clause against Provident under the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999?

options.en: Sky may have a right of action if there is a benefit to it, as the third party expressed in a term of the supplemental deed, even if it appears that the parties to the deed did not expressly intend it to do so

A third party would only have a right of action if there is a benefit to the third party expressed in a term of the supplemental deed, as long as the parties to the deed expressly intended it to do so

Although Sky was not a party to the supplemental deed, the non-express reference to "any previous tenant" would cover it, since under the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 they are entitled to enforce this limitation against Provident
Sky is entitled to enforce this limitation against Provident because the clause in the supplemental deed made grammatical sense

Even though the limitation on liability did not contain an express provision allowing Sky to rely on it, its partners would be entitled to the benefit of the restriction by virtue of the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999

explanation.en: B is correct. The meaning of the clause must be clear. It must have the effect of giving the third party protection by virtue of the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999. Lead case: Prudential Assurance Co Ltd v Ayres and Ors [2008] EWCA CiV 52 (CA). Statute; rule; constitution: Section 1(1)(b) of the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999.

stem: The Canine Welfare Society (CWS) contracted with Ken's Kennels for the supply of puppies to sell to reputable individuals. Maureen bought one of the puppies from Ken's Kennels, subject to an express provision in the contract of sale, that CWS may enforce contractual rights against her if she is found to be mistreating the puppy. The CWS have received credible evidence that Maureen has mistreated the puppy.
ask: Can the CWS bring such an action against Maureen under the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999, even though it does not benefit from the contract?

options.en: No, because there were insufficient ties of love and affection from Maureen to the puppy for privity to extend to both of them
No, because CWS, as a third party, does not have the ability of to bring an action, even if the contract gives it an express right to do so
Yes, because the contracting parties, Ken's Kennels and Maureen, expressly provided for such a right of enforcement in the contract
Yes, as long as the contract benefits CWS as the third party, by implication, this will be enough to raise the presumption that it has a right to enforce the contract
Yes, CWS has a right of action if there is a benefit to it as the third party expressed in a term of the contract, even if it appears that Ken's Kennels and Maureen did not expressly intend to do so

explanation.en: C is correct. Section 1(1)(a) of the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 states that a third party may enforce a term of the contract if the contract expressly provides that it may. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 1(1) (a) of the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999.

stem: Douglas sent a letter offering to buy shares from a company at 50 pence a share. Six months later the company accepted his offer, by which time the value of the shares had fallen to 40 pence a share. Douglas had not withdrawn the offer but refused to go through with the sale, and the company has brought an action for specific performance of the contract.
ask: Which of the following statements best explains Douglas's legal position regarding the company's claim against him?

options.en: Since it appears that the company relied on Douglas's offer, the offer should remain open because it would be unconscionable to allow Douglas to withdraw it just because the share price fell
Since no time limit was specified, then the offer remains open and the company's action for specific performance will likely succeed
The company's acceptance of Douglas's offer, by letter, to buy the shares, constituted an acceptance of his offer
The period between offer and acceptance seems unreasonable and therefore no contract is likely to still exist six months after Douglas's offer and the company's acceptance
Since the value of the shares had fallen to from 50 to 40 pence a share in the interim, Douglas should not be obliged to go ahead with the sale, on grounds that he had made such a bad bargain

explanation.en: D is correct. The offer would no longer be open as due to the nature of the subject matter of the contract the offer lapsed after a reasonable period of time. Therefore there was no contract and the company's action for specific performance would be unsuccessful. Lead case: Ramsgate Victoria Hotel Co v Montefiore (1866) LR 1 Ex 109.

stem: Eight months ago, Alfred, a private individual, sold a second hand car to a dealership in part exchange for a new car. When presenting the registration book to the dealer, Alfred had falsely, but honestly, verbally stated that the second hand car was a 2008 model, when in fact it was a 2001 model. The dealership now intends to sue Alfred for damages.
ask: How would you advise Alfred regarding the dealerships claim against him?

options.en: The dealership has no claim against Alfred because the term caveat emptor applies in these situations, meaning the courts will not save buyers from the consequences of their bad bargains
Because the dealership has the greater skill and knowledge of such matters, the statement should not be regarded as a term
Alfred either was or should have been in a position to guarantee the age of the car, since the law clearly states that he who asserts must prove
Alfred is bound to his statement, because it was not something detached from the contract, but was a part of the contract and was in legal terminology a condition
The statement made by Alfred at the time of the making of the contract was a statement made contractually and he must therefore be bound by it

explanation.en: B is correct. As buyer is a car dealer and Alfred has no expertise, and only repeated the year of manufacture from the registration book, he is taken to know less than the buyer, and thus, the statement was a representation not a term. Lead case: Oscar Chess Ltd v Williams [1957] 1 WLR 370.

stem: Venture Inc insisted to AB Shipping Ltd ("AB") that as part of any contract for the transport of its cargo by sea, AB should not carry the cargo on deck. AB gave verbal assurance that Venture's cargo would be carried below deck, but issued printed standard conditions for the contract which allowed for freight to be carried on deck.
ask: Venture's cargo was carried on deck, and was lost overboard In such a scenario is the verbal assurance likely to take precedence over the written conditions?

options.en: No, because there was no contractual promise that these containers should be carried under deck
No, because even if there was a contractual promise that the goods would be carried under deck, AB can rely on the printed terms and conditions
Yes, although the oral assurance was not included in the written terms of the contract, it was nonetheless part of the contract through the verbal assurance
Yes, because every representation made in the course of such dealing is to be treated as a warranty
No, because AB should not be liable in damages for an innocent misrepresentation

explanation.en: C is correct. The statement that Venture's cargo would be carried below deck was a contractual term, and it would be entitled to succeed. Lead case: Evans & Son Ltd v Andrea Merzario Ltd [1976] 2 All ER 930.

stem: Julia's lease was up for renewal, and the landlord tried to insert a written clause stating that the apartment should not be used for any employment activities. When Julia objected, saying that she generally works from home, the landlord assured her orally that if she signed the lease, she would be allowed to continue working from home. The landlord is subsequently trying to rely on this written clause to evict Julia, claiming that Julia is in breach of it by working there.
ask: In such a scenario could Julia rely on a collateral contract giving her the right to work from home?

options.en: No, Julia is unlikely to be able to rely on a collateral contract, because there was no contractual promise giving her the right to work from home
Yes, under these circumstances, Julia is likely to be able to rely on a collateral contract giving her the right to work from home
No, because even if there was a contractual promise giving her the right to work from home, the landlord can rely on the printed terms and conditions
Yes, because promissory estoppel would apply as it would be inequitable for the landlord to go back on the future promise
No, because the landlord will not be held liable for innocent misrepresentation; the court is unlikely to decide that there was a collateral contract

explanation.en: B is correct. A written document is not deemed to be exhaustive of the parties intentions when there is clear evidence of a collateral contract. Lead case: City of Westminster Properties v Mudd [1959] Ch 129; [1958] 2 All ER 733.

stem: Justin advertised a car in a private sale as a 'Falcon, convertible, silver, 2009'. Eric, who was a private buyer, later discovered it was actually two cars stuck together and the description only fitted the rear half of the car.
ask: Would Justin be liable under the Sale of Goods Act even though he innocently described the state of the car?

options.en: Yes, because promissory estoppel would apply, as it would be inequitable for Justin to go back on his representations to Eric
No, because under the Act, Justin would only be liable for the sale of the car if he had knowingly and falsely described the details
Yes, because under the Act, a seller is still liable for the innocent sale of goods that have been falsely described
No, Eric has no claim against Justin because the term caveat emptor applies in these situations, meaning the courts will not save buyers from the consequences of their bad bargains
No, because the Act does not apply to private sales, only those in the course of a business and Justin's was a private sale to Eric

explanation.en: C is correct. s13 of the Sale of Goods Act implies a condition that goods will match their description. Lead case: Beale v Taylor [1967] 3 All ER 253. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 13 Sale of Goods Act 1979.

stem: A car dealership bought a car from Natalie for £3000 and resold it for £4000 to Olivia who used it for five months, before discovering that the car had never belonged to Natalie, who had bought it in good faith from someone without title. After the car had been claimed by the original owner, the dealership paid off Olivia by refunding her the £4000 and claimed to recover in turn the £3000 which it had paid to Natalie.
ask: With reference to the Sale of Goods Act, would the dealership be entitled to recover the whole purchase price?

options.en: Yes, the dealership would be entitled to recover the whole purchase price, but Natalie would be entitled to set off anything for the five month use of the car which Olivia had enjoyed
Yes, the dealership would be entitled to recover the whole purchase price and Natalie would not be entitled to set off anything for the five month use of the car which Olivia had enjoyed
No, the dealership would not be entitled to recover the whole purchase price, but Natalie would be entitled to set off anything for the five month use of the car which Olivia had enjoyed
No, because a car dealership should be taken to have better knowledge of such matters than Natalie, since the dealership has the greater skill and knowledge of such matters
No, because the dealership cannot recover any money paid, since use has been made of the car in the intervening period

explanation.en: B is correct. The dealership would be allowed to recover what it had paid to Natalie in full, on grounds of a total failure of consideration, and Olivia's intervening use of the car is irrelevant. Lead case: Rowland v Divall [1923] 2 KB 500. Comment: The essence of a sale of goods contract is not the use of the goods, but the transfer of ownership. The breach of s 12(1) Sale of Goods Act meant that ownership had never been transferred, and dealership would be entitled to recover all its money. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 12(1) Sale of Goods Act 1979.

stem: Jacqueline had bought the latest four-wheeled 'Bull Charger' all terrain vehicle, but it had numerous minor defects such as deterioration of the oil seals and defects in the engine and gear box, which made it unduly noisy and caused misfiring at all speeds. There were also numerous minor defects in the bodywork, although it was fit to drive.
ask: With reference to the Consumer Rights Act, would the lack of satisfactory quality allow Jacqueline to repudiate the contract even if the Bull Charger was fit to drive?

options.en: No, because it is common knowledge, new cars of all kinds from time to time produce snags of this kind after first delivery
No, because a buyer must establish that the defects made the Bull Charger unroadworthy and useable in the sense that it was not unsafe or in immediate peril of breaking down
No, because none of the defects were such as to render the vehicle unroadworthy, unusable or unfit for any of the normal purposes for which a Bull Charger might be used
Yes, because even the most superficial of cosmetic blemishes, dents and scratches, give good grounds for repudiation
Yes, it seems the faults revealed were sufficient to render the Bull Charger unmerchantable, and if a person pays a high price, she can expect a correspondingly high standard of quality

explanation.en: E is correct. A series of defects in an expensive model would likely make it unmerchantable (not of satisfactory quality) even though it was fit to drive. A key component in the s.9(2) CRA analysis is that if a person pays a high price, he can expect a similarly high standard of quality. Lead case: Rogers v Parish (Scarborough) Ltd [1987] OB 933. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 9(2) Consumer Rights Act 2015.

stem: Kerry's Car Wash presented Jean with a receipt for her car, which she left to be cleaned, while she went shopping in the mall opposite. Before she signed the receipt, she inquired what was meant by the confusing small print and the attendant, in all innocence, assured her that it was a clause excluding liability for damage to wing mirrors and head lamps only. When she returned to collect her car, she noticed severe abrasions to the paint work and the front window screen was cracked, but the car wash is relying on the clause which actually excluded liability for all damage whatsoever.
ask: Which of the following statements best describes the parties' legal position?

options.en: In the absence of actual fraud, an exclusion clause is effective
A misrepresentation innocently made does not negate the effectiveness of an exclusion clause
Liability does not attach to a statement, whether it is only half the truth or an outright lie, once a signed contract is in place
A half-truth, even if innocently made as to the extent of a clause, still amounts to a misrepresentation
Any exclusion clause effectively excludes liability once it becomes part of the contract

explanation.en: D is correct. Even though the attendant's statement was innocently made, and true as far as the attendant understood the clause, half-truths such as the one made by the attendant can amount to a misrepresentation. Because the extent of the exclusion was not revealed, Kerry's Car Wash would effectively be estopped from relying upon it. Lead case: Curtis v Chemical Cleaning and Dyeing Co Ltd [1951] 1 KB 805.

stem: Karl rented six computer programme packs from Zenith Inc to update the computers at his internet café and which were delivered by courier, together with a receipt containing numerous printed conditions, one of which specified that all programmes had to be returned within five working days; otherwise a late fee of £75 would be charged for each unreturned programme pack. Karl, who had not previously used Zenith's services, did not read the conditions and returned all the programme packs six weeks later than scheduled. Zenith has invoiced Karl for £13,500, but Karl refuses to pay.
ask: Is Zenith likely to succeed in an action to recover that sum?

options.en: Yes, because in the absence of fraud or misrepresentation the condition is effective
No, because Karl was neither under any obligation to read the receipt nor to make himself aware of the condition
Yes, because the terms of the receipt formed part of a contract between the parties; and, therefore Zenith are entitled to enforce those terms against Karl
Yes, because by serving the receipt with delivery, Zenith did what was reasonably fair to bring to Karl's attention the existence of this particular condition

No, because where a condition in a set of printed conditions is particularly unusual or onerous, such as for late fees, the party seeking to enforce it must show that the particular condition was fairly brought to the attention of the other party

explanation.en: E is correct. The unusual and one-sided nature of the clause in question would likely make it incumbent on Zenith to do more than it had done to bring it to Karl's attention. Lead case: Interfoto Picture Library v Stiletto Visual Programmes [1988] QB 433. Comment: Please note, Interfoto Picture Library v Stiletto Visual Programmes was not an exlusion clause case, but is used to illustrate how courts will strike down exceptional, and unusually onerous conditions. Lead case: Hollier v Rambler Motors [1972] 2 QB 71; [1972] 1 AlI ER 399.

stem: Marjorie arrived at a hotel as a guest and paid for a room in advance at the reception desk. There was a notice clearly displayed in the hotel bedroom, which Marjorie read, stating: 'Proprietors will not hold themselves responsible for articles lost or stolen, unless handed to reception for safe custody.' Owing to the negligence of the hotel, a thief managed to get into the room, which had been taken by Marjorie, and stole a quantity of her articles.
ask: Would the hotel proprietors be able to rely on the notice as a term of the contract?

options.en: No, because Marjorie wasn't under any obligation to read the notice and to make herself aware of the condition
Yes, because the exclusion clause was sufficiently drawn to Marjorie's attention to be considered as part of the agreement between her and the hotel
No, because the contract was completed at the reception desk and no subsequent notice could affect her rights
Yes, because even if the hotel had not taken reasonable steps to bring the extent of the exclusion clause to Marjorie's attention, there was a signed contract in place
Yes, because such notices are so standard and ubiquitous, the proprietors would be entitled to assume that Marjorie had previously read such a notice even if this was not in fact the case

explanation.en: C is correct. The contract was completed at the reception desk, and no subsequent notice could affect her rights. Notice of the exclusion clause was, therefore, too late for the hotel proprietors to be able to rely on it. Lead case: Olley v Marlborough Court Hotel [1949] 1 KB 532. Comment: Please note that the liability of a hotel owner for the loss of guests' property is now affected by the Hotel Proprietors Act 1956.

stem: Bobby, who could not read, travelled from London to Brighton for the day, and on arrival in Brighton deposited his bag at the railway station's luggage store for safekeeping. He was given a ticket, which, on its face was printed a number, and a direction to read the back of the ticket, which contained a clause excluding liability for the loss or theft of any item, and a sign to the same effect was hung in the luggage room. Bobby had a nice day by the seaside, but when he went to collect his bag, the attendant told him that it had been stolen.
ask: Had reasonable notice of the clause excluding liability been given to Bobby despite his illiteracy?

options.en: Yes, reasonable notice had been given despite Bobby's illiteracy
No, obviously persons who are minded to go for a day journey of this sort do not take the trouble to make an examination of all the terms and conditions of each and every contract
No, because any conditions contained in the notice came too late, as the contract was already made
Yes, because such notices are so standard and ubiquitous; the railway station would be entitled to assume that Bobby had previously read such a notice even if this was not in fact the case
No, even if the railway station attendant had to have taken reasonable steps to bring the exclusion clause to the attention of Bobby, he cannot rely on it if there is no signed contract

explanation.en: A is correct. The fact that Bobby was illiterate does not help him, although the position might be different if the attendant had actual knowledge of Bobby's inability to read the terms and conditions. Lead case: Olley v Marlborough Court Hotel [1949] 1 KB 532; [1949] 1 All ER 127.

stem: Daniel was considering buying 80 acres of land with a view to rearing dairy cattle upon it, and asked the selling farmer, Giles, if in his opinion that amount of land could support a 700 head of cattle. Giles pointed out that he was not a cattle farmer, and had never tried cattle-farming on the land, but thought it could realistically support 700 head of cattle. Giles' opinion has turned out to be inaccurate and the land can only sustain 400 head of cattle and Daniel argues that the statement was a misrepresentation.
ask: Did Giles's statement amount to an actionable misrepresentation?

options.en: No, because Giles's assessment of the matter was no more than an expression of opinion, and not a statement of fact
Yes, because Giles's assessment of the matter was not an expression of opinion, and more a statement of fact
No, because a statement of opinion cannot involve a statement of fact
Yes, because Daniel relied upon Giles's representation so it is irrelevant whether it was stated as a specific fact, or a statement of opinion
Yes, because any statement made by an owner who has been occupying his own farm as to its carrying capacity would be regarded as a statement of fact

explanation.en: A is correct. Giles's assurance of the suitability of land for cattle rearing, when Daniel was aware that he had no knowledge or experience of this type of farming, would be an opinion rather than a fact. A vendor of land would not be liable for stating that it would support 700 livestock where he had no personal knowledge of the facts, the land never having been used for cattle rearing and the buyer knew this and understood that the vendor was only stating an opinion. Note that option C is incorrect, as a statement of opinion by one who knows the true facts, where the other party does not know the true facts, may amount to a statement of fact. This is because, by implication, the person making the statement states that he knows facts which justify his opinion. However, this is not the case here. Lead case: Bisset v Wilkinson [1927] AC 177.

stem: Krishnan wished to sell his medical practice, and while negotiating with Liam, he stated that his practice earned him £80,000 per year. When Krishnan made this statement, it was true, but because of his failing health, by the time it was actually sold to Liam, Krishnan's earnings from the practice were less than £20,000 per year.
ask: Did Krishnan's statement amount to an actionable misrepresentation?

options.en: Yes, because Krishnan's failure to notify Liam of the fact that his earlier statement was no longer true amounted to a misrepresentation
No, because Krishnan was not obligated to notify Liam of the fact that his earlier statement was no longer true
No, because Krishnan's assessment of the matter was no more than an expression of opinion, and not a statement of fact
No, Krishnan had no duty to Liam because there was no pre-existing confidential or a fiduciary relationship requiring of Krishnan a duty of entire disclosure
Yes, because any statement made by an owner who has been running his own practice as to its earning capacity would be regarded as a statement of fact

explanation.en: A is correct. There exists an obligation to provide information to the other party if the facts materially change between the issuing of the statement and the acceptance of it. Lead case: With v O'Flanagan [1936] Ch 575.

stem: Kenny was considering entering in to a pub tenancy agreement with Castle Brewery and spoke to one of Castle's most experienced representatives who estimated that the likely quantity of beer sold by the pub would reach 4,000 barrels per year. Kenny was doubtful as to the likelihood of the estimate, but deferred to Castle's representative's greater familiarity of the pub-retailing business. The expert failed, however, to consider the fact that the local authority had only granted an opening licence until 11pm, not 2am as envisaged, and Kenny now finds that, after one year, the quantity of beer sold by the pub has failed to reach 2,200 barrels per year.
ask: Which statement is the most accurate regarding whether the representative's statement amounted to an actionable misrepresentation that would give rise to damages?

options.en: The representative's statement was no more than an expression of opinion, and not a statement of fact, so does not give rise to an action for misrepresentation
The parties were contracting with one another, so the representative was entitled to observe silence, even in regard to facts which he believed might influence Kenny
The representative had no duty to Kenny because there was no pre-existing confidential or a fiduciary relationship giving rise to a duty of full disclosure
Although the estimate was an expression of opinion, it contained an implied promise that it was made with reasonable care and skill
In such situations the law is clear; an innocent misrepresentation is not actionable and gives no right to damages

explanation.en: D is correct. Because it was a statement made by an experienced expert, Castle would be liable due to its negligence in failing to take reasonable care in preparing the forecast. Lead case: Esso Petroleum Co Ltd v Mardon [1976] QB 801; [1976] 2 All ER 5.

stem: Property owned by Diana was sold by auction to James. There was an inaccurate statement in the auction particulars, which was re-affirmed by the auctioneer, to the effect that rent reviews of three leases to which the properties were subject had not been finalised. James is now seeking to rescind the contract for misrepresentation on grounds that the misrepresentation induced him to enter into a contract.
ask: Which of the below statements most accurately reflects the law's current approach as to whether an inducement to a contract was material?

options.en: The misrepresentation would have to be the sole or main factor inducing the representee in to the contract
There would only be an inducement if the representation had been verified by a third- party and the representee relied on the verification

The reasonableness or otherwise of a claimant's behaviour is not relevant to the burden of proof, but the less reasonable the inducement, the less difficult it would be for the claimant to convince the court that he had been affected by the misrepresentation

If the misrepresentation would have induced a reasonable person to enter into the contract, courts will presume that it did and the burden of proof is on the person relying on the representation to show that he did not actually rely on the misrepresentation

If the misrepresentation would have induced a reasonable person to enter into the contract, courts will presume that it did and the burden of proof shifts to the person making the representation to show that the person relying on the representation did not actually rely on the misrepresentation

explanation.en: E is correct. If the misrepresentation would have induced a reasonable person to enter into the contract, the court will presume that it did and the onus of proof is then placed on the representor to show that the representee did not in fact rely on the misrepresentation. A representation is material if it is something that induces the person to whom it is made, whether solely or in conjunction with other inducements, to contract on terms on which he does contract. Lead case: Museprime Properties Ltd v Adhill Properties Ltd [1990] 2 EG 196; (1990) 61 P & CR 111.

stem: Jack bought an operating removal's business from Stanley, who apprised Jack of the value of the business and gave him photocopies of the business accounts. In fact, Jack did not trouble himself to check the accounts which, had he done so, would most likely have revealed the level of Stanley's misrepresentation.
ask: Would Jack's oversight prevent him rescinding the contract based on misrepresentation?

options.en: No, because Stanley had no duty to Jack because there was no pre-existing confidential or a fiduciary relationship requiring of Stanley a duty of entire disclosure
Yes, because any statement made by an owner who has been running his own business as to its accounts would be regarded as a statement of fact
No, if Jack had relied on the false statement he would be entitled to rescind the contract
No, because Jack wasn't actually deceived because he rejected the chance to discover the truth
Yes, because Stanley's accounts contained an implied promise that it was made with reasonable care and skill

explanation.en: C is correct. It is irrelevant that the claimant has the opportunity to verify the veracity of the representation but does not take it. Where a person makes a misrepresentation, it is not sufficient to mitigate the falsehood by providing documents containing the true position. The fact that the Jack chose not to verify the position when given the opportunity does not prevent him from rescinding the contract, as he had relied on the original false representation by Stanley (Redgrave v Hurd (1881) 20 Ch D 1).

stem: David bought Nick's catering and sandwich business, who claimed that it had an annual turnover of £87,000 and that most of the trade was over the counter. In fact, this wasn't true and the vast majority of the trade was wholesale, requiring a representative to canvass for orders, which meant that turnover was less than £47,000 after the representative had taken his cut.
ask: Which of the following would be best practice to advise David to sue Nick under?

options.en: Fraudulent misrepresentation (tort of deceit)
Negligent misrepresentation under common law
Innocent misrepresentation
Negligent misrepresentation under the Misrepresentation Act 1967
Negligent misstatement

explanation.en: D is correct. Always better to sue under the Misrepresentation Act 1967 because it's easier to prove than fraudulent misrepresentation. Further, (1) the burden of proof is on the misrepresentor and (2) the measure of damages is the same as that for fraudulent misrepresentation. Lead case: Doyle v Olby (Ironmongers) Ltd [1969] 2 QB 158. Statute; rule; constitution: s.2(1), 2(2) Misrepresentation Act 1967.

stem: After a dispute over contributions to its members, the United Stevedores' Trade Union (USTU) threatened to encourage its members to break their contracts with the owners of the good ship "Teutonic" by refusing to handle it or any of its cargo in port in Liverpool unless the owners agreed to pay £ 250,000 in to the union's welfare fund. The ship owners would have lost a valuable consignment in Rotterdam if they couldn't get the ship out of Liverpool before the weekend, so under protest, paid the £250,000 in to the union's welfare fund. Although it subsequently learned that the industrial action was unlawful, at the time it was taken, the union honestly thought it was lawful.
ask: Would the ship owners likely succeed in an action to recover this payment on grounds of duress?

options.en: No, the payments are irrecoverable, because the demand had arisen out of a trade dispute, and so was a legitimate exercise of pressure and did not constitute duress
No, not every threat of non-performance will amount to economic duress, since there is a distinction between duress and hard bargaining
Yes, because such a threat of economic embargo, such as breaking the contract, will always be illegitimate even if it was a lawful act at the time
No, because the threat to do the unlawful act such as breaking the contract would only be illegitimate if the union was aware that it was an unlawful act at the time
Yes because the threat to do the unlawful act, such as breaking the contract, will always be illegitimate even if the union thought it was a lawful act at the time

explanation.en: E is correct. If the threatened industrial action was unlawful under English law, the payment would be recoverable. Lead case: Universe Tankships Inc of Monrovia v International Transport Workers Federation, The Universe Sentinel [1983] 1 AC 366; [1982] 2 All ER 67.

stem: André received a commission to compose a symphony for a film score from Galaxy Productions, but before the submission date of his symphony, Galaxy decided it was going to make an action movie, rather than the love story for which André had been busy preparing. André has demanded at least £500 towards the work which he has completed thus far, but Galaxy have refused saying that it has received no benefit.
ask: Which statement best summarises André's legal position?

options.en: As a special contract is already in existence and open, André is unable to sue in quantum meruit
Since the contract did not exist any longer, the work was abandoned; under these circumstances André will lose the fruit of his labour
Since André has performed work for Galaxy, he may claim in respect of the reasonable value of the work he has done on the basis of a quantum meruit
Since André has not performed delivery exactly within the terms of the contract; Galaxy is entitled to reject the half-finished symphony
When a frustrating event occurs, such as this, the contract is terminated and neither party has any further obligations to the other

explanation.en: C is correct. Because André is prevented by Galaxy from performing all his obligations, he can recover a reasonable price for what he has in fact done on a quantum meruit basis in an action in quasi-contract. Lead case: Planché V Colburn (1831) 8 Bing 14; [1824-34] All ER Rep 94.

stem: Dinah employed Johnny to decorate and furnish her flat at a fixed cost of £750. Johnny completed the work, although Dinah did find some faults which amounted to £55 to put right. Dinah moved into the flat but refuses to pay Johnny the balance outstanding under the contract. The contract provided for payment of 'net cash as the work proceeds and balance on completion', so that Dinah had already paid £350 and Johnny is now asking to recover the remaining £400.
ask: Which statement best summarises Johnny's legal position regarding the remaining £400?

options.en: The contract had been performed, albeit badly performed, and Johnny can recover for the work done, less deductions for the fact that it did not conform to the contract requirements
Dinah can reject that price altogether and simply pay a reasonable price for all the work that was done based on a quantum meruit
Since the contract no longer exists, the work was abandoned; under these circumstances Johnny will lose the fruit of his labour
Since Johnny has not performed exactly within the terms of the contract; Dinah is entitled to refuse to pay Johnny the balance outstanding under the contract
In unilateral contracts, such as this, Johnny is forced to perform his side of the bargain before any performance obligation falls upon Dinah

explanation.en: A is correct. Substantial performance allows a party to enforce a contract. Note, there is a distinction between failing to complete, and completing badly. Lead case: Hoenig v Isaacs [1952] 2 All ER 176

stem: Lou agreed to employ Sonny on 20 June to work as a sales representative, and accompany him when he meets clients in the Far East. On 1 June, however, Lou emailed Sonny informing him that his services would no longer be required. Sonny is considering bringing an action for damages immediately, without waiting for 20 June.
ask: Which is the best advice to give to Sonny?

options.en: Sonny must wait until performance is due, and then seek damages for non- performance at that stage
Since there can be no actual breach of a contract by reason of non-performance, so long as the time for performance has not yet arrived, there has been no actionable breach
Sonny has no actionable claim since he has done nothing to avert the injurious effects which he claims have flowed from the non-fulfilment of the contract
Since an anticipatory breach entitles the innocent party to terminate performance of the contract immediately, Sonny can claim damages on the date of the acceptance of the breach
In unilateral contracts, such as this, Sonny will be forced to perform his side of the bargain before any performance obligation falls upon Lou

explanation.en: D is correct. Lou's repudiation would allow Sonny to accept the repudiation immediately and sue for breach of contract without having to wait for the date of intended performance. Lead case: Hochster v De La Tour (1853) 2 E & B 678; [1843-60] All ER Rep 12.

stem: A cargo vessel, which was carrying dates, sank in shallow water as it entered the river Thames from the Persian Gulf. The vessel was raised and the cargo salvaged, but on arrival at the port of discharge the dates were found to be in a state of fermentation, and contaminated with sewage. The freight was payable by the charterer on arrival at the port.
ask: Was the contract frustrated?

options.en: No freight would be payable in respect of the dates, for the dates had ceased to be dates in a mercantile sense, whatever they may have been in appearance
The contract was not frustrated, since it is enough that on arrival the dates existed in species as dates, even if they were not merchantable
The dates might have deteriorated, but they were still merchantable as dates, so the contract was not frustrated
Obligations are not discharged by a frustrating event, and a party who fails to perform as a result of such an event would still be in breach of contract
The contract was not frustrated, because total destruction of the goods is necessary; mere destruction of the merchantable quality of the goods is insufficient

explanation.en: A is correct. The contract was frustrated, because total destruction of the goods is not necessary; mere destruction of the merchantable quality of the goods is sufficient. Lead case: Asfar v Blundell [1896] 1 QB 123.

stem: Dwayne Vegas was hired by the members of boy band, "Slush" to be their lead singer for two shows, seven days a week for their forthcoming cabaret summer season in Blackpool. Due to severe laryngitis, however, Dwayne's doctor has advised him that can only perform three nights a week, with no matinee afternoon shows. Slush has now terminated his contract.
ask: Was the contract between Dwayne and Slush frustrated?

options.en: Slush's obligations were not discharged by Dwayne's laryngitis and should they fail to meet them, they would be in breach of contract
The contract was not frustrated, because Dwayne's incapacity must be total; mere vocal interruption is insufficient
Commercially it would be impossible for Dwayne to perform the contract and the contract is frustrated
Obligations are not discharged by a frustrating event, and a party who fails to perform as a result of such an event would still be in breach of contract
The contract was not frustrated, because Dwayne was capable of partial performance

explanation.en: C is correct. In a business sense, it would be impossible for the singer to perform the contract and for that reason the contract would be discharged for frustration.

stem: Trudy agreed to pay a premium price to hire from Trevor a suite overlooking Horse Guards Parade for the particular purpose of watching the royal wedding procession of William and Kate on 29 April. Trudy paid £450 as a deposit and was to pay the balance of £350 on 28 April, but owing to security fears, the route of William and Kate's procession was changed at the last moment, which meant the processions would not go anywhere near Horse Guards. Trevor is demanding she pays the outstanding balance but Trudy has refused and demands the return of her deposit on the ground that the contract was frustrated.
ask: Which of the following would be the best advice to Trudy?

options.en: Trudy's obligations were not discharged by the change of route and should she fail to meet them, she would be in breach of contract
The purpose of the contract was defeated by the radical change in circumstances; namely the absence of a procession, so the contract was frustrated
The contract was not frustrated, because the frustration must be total, and the fact is; she still had use of the suite
Although there was no procession, literal performance was possible so the contract was not frustrated
The particular purpose of the contract was defeated by the radical change in circumstances; namely the incapacity or unavailability of a particular party

explanation.en: B is correct. Although literal performance was possible, in that the suite could have been made available to Trudy at the appropriate time, and she could have sat in it and looked out of the window, in the absence of the procession it had no point, and the whole purpose of the contract had disappeared. Lead case: Krell v Henry [1903] 2 KB 740.

stem: Percy agreed to pay Beatrice £750 to hire the cruise ship "Shanty" from Beatrice for 29 April 'for the purpose of viewing the royal regatta and for a day's cruise round the fleet'. On 28 April the royal regatta,
ask: Which the Queen was due to conduct, was officially cancelled because the Queen was ill, but the fleet remained in place. Beatrice brought a claim for the outstanding balance owing, but. Percy is seeking to repudiate the contract all together. Was the contract frustrated?

options.en: The contract was frustrated because a supervening event prevented Beatrice supplying, and Percy from obtaining, what Beatrice had contracted to provide and Percy acquire under the contract
The contract was not frustrated because the destruction of the subject matter prior to the formation of a contract will render it void for common mistake

The contract was frustrated because the particular purpose of the contract was defeated by the radical change in circumstances; namely the incapacity or unavailability of the Queen at the royal regatta

The contract was frustrated because the particular purpose of the contract, namely the special object of seeing both the royal regatta and reviewing the fleet was defeated by the radical change in circumstances; the absence of a royal regatta

The contract was not frustrated because the object of the voyage was not limited to the royal regatta, but also extended to a cruise round the fleet, and since the fleet was still in place, the tour could go still ahead

explanation.en: E is correct. Although the Queen was ill and the royal regatta was cancelled, the fleet was still in place and so the tour of it could go ahead, so the effect on the contract was not sufficiently fundamental to lead to it being regarded as frustrated. Lead case: Herne Bay Steamboat Co v Hutton [1903] 2 KB 683.

stem: Richard entered into a contract with a local authority to build a railway bridge, but after the outbreak of war, the government ordered him to stop work so that the men and equipment could be used in the war effort. The government order could have lasted as long as the war lasted and no one knew how long this could have been. The construction contract contained a clause which provided that in the event of delays 'however occasioned' the contractor would be given additional time in which to complete the project.
ask: Did the government order bring the contract to an end?

options.en: The contract was not frustrated, because the clause in the contract dealing with the possibility of an extension of time, in the case of delay, covered an interruption of such a character and duration, even if that interruption fundamentally altered the conditions of the contract
The contract was not frustrated because such an interruption would have been in the contemplation of the parties at the time the contract was made

The contract was frustrated because the clause could not have contemplated such a fundamental change of circumstances that would change the whole basis of the contract as a result of the government order
The contract was frustrated because of its illegality at the time of its formation
The contract was not frustrated, because as a matter of construction the clause covered the extraordinary situation which had arisen

explanation.en: C is correct. A contract will be frustrated if a supervening event makes performance of the contract impossible or radically different from what the parties originally envisaged. Lead case: Metropolitan Water Board v. Dick Kerr and Company [1918] AC 119.

stem: A contract was in place to promote a 'Guns N' Roses' concert, but when the Spanish government decided to close the stadium where it was supposed to take place, the contract was frustrated. The claimant had paid $400,000 to the defendant before the stadium's closure and pursued the defendant for recovery. Meanwhile, the defendant had sustained costs of approximately $50, 000 in outlays and argued that it should be allowed to keep this amount.
ask: With deference to the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943, which outcome would be most appropriate to do justice to the parties?

options.en: To do justice under the Act, the party receiving the benefit will be ordered to pay a just sum in return for it
To do justice under the Act, $350,000 would have to be returned to the claimant
To do justice under the Act, the court must allow the losses to lie where they fell, which is the consequence of an application of common law rules on mistake
To do justice under the Act, the full $400,000 would have to be returned to the claimant without deduction for the defendant's expenses
To do justice under the Act, the full $50,000 would have to be returned to the defendant

explanation.en: D is the best answer. Taking into account the claimant's loss (approximately $400,000), justice would be done by allowing the claimant to recover the advance payment in full without any deduction for the defendant's expenses. Any financial obligation due (as in Chandler v Webster) is excused, subject to where expenses have been incurred by the payee. In this instance, the courts may award an amount up to what was payable prior to the frustrating event. Gamerco SA v ICM/Fair Warning (Agency) Ltd demonstrates the application of s.1(2) Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943. In that case, a large pre- payment of $412,500 was returned to Gamerco SA, where they had incurred expenses prior to a frustrated contract for a series of concerts, despite both sides having begun performance (in the form of advertising). Lead case: Gamerco SA v ICM/Fair Warning (Agency) Ltd [1995] 1 WLR 1226. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 1(2) The Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943. Note: Section 1(2) of the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943 allows money paid under a frustrated contract to be recoverable, even where there is not a total failure of consideration. However, the court has a broad discretion, and is not bound by specific formulas (e.g., equal sharing of losses) when applying the proviso under s 1(2). In this respect, the defendant (D) bears the burden of establishing that: (1) D incurred expenses paid or payable; (2) before the discharge of the contract; (3) in performance of the contract (if applicable); or (4) for the purposes of the performance of the contract; and (5) that it is just in all the circumstances to allow D to retain the whole or any part of the sums so paid or payable. Therefore B is not the best answer.

stem: The renowned entertainer, Sammy Smile, agreed to perform at Brian's Phoenix Club for the whole of June. Sammy told Brian that he can't perform between the dates of 11-15 June because his daughter needs an operation. Brian has discovered that Sammy will be appearing at the rival Coconut Grove Club between those dates.
ask: May Brian compel Sammy to continue the Phoenix Club; if so, which is the most appropriate remedy?

options.en: Yes, Brian can compel Sammy to continue performing at the Phoenix Club, and the most appropriate remedy is specific performance

No, Brian cannot compel Sammy to continue performing at the Phoenix Club, because courts will not compel the performance of a contract of personal service on the ground that it effectively amounts to involuntary servitude
Yes, Brian can compel Sammy to continue performing at the Phoenix Club, and the most appropriate remedy is quantum meruit
No, Brian cannot compel Sammy to continue performing at the Phoenix Club, because a party that wishes to do equity must come to the court with clean hands
Yes, Brian can compel Sammy to continue performing at the Phoenix Club, and the most appropriate remedy is a prohibitory injunction

explanation.en: B is correct. Please note, courts will not enforce a contract for personal services and this is now enshrined in Section 236 Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992. Lead case: Johnson v Shrewsbury and Birmingham Rly (1853) 3 DM & G 358. Statute; rule; constitution: Section 236 Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992.

stem: Pablo Fablo, Burnpool City's star striker in the English Premier League, contracted with Buddy to upgrade his swimming pool and during the contract negotiations, Pablo explains to Buddy that he intends to pay for the work out of the £250,000 bonus he is due to receive from City when he completes his 40th appearance in one season for the club. Two days before Pablo is due to make his 40th appearance, Buddy gives the thumbs up for Pablo to use the pool, and watches in horror as Pablo dives in to the deep end, only to suffer horrific injuries after hitting the bottom of the pool. Pablo is out for the rest of the season and will lose his bonus as a result of Buddy not deepening the pool as specified in the contract.
ask: Which is the most advisable measure of damages Pablo should pursue under the circumstances?

options.en: Since Pablo made Buddy aware of this bonus during negotiations, and as such it was reasonably in Buddy's contemplation, Pablo would be advised to make a claim for expectation damages
Pablo would be compensated for the losses which have arisen from Buddy's wrongful action by putting Pablo back into the position he was in prior to the breach of contract being committed
Since the accident happened after the building of the swimming pool, any losses resulting from Pablo missing out on his bonus are likely to be regarded as too remote and therefore irrecoverable
The court would allow the recovery of the 'cost of cure', namely putting the swimming pool back in to the condition it should have been in, if the breach had not occurred
While Pablo is entitled to a remedy for his loss of profit in principle, all he may in fact receive are nominal damages as the loss is entirely incapable of assessment

explanation.en: A is correct. Since Pablo made Buddy aware of this bonus during negotiations and as such it was reasonably in his contemplation, Pablo would be advised to make a claim for expectation damages, as it was only the injury to Pablo caused by Buddy that prevented him playing and earning his bonus. Lead case: Hadley v Baxendale (1854) 9 Exch 341. Comment: This is not a normal loss and so damages will only be payable under the second test in Hadley v Baxendale, otherwise they will be 'too remote'.

stem: Charlie entered into a contract with Buddy to build an extension on to his pub near Pall Mall, in order to increase the pub's seating capacity. Instead of finishing the work by the beginning of April, as agreed, Buddy only completed the work by the end of May.
ask: Which measure of damages is Charlie best advised to pursue Buddy for as a result of not having the extra seating capacity?

options.en: Charlie would be compensated for the losses which have arisen from Buddy's wrongful action by putting Charlie back into the position he was in prior to the breach of contracted being committed
Since time was of the essence, Charlie will be able to terminate the contract for breach of a contractual condition under the Sale of Goods Act 1979
