Charlie can recover damages for all profits lost as a result of the extension not being completed on time
The court would allow the recovery of the 'cost of cure', namely putting the building into the condition it should have been in if the breach had not occurred
Since Charlie was not making any profit from the extension in the first place, no profit was certain to be made, and therefore there may be no recovery, except for nominal damages for loss of amenity

explanation.en: C is correct. Damages are an automatic common law right following a breach of contract. Lead case: Hadley v Baxendale (1854) 9 Exch 341.

stem: Charlie entered into a contract with Buddy in January to build an extension onto his pub near Pall Mall, in order to increase the pub's seating capacity. Instead of finishing the work by the beginning of April, as agreed, Buddy only completed the work by the end of May, which meant that Charlie missed out on the money-spinning royal wedding trade, as Kate and William announced the date of their wedding in March. While neither party had reasonably contemplated the announcement of the wedding, Charlie is seeking damages.
ask: Which statement best reflects the most likely outcome?

options.en: Charlie can recover damages for all the extra profits he would have made during the royal wedding had it not been for Buddy's failure to complete the extension on time
Charlie would be compensated for all losses which have arisen from Buddy's wrongful action by putting Charlie back into the position he was in prior to the breach of contracted being committed

Since time was of the essence, Charlie will be able to terminate the contract for breach of a contractual condition under the Sale of Goods Act 1979, which takes in to account all special losses such as these

Any losses resulting from missing out on extra revenues associated with the royal wedding are likely to be recovered, as there is little doubt that this is a special loss, and it would be reasonable to assume that it was within the reasonable contemplation of both parties

Since the royal wedding was only announced in March, after Charlie and Buddy had signed the contract, any losses resulting from missing out on the extra revenues associated with the royal wedding are likely to be regarded as too remote and therefore irrecoverable

explanation.en: E is correct. Damages must not be too remote and arise as a natural consequence of the breach or else be in the contemplation of both parties when the contract was formed. Lead case: Hadley v Baxendale (1854) 9 Exch 341.

stem: Chloe was one of the young hopefuls out of 40 waiting to audition for the chance to be awarded a record deal, after viewers had voted for her on the hit TV show England's Got Talent. In breach of contract, however, the TV company failed to give her the opportunity to attend the actual audition, and Chloe now seeks to recover damages from the TV company, since she feels that she has missed out on a lucrative record deal.
ask: Which statement best describes the likely outcome of her action against the TV company?

options.en: While Chloe may not recover for the loss of chance of being selected for the record deal, she may recover for consequent losses flowing from the record deal that she unjustly missed out on
While Chloe may not recover for losses concerning any potential record deal, as any profit is speculative, she may recover for the loss of chance of being selected for it
Chloe may recover for consequent losses flowing from the potential record deal that she unjustly missed out on, and for the loss of chance of being selected for it
While Chloe is entitled to a remedy for her loss of a chance in principle, all she may in fact receive are nominal damages as the loss is entirely incapable of assessment
Chloe may neither recover for losses concerning the record deal that she unjustly missed out on, nor for the loss of chance of being selected for it

explanation.en: B is correct. Although any profits from a possible contract is pure speculation, it does not matter that there was no certainty in winning the audition; it is enough that Chloe has lost the chance of winning per se. Lead case: Chaplin v Hicks [1911] 2 KB 786.

stem: After reading the company's brochure promising the 'holiday of a lifetime', Damon and Anna booked a 26- day cruise on the maiden voyage of the "Princess Margaret", at a discounted price of £15,000. During rough weather, however, the portals leaked and the constant loud thud from the ship's engine made sleep impossible. Following unsuccessful attempts to agree a suitable alternative cabin, Damon and Anna disembarked at Seville after 7 days, and were refunded £12,000, leaving the net cost of their holiday as £3,000.
ask: Which different heads of loss could Damon and Anna realistically claim for?

options.en: Since non-pecuniary losses are generally not recoverable, Damon and Anna would not be entitled to a damages award
There would only be damages for disappointment and distress, but nothing for pecuniary loss (or diminution in value of the holiday), since they freely chose to disembark in Seville
They should claim for the £12,000 in reliance losses, to put them back in the position they were in before embarking on the holiday
Pecuniary loss (or diminution in value) of the amount actually paid after the refund, and damages for disappointment and distress
Pecuniary loss (or diminution in value) of the full cost of the holiday, and damages for disappointment and distress

explanation.en: D is correct. As to diminution in value, the starting point would be the discounted price actually paid, namely £3,000 for the 7 days that they were at sea, not the price of the advertised holiday! As to disappointment and distress, Damon and Anna could reasonably have expected to experience the 'holiday of a lifetime'. Lead case: Milner v Carnival Plc (t/a Cunard) [2010] EWCA Civ 389.

stem: Paralivian striker Pablo Fablo agreed to sign for Burnpool City in the English Premier League. City paid £5,000,000 to Pablo's agent and brother in agent's fees to facilitate the transfer, and were hoping that if he was successful, they could sell Pablo for a profit at the end of the season. At 11.55pm on 31 August, five minutes before the transfer window was due to close, Pablo repudiated the contract, giving City no time to find a replacement striker.
ask: Which is the most advisable measure of damages City should pursue under the circumstances?

options.en: City may neither recover for losses concerning the agent's fees, nor for the profit they might have made had Pablo gone there and succeeded
Since City may not recover for losses concerning agent's fees, they would be advised to make a claim for potential loss of profit
City may recover for losses concerning the agent's fees, and for the profit they might have made had Pablo gone there and succeeded
While City is entitled to a remedy for their loss of profit in principle, all they may in fact receive are nominal damages as the loss is entirely incapable of assessment
Since City cannot say what their profit would have been on his contract had Pablo gone there and performed it, they would be advised to make a claim for their wasted expenditure

explanation.en: E is correct. Because City would have difficulty proving expectation damages, they should pursue a claim for their reliance loss instead. Lead case: Anglia Television Ltd v Reed [1971] 3 All ER 690.

stem: The Republic of New Queen's Territory (NOT) advertised a wrecked tanker for sale, which was supposed to be off the coast of Papua New Guinea. Salvage Bros won the tender, paid the tender price of £2,000 and then equipped an expedition to go and salvage it. Although NOT supplied precise co-ordinates so that Salvage Bros could locate it, it turned out that there was no tanker.
ask: What would be the likely effect of the non-existence of the tanker on the agreement between NOT and Salvage Bros?

options.en: The contract would be void for common mistake, namely mistake as to the quality of the subject-matter
The contract would not be void for common mistake, because NOT had warranted the existence of the tanker
Since both parties made the contract but regarding different facts, the contract would be void for mutual mistake
The contract would be void for common mistake, namely mistake as to the existence of the subject matter of the contract, or res extincta
The contract would be void for common mistake, namely mistake as to the possibility of performing the contract

explanation.en: B is correct. Here one of the parties has specifically promised that the subject matter exists, then mistake has no role to play, and the other party can sue for breach of the promise. Lead case: McRae v Commonwealth Disposals Commission (1951) 84 CLR 377.

stem: Herbert agreed to sell to Teddy a consignment of coal, to arrive on a ship called the "Silesian Princess" from Poland. In fact, there were two ships named the Silesian Princess sailing from Poland that summer, one in June, the other in August.
ask: Teddy argued that he had intended only to purchase deliveries from the June Silesian Princess, whereas Herbert argues that he had only had the August ship in mind Which type of mistake does it appear that the parties have been labouring under; why?

options.en: Common mistake, because the mistake is as to the quality of the subject-matter
Unilateral mistake, because one party has made a mistake about the terms of the offer
Common mistake, because the mistake is as to the possibility of performing the contract
Common mistake, because the mistake is as to the existence of the subject matter of the contract, or res extincta
Mutual mistake, because the parties are at cross-purposes

explanation.en: E is correct. There is mutual mistake because the parties are at cross-purposes. Since there was a mistake as to the subject matter of the contract, there was in effect no contract between the parties, or at least no contract that clearly identified the agreement made. The claimant's action would fail. Lead case: Raffles v Wichelhaus (1864) 2 H & C 906; 159 ER 375.

stem: Hank mistakenly quoted to Chuck the sale price for his salmon catch 'per kilo', when he actually meant to say the customary 'per pound'. Hank's mistake meant that he priced the catch three-quarters less than he intended to sell at. After Chuck accepted Hank's terms, Hank refused to supply on this basis, claiming that the buyers were trying to take unfair advantage of a genuine mistake.
ask: Which type of mistake does it appear that the parties have been labouring under and why?

options.en: Common mistake, because the mistake is as to the quality of the subject-matter
Unilateral mistake, because one party has made a mistake about the terms of the offer
Mutual mistake, because the parties are at cross-purposes
Common mistake, because the mistake is as to the existence of the subject matter of the contract, or res extincta
Common mistake, because the mistake is as to the possibility of performing the contract

explanation.en: B is correct. This is a unilateral mistake, since only one party is mistaken. There was a pricing up error. The seller had thought that he was pricing per pound, but the cost was actually calculated per item. If one party to a proposed contract knows or really ought to have known that the offeror does not intend the terms of the offer to be those that the natural meaning of the words would suggest, and that the terms offered were a mistake, he cannot, by purporting to accept the offer, bind the offeror to a contract. Lead case: Hartog v Colin & Shields [1939] 3 All ER 566.

stem: Margaret has just finished her first year as an LLB student at university, and has met her first boyfriend Clint, who she intends to marry. Her father tells her that if she doesn't marry Clint, but marries Martin instead, he will pay her a lump sum of money, and after agreeing to this, Margaret drafts a contract to this effect. She married Martin but her father refuses to pay the lump sum.
ask: Will Margaret be able to enforce the contract?

options.en: Since there is no recognized policy proscribing acts that are prejudicial to family life, the contract is unenforceable
Even if the contract is illegal, it will be enforceable in equity
Since the agreement is prejudicial to family life it is unenforceable
Since the agreement is contrary to public policy it is unenforceable
Since the agreement is prejudicial to public safety it is unenforceable

explanation.en: C is correct. A promise by A to make a payment if she marries anyone else other than B will be unenforceable. A contract prejudicial to family life is unenforceable if it is prejudicial to the institution of marriage, e.g, contracts not to marry. Lead case: Lowe v Peers (1768) 4 Burr 2225.

stem: Adam and Eve agreed to exchange Adam's apple for Eve's pet reptile, which they did immediately. The possession of the goods and the right of the goods were transferred together.
ask: Which of the following best describes how such an agreement, if any, is defined under the doctrine of consideration?

options.en: Consideration may be exhausted where one party promises to do something in return for the act of another, rather than for the mere promise of future performance of an act
Consideration may be executed where one party promises to do something in return for the act of another, rather than for the mere promise of future performance of an act
Consideration may be executory where one party promises to do something in return for the act of another, rather than for the mere promise of future performance of an act
Consideration may be excised where one party promises to do something in return for the act of another, rather than for the mere promise of future performance of an act.
Consideration may be expurgated where one party promises to do something in return for the act of another, rather than for the mere promise of future performance of an act

explanation.en: B is correct. If one party makes a promise, in exchange for an act (or forbearance) by the other party, when that act is completed, the consideration is executed, e.g. in a unilateral contract where A offers a £50 reward for the return of her lost handbag: if B finds the bag and returns it, B's consideration is executed; if B fails to find the bag, A is not contractually bound to pay anything.

stem: Adam and Eve agreed to exchange Adam's apple for Eve's pet reptile, which they did the following week. The right of the goods was transferred but not their possession.
ask: Which of the following best describes how such an agreement, if any, is defined under the doctrine of consideration?

options.en: Consideration may be exhausted where the parties exchange promises to perform acts in the future
Consideration may be executed where the parties exchange promises to perform acts in the future
Consideration may be executory where the parties exchange promises to perform acts in the future
Consideration may be expunged where the parties exchange promises to perform acts in the future
Consideration may be exercised where the parties exchange promises to perform acts in the future

explanation.en: C is correct. Consideration is called "executory" where there is an exchange of promises to perform acts, in the future, e.g. a bilateral contract for the supply of goods whereby A promises to deliver goods to B, at a future date, and B promises to pay, on delivery: both parties are contractually bound, although neither has yet performed his side of the bargain.

stem: Larry said to Sue, "I will sell you this watch for £5". Sue replied, "I agree".
ask: Which of the following best describes the status of the parties?

options.en: Larry has made an invitation to treat and Sue is the offeror
Larry has made an invitation to treat and Sue is the offeree
Sue has made an invitation to treat and Larry is the offeree
Sue is the offeror and Larry is the offeree
Larry is the offeror and Sue is the offeree

explanation.en: E is correct. An express offer has been made in this instance. Larry is the offeror and Sue the offeree.

stem: Sue said to Larry, "I will give you £5 for that watch". Larry replied, "I agree".
ask: Which of the following best describes the status of the parties?

options.en: Larry has made an invitation to treat and Sue is the offeror
Larry has made an invitation to treat and Sue is the offeree
Sue has made an invitation to treat and Larry is the offeree
Sue is the offeror and Larry is the offeree
Larry is the offeror and Sue is the offeree

explanation.en: D is correct. An express offer has been made in this instance. Sue is the offeror and Larry the offeree.

stem: Bobby posted a letter accepting Liz's offer to sell goods. Bobby subsequently telephoned Liz and withdrew his acceptance by asking Liz to ignore the letter of acceptance when it arrives.
ask: Which of the following best advises the parties regarding their respective obligations, if any?

options.en: Liz is bound by the letter once it was posted. Bobby may reserve his right to withdraw his acceptance during the transit of the letter
Bobby can withdraw his acceptance offer by telephoning Liz and asking her to ignore the letter of acceptance when it arrives
Bobby cannot withdraw his acceptance offer by telephoning Liz and asking her to ignore the letter of acceptance when it arrives
Bobby can withdraw his acceptance offer by telephoning Liz and asking her to ignore the letter of acceptance since the letter has not yet been delivered
Liz is bound by the letter once it was posted since Bobby may reserve his right to withdraw his acceptance during the transit of the letter

explanation.en: C is correct. An acceptance cannot be recalled once it has been posted even though it has not reached the offeror and Liz could hold Bobby bound by the contract if she wishes to do so. Lead case: Byrne v Van Tienhoven (1880).

stem: Samir sold goods to Amira under circumstances of mistake. Amira then resold the goods to Kamal.
ask: Which of the following best describes how the contract is affected under these circumstances, if at all?

options.en: The contract is void and Kamal gets no title of the goods
The contract is voidable and Kamal gets no title of the goods
The contract is void and Kamal gets title of the goods
The contract is voidable but Kamal gets title of the goods
The contract is both void and Kamal gets title of the goods or the contract is voidable and Kamal gets no title of the goods

explanation.en: A is correct. A contract affected by mistake is void; where A sells goods to B under circumstances of mistake and B resells them to C, then C gets no title and A can recover the goods from him or sue him for damages in conversion.

stem: Samir sold goods to Amira under circumstances of misrepresentation. Amira then resold the goods to Kamal, who took them bona fide and for value before Samir had rescinded his contract with Amira.
ask: Which of the following best describes how the contract is affected under these circumstances, if at all?

options.en: The contract is void and Kamal gets no title of the goods
The contract is voidable and Kamal gets no title of the goods
The contract is void but Kamal gets title of the goods
The contract is voidable and Kamal gets title of the goods
The contract is both void and Kamal gets title of the goods or the contract is voidable and Kamal gets no title of the goods

explanation.en: D is correct. A contract affected by misrepresentation is voidable and Samir would only have a remedy against Amira.

stem: Lee bought a bicycle from Paul thinking it was worth £100. In fact it was only worth £50.
ask: Which of the following best describes how the contract is affected under these circumstances, if at all?

options.en: The contract is good and Lee must bear the loss even if there has been a mistake of fact and law
The contract is not good and Lee need not bear the loss due to mistake of fact
The contract is not good and Lee need not bear the loss due to mistake of law
The contract is not good and Lee need not bear the loss, even if there has been no misrepresentation by Paul
The contract is good and Lee must bear the loss if there has been no misrepresentation by Paul

explanation.en: E is correct. The maxim caveat emptor applies in this situation. The doctrine of mistake does not cover errors of judgment as to value.

stem: Bubbles Ltd agreed to deliver three dozen bottles of shampoo to Groovy Groceries Ltd. Only two dozen bottles were delivered. Groovy Groceries Ltd has rejected the entire consignment.
ask: Which of the following best describes the respective rights of the parties in these circumstances?

options.en: Groovy Groceries Ltd. must pay for the consignment at the contract rate
Groovy Groceries Ltd. is entitled to reject the entire consignment
The contract is frustrated and neither party has any binding obligations to the other
Since the breach was so trivial, variation is acceptable, due to the doctrine of partial performance
Rejection of the consignment by Groovy Groceries Ltd. dissolves the contract and permits Bubbles Ltd to sue for breach of contract

explanation.en: B is correct. Where performance is partial by A and B has rejected A's partial performance, then B may exercise its right to reject the whole consignment. Lead case: Re Moore & Co and Landauer & Co [1921].

stem: Bubbles Ltd agreed to deliver three dozen bottles of shampoo to Groovy Groceries Ltd. Only two dozen bottles were delivered. Groovy Groceries Ltd accepted delivery of two dozen bottles.
ask: Which of the following best describes the respective rights of the parties in these circumstances?

options.en: Groovy Groceries Ltd. must pay for the consignment at the contract rate
Groovy Groceries Ltd. is entitled to reject the entire consignment
The contract is frustrated and neither party has any binding obligations to the other
Since the breach was so trivial, variation is acceptable, due to the doctrine of partial performance
Rejection of the consignment by Groovy Groceries Ltd. dissolves the contract and permits Bubbles Ltd to sue for breach of contract

explanation.en: A is correct. Where the party to whom the promise of performance was made, B accepts partial performance of the contract by A, he must pay A for the goods he has accepted/the benefit he has received. Lead case: Sumpter v Hedges (1898). Statute; rule; constitution: Section 30(1) Sale of Goods Act 1979.

stem: Jacob and Joseph agreed with each other that they will continue to negotiate with each other with regard to property belonging to Jacob until they reach a binding agreement. In the course of negotiations between them Jacob decided to sell the property to Ruben.
ask: Which of the following represents the best advice to give to the parties?

options.en: The agreement to negotiate has no legal effect and Joseph will have no successful claim
The agreement to negotiate has no legal effect, however Joseph may still have successful claim against Ruben
The agreement to negotiate is binding and Joseph will have a successful claim against Ruben
The agreement to negotiate is binding and Joseph will have a successful claim against
The agreement to negotiate is binding and Joseph will have a successful claim against Jacob and Ruben

explanation.en: A is correct. An agreement to continue negotiations until an agreement has been reached is not enforceable as having no legal content. Lead case: Walford v Miles [1992].

stem: A seller failed to deliver goods. The buyer was able to purchase elsewhere at no extra cost. The buyer is considering bringing a claim against the seller for breach of contract.
ask: Which of the following best describes the type of damages, if any, the court is likely to award?

options.en: In such a scenario, the court is likely to award the buyer exemplary damages
In such a scenario, the court is likely to award the buyer punitive damages
In such a scenario, the court is likely to award the buyer nominal damages
In such a scenario, the court is likely to award the buyer liquidated damages
In such a scenario, the court is likely to award the buyer unliquidated damages

explanation.en: C is correct. The court is likely to award nominal damages, i.e. an award of a small sum, e.g. £2, to reflect the view that the damage suffered by the buyer was purely technical. Please note, E is broadly correct, in the sense that the court is likely to award a sum of damages which correctly reflects the extent of the buyer's loss (i.e. unliquidated damages), but C is more specific, in clarifying that such a sum is likely to be nominal in value.
